The river stopped flowing, and they stood on the dry riverbed. It may be helpful to make this explicit in some languages. For example, you could say:

The priests who carried the ark stood on dry ground in the middle of the Yarden River

4:10b

until the people had completed everything Yahweh had commanded Yehoshua (Joshua) to tell them,

  • until the people finished doing everything that Yahweh commanded Yehoshua.

  • until everyone crossed. This is what Yahweh commanded Yehoshua to tell them to do.

until the people had completed everything Yahweh had commanded Yehoshua to tell them: The clause until the people had completed everything Yahweh had commanded Yehoshua to tell them indicates that the people did everything that Yahweh commanded them to do. Yahweh gave his command to Yehoshua. Yehoshua repeated the command to the Israelis (Israelites), and the Israelis obeyed the command.

4:10c

just as Mosheh (Moses) had directed Yehoshua.

  • The Israelis did everything as Mosheh commanded Yehoshua.

  • The people obeyed all Yehoshua’s commands, which he received from Mosheh.

just as Mosheh had directed Yehoshua (Joshua): The phrase just as Mosheh had directed Yehoshua indicates that Yahweh first gave these commands to Mosheh before Mosheh died. Mosheh then told Yehoshua what Yahweh wanted the Israelis to do when they reached the Yarden (Jordan).

4:10d

The people hurried across,

  • The people crossed the river as quickly as they could.

  • The people hurried across.

The people hurried across: The clause The people hurried across means that the Israelis (Israelites) crossed the Yarden River as quickly as they could. They hurried across it.

title: Joshua 4:11
content:
Section 4:1–5:1 The Israelis (Israelites) commemorated the crossing of the Yarden (Jordan) River

Twelve men from among the Israelis each took a stone from the middle of the Yarden River. With these stones Yehoshua (Joshua) built a monument to remind the Israeli (Israelite) people, and their descendants, about how God helped them cross the river.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Setting up memorial stones

Twelve memorial stones

A reminder that God brought them to the promised land

Paragraph 4:10–11

This paragraph is a summary about the crossing of the Yarden River. The priests obeyed God’s command. They stood in the middle of the river while the rest of the Israelis crossed it. Finally, the priests with the ark of the covenant finished crossing the river.

4:11a

and after everyone had finished crossing,

  • When all the Israelis (Israelites) finished crossing,

  • When everyone crossed the river,

and: The word and indicates that the next action in the story is about to take place.

after: Another time connector might be clearer such as “as soon as.” Use a time connector that is natural in your language.

everyone had finished crossing: The word everyone refers to all the Israeli (Israelite) people except for the priests carrying the ark.

4:11b

the priests with the ark of Yahweh crossed in the sight of the people.

  • the ark of Yahweh and the priests crossed while the people watched.

  • the priests carried the covenant box of Yahweh across the river as the people watched.

the priests with the ark of Yahweh: The Hebrew language places the ark of Yahweh first to emphasize its importance. However, the priests were still carrying the ark. It may be more natural in some languages to translate this phrase as “the priests who were carrying the ark of Yahweh.”

ark: See 3:3 for ideas of how to translate the word ark.

crossed: The word crossed means that the priests crossed the Yarden (Jordan) River to the other side.

in the sight of the people: There are two ways to interpret the phrase in the sight of the people:

  1. The priests crossed the river while the people watched. For example:

    …crossed as the people looked on (NET) (BSB, NET, RSV, NCV, NIV, NLT, NRSV, KJV)

  2. The priests crossed the river and went ahead of the people. For example:

    …went on ahead of the people (GNT) (GNT, NAB, NJB, NJPS, REB)

It is recommended that you follow interpretation (1). The clause “crossed in the sight of the people” points to 4:15–18. The people came out of the river. Then they watched as the priests finished crossing the river.

title: Joshua 4:12
content:
Section 4:1–5:1 The Israelis (Israelites) commemorated the crossing of the Yarden (Jordan) River

Twelve men from among the Israelis each took a stone from the middle of the Yarden River. With these stones Yehoshua (Joshua) built a monument to remind the Israeli (Israelite) people, and their descendants, about how God helped them cross the river.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Setting up memorial stones

Twelve memorial stones

A reminder that God brought them to the promised land

4:12a

The Re’uvenim (Reubenites), the Gadim (Gadites), and the half-tribe of Menasheh (Manasseh)

  • ¶ The clans of Re’uven (Reuben), Gad, and half of the clan of Menasheh

  • ¶ The men of the clan of Re’uven, Gad, and the eastern half of the clan of Menasheh

The Re’uvenim: The word Re’uvenim refers to men of the tribe of Re’uven.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

men from the tribe of Re’uven

the Gadim: The word Gadim refers to men of the tribe of Gad.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

men from the tribe of Gad

and the half-tribe of Menasheh (Manasseh): The phrase the half-tribe of Menasheh refers to the families of the tribe of Menasheh who asked Mosheh (Moses) for permission to settle on the east side of the Yarden (Jordan) River along with the tribes of Re’uven (Reuben) and Gad. This request and Mosheh’s answer is found in Numbers 32:16–33.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

men from the east part of the tribe of Menasheh

There is implied information here. These men were also soldiers. This is made clear in 4:12b. For example:

The armed warriors from the tribes of Re’uven, Gad, and the half-tribe of Menasheh (NLT)

4:12b

crossed over before the Israelis (Israelites), armed for battle

  • crossed over the river with their weapons ahead of the other Israelis,

  • crossed the river first, carrying their weapons of war.

crossed over before the Israelis, armed for battle: The phrase crossed over…armed for battle indicates that the tribes of Re’uven (Reuben), Gad, and the half-tribe of Menasheh (Manasseh) took their weapons with them when they crossed over the Yarden (Jordan) River. They were ready to fight. They did this to show that they would keep the promise they made to Yehoshua (Joshua) in 1:16–18. They promised to help the other tribes of Yisrael (Israel) conquer the land of Kena’an (Canaan).

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

they crossed the river carrying their weapons

before the Israelis: The phrase before the Israelis indicates that the tribes of Re’uven, Gad, and the half-tribe of Menasheh crossed the river ahead of the other tribes.

4:12c

as Mosheh (Moses) had instructed them.

  • as Mosheh commanded them to do.

  • because Mosheh commanded them to do this before he died.

as Mosheh had instructed them: The phrase as Mosheh had instructed them indicates that these tribes obeyed the command that Mosheh gave them before he died. This command is recorded in Numbers 32:16–32 and Deuteronomy 3:12–20.

had instructed: The phrase had instructed means “had commanded.”

title: Joshua 4:13
content:
Section 4:1–5:1 The Israelis (Israelites) commemorated the crossing of the Yarden (Jordan) River

Twelve men from among the Israelis each took a stone from the middle of the Yarden River. With these stones Yehoshua (Joshua) built a monument to remind the Israeli (Israelite) people, and their descendants, about how God helped them cross the river.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Setting up memorial stones

Twelve memorial stones

A reminder that God brought them to the promised land

4:13a

About 40,000 troops armed for battle

  • About forty thousand Israeli soldiers carried their weapons ready for war

  • There were about forty thousand men prepared to enter battle.

About 40,000 troops armed for battle: There is an interpretation issue here. There are two ways to understand the number 40,000.

  1. There were a total of 40,000 Israeli (Israelite) soldiers who crossed the Yarden (Jordan) River. This was the total number of soldiers for all twelve tribes combined. For example:

    About forty thousand battle-ready troops (NET) (BSB, NET, RSV, ESV, NIV, NABRE, NJPS, GNT, KJV)

  2. There were 40,000 soldiers from the two and one half eastern tribes. This number does not include the soldiers from the western tribes. For example:

    Forty thousand soldiers from the tribes of Re’uven (Reuben), Gad, and East Menasheh (Manasseh) (CEV) (CEV, NLT)

It is recommended that you follow interpretation (1). A total of 40,000 Israeli soldiers corresponds with the numbers of soldiers referred to in Yehoshua (Joshua) chapters 7–8 and the two battles at Ay (Ai). See especially 8:3–12. This is the interpretation followed by many English versions, and by several commentaries.

armed: The word armed means that they carried their weapons with them.

for battle: The phrase for battle means that they were ready to fight in a war.

Here is another way to translate this part of the verse:

There were about forty thousand soldiers who carried their weapons and were ready to fight

4:13b

crossed over before Yahweh

  • and marched past the ark of Yahweh,

  • They marched past the ark of Yahweh ready to fight.

crossed over before Yahweh: The phrase crossed over means that the forty thousand soldiers crossed over the Yarden (Jordan) River.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

crossed the Yarden River in the presence of Yahweh

4:13c

into the plains of Yeriho (Jericho).

  • heading toward the plains of Yeriho.

  • They went along the road to the plains in front of Yeriho city.

into the plains of Yeriho: The plains of Yeriho refers to the plain between the Yarden River and the town of Yeriho. This indicates that the forty thousand soldiers marched into this plain.

title: Joshua 4:14
content:
Section 4:1–5:1 The Israelis (Israelites) commemorated the crossing of the Yarden (Jordan) River

Twelve men from among the Israelis each took a stone from the middle of the Yarden River. With these stones Yehoshua (Joshua) built a monument to remind the Israeli (Israelite) people, and their descendants, about how God helped them cross the river.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Setting up memorial stones

Twelve memorial stones

A reminder that God brought them to the promised land

4:14a

On that day Yahweh exalted Yehoshua in the sight of all Yisrael (Israel),

  • ¶ All the people of Yisrael saw how Yahweh honored Yehoshua that day.

  • ¶ That day Yahweh showed all the Israelis (Israelites) that Yehoshua (Joshua) was a great leader.

On that day: The phrase On that day refers to the day that the Israelis crossed the Yarden (Jordan) River.

Yahweh exalted Yehoshua: The phrase Yahweh exalted Yehoshua means that Yahweh honored Yehoshua when he made the Yarden River stop flowing. Yahweh showed the Israelis that Yehoshua was a leader whom they must respect because Yahweh had done this miracle by speaking through Yehoshua.

in the sight of all Yisrael: The phrase in the sight of all Yisrael indicates that all the people of Yisrael saw what Yahweh had done.

4:14b

and they revered him

  • They respected him greatly because of this

  • So they honored him

and: The word and marks the result of what Yahweh did through Yehoshua’s (Joshua’s) leadership. It might be more natural in some languages to translate this word with a word or phrase that expresses result, such as:

therefore

because of this

they revered him: The clause they revered him indicates that the Israelis (Israelites) honored and respected Yehoshua.

4:14c

all the days of his life,

  • for as long as he lived,

  • for the rest of his life,

all the days of his life: The phrase all the days of his life refers to the rest of Yehoshua’s (Joshua’s) life, or for as long as Yehoshua lived.

4:14d

just as they had revered Mosheh (Moses).

  • in the same way that they respected Mosheh.

  • as much as they formerly honored Mosheh.

just as: The words just as mean “in the same way.”

they had revered Mosheh: The clause they had revered Mosheh indicates that the Israelis (Israelites) had honored and respected Mosheh.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

in the same way that they had honored Mosheh

title: Joshua 4:15
content:
Section 4:1–5:1 The Israelis (Israelites) commemorated the crossing of the Yarden (Jordan) River

Twelve men from among the Israelis each took a stone from the middle of the Yarden River. With these stones Yehoshua (Joshua) built a monument to remind the Israeli (Israelite) people, and their descendants, about how God helped them cross the river.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Setting up memorial stones

Twelve memorial stones

A reminder that God brought them to the promised land

4:15

Then Yahweh said to Yehoshua,

  • ¶ Then Yahweh told Yehoshua:

  • ¶ Yahweh commanded Yehoshua (Joshua):

Then: The word Then indicates that the next action in the story is about to take place.

Yahweh said to Yehoshua: It may be more natural in some languages to use a word such as:

Yahweh ordered Yehoshua

Yahweh commanded Yehoshua

title: Joshua 4:16
content:
Section 4:1–5:1 The Israelis (Israelites) commemorated the crossing of the Yarden (Jordan) River

Twelve men from among the Israelis each took a stone from the middle of the Yarden River. With these stones Yehoshua (Joshua) built a monument to remind the Israeli (Israelite) people, and their descendants, about how God helped them cross the river.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Setting up memorial stones

Twelve memorial stones

A reminder that God brought them to the promised land

4:16a

“Command the priests who carry the ark of the Testimony

  • “Tell the priests who are carrying the covenant box

  • “Order the priests to bring the box with the Ten Commandments in it

Command the priests who carry the ark of the Testimony: The phrase the priests who carry the ark refers to the priests who carried the ark into the middle of the Yarden (Jordan) River.

the ark of the Testimony: The Testimony refers to the stone tablets on which Mosheh (Moses) had written the Ten Commandments. The ark of the Testimony and the “ark of the covenant” refer to the same box.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

the ark of the covenantal laws (NET)

the box with the Ten Commandments in it

Some English versions translate this phrase in the same way that they translate “ark of the covenant.”

4:16b

to come up from the Yarden.”

  • to come out of the Yarden River.”

  • up out of the river bed.”

to come up from the Yarden (Jordan): The phrase come up from the Yarden means that the priests should carry the ark from the middle of the riverbed where they were standing, across to the other side of the Yarden River.

In some languages, it might be more natural to change the indirect quote into a direct quote. For example, you could say:

Command the priests, “Come up out of the Yarden.”

title: Joshua 4:17
content:
Section 4:1–5:1 The Israelis (Israelites) commemorated the crossing of the Yarden (Jordan) River

Twelve men from among the Israelis each took a stone from the middle of the Yarden River. With these stones Yehoshua (Joshua) built a monument to remind the Israeli (Israelite) people, and their descendants, about how God helped them cross the river.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Setting up memorial stones

Twelve memorial stones

A reminder that God brought them to the promised land

4:17a

So Yehoshua commanded the priests,

  • So Yehoshua told the priests:

  • Then Yehoshua (Joshua) gave this command to the priests:

So Yehoshua commanded the priests: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as So indicates that the next action in the story is taking place. In this case, it also shows that Yehoshua’s action is a response to God’s command.

Here are some other way to translate this part of the verse:

and so Yehoshua commanded the priests

in obedience to God, Yehoshua commanded the priests

4:17b

“Come up from the Yarden (Jordan).”

  • “Bring the ark up from the riverbed.”

  • “Carry the ark up out of the river.”

Come up from the Yarden: The clause Come up from the Yarden indicates that the priests should come up from the dry riverbed and cross to the west side of the Yarden River. It may be redundant in some languages to repeat this command, which uses almost the same words as in 4:16b. It may be more natural to summarize the action. For example:

Yehoshua (Joshua) did so (GNT)

So Yehoshua gave the command (NLT)

title: Joshua 4:18
content:
Section 4:1–5:1 The Israelis (Israelites) commemorated the crossing of the Yarden (Jordan) River

Twelve men from among the Israelis each took a stone from the middle of the Yarden River. With these stones Yehoshua (Joshua) built a monument to remind the Israeli (Israelite) people, and their descendants, about how God helped them cross the river.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Setting up memorial stones

Twelve memorial stones

A reminder that God brought them to the promised land

4:18a

When the priests carrying the ark of the covenant of Yahweh

  • Then the priests who were carrying the ark of the covenant of Yahweh

  • The priests who were carrying the covenant box of Yahweh

The Hebrew word that the BSB leaves untranslated but many English versions translate as “and” signals the next event in the storyline.

the ark of the covenant of Yahweh: See how you translated this in 3:3.

4:18b

came up out of the Yarden (Jordan)

  • came up out of the riverbed.

  • brought the ark up from the middle of the river.

came up out of the Yarden: The clause came up out of the Yarden indicates that the priests came up from the middle of the dry riverbed to the west side of the Yarden River.

4:18c

and their feet touched the dry land,

  • When their feet touched dry ground

  • As soon as their feet stepped onto dry land,

touched the dry land: The phrase touched the dry land means that the priests stepped up out of the riverbed, and onto the dry ground. It may be more natural in some languages to leave the words touched implicit. For example:

And their feet were on high ground (NLT)

4:18d

the waters of the Yarden (Jordan) returned to their course

  • the river water began to flow

  • the Yarden River flowed again

the waters of the Yarden: Another way to translate this is:

the Yarden River

returned to their course: The phrase returned to their course means that the water began to flow again, as it had before the priests first stepped into the river.

4:18e

and overflowed all the banks as before.

  • and flooded its banks again, as it was before.

  • and the water was as high as it was before.

and overflowed all the banks as before: In 3:15 it says that the Yarden (Jordan) River was in flood. The clause overflowed all the banks as before indicates that the river now returned to being flooded again. The water was as high as it was before the priests stepped into it.

title: Joshua 4:19
content:
Section 4:1–5:1 The Israelis (Israelites) commemorated the crossing of the Yarden (Jordan) River

Twelve men from among the Israelis each took a stone from the middle of the Yarden River. With these stones Yehoshua (Joshua) built a monument to remind the Israeli (Israelite) people, and their descendants, about how God helped them cross the river.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Setting up memorial stones

Twelve memorial stones

A reminder that God brought them to the promised land

4:19a

On the tenth day of the first month the people went up from the Yarden

  • ¶ The Israelis (Israelites) crossed the Yarden (Jordan) River on the tenth day of the first month.

  • ¶ On the tenth day of the first month of the year, Yisrael (Israel) crossed the Yarden River.

On the tenth day of the first month: The first month refers to the month of the Hebrew calendar that was called Aviv (Abib), and later called Nisan. This month began with the first new moon occurring after March 11. So, the people crossed the Yarden River between March 21 and April 18.4:19 Bratcher and Newman, p. 55.

the people went up from the Yarden: The Israelis walked out of the Yarden River and up onto the western bank.

4:19b

and camped at Gilgal on the eastern border of Yeriho (Jericho).

  • They set up their camp in Gilgal, east of the city of Yeriho.

  • They set up their tents in a place called Gilgal, which was east of the land controlled by Yeriho.

and camped: The word camped means that they set up a temporary camp or dwelling place. If there is no appropriate word in your language for “camp” you can translate it:

they set up temporary homes

at Gilgal: Gilgal is the name of a place between Yeriho and the Yarden (Jordan) River. At the time when the Israelis (Israelites) camped there, Gilgal was not yet a town. It was given the name Gilgal at the time of their encampment and probably later it became a town. The exact location of Gilgal is not known.

on the eastern border of Yeriho: Yeriho was a town with a large wall around it for protection against enemies.

title: Joshua 4:20
content:
Section 4:1–5:1 The Israelis (Israelites) commemorated the crossing of the Yarden (Jordan) River

Twelve men from among the Israelis each took a stone from the middle of the Yarden River. With these stones Yehoshua (Joshua) built a monument to remind the Israeli (Israelite) people, and their descendants, about how God helped them cross the river.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Setting up memorial stones

Twelve memorial stones

A reminder that God brought them to the promised land

4:20a

And there at Gilgal Yehoshua set up

  • Yehoshua set up at Gilgal as a monument

  • Yehoshua (Joshua) commanded the men to set up as a memorial at Gilgal

Yehoshua set up: It is likely that Yehoshua commanded the men to set up the stones. He probably did not do this himself. However, this is not certain. You may wish to rearrange the parts of this verse, for example:

The men who had carried the twelve rocks from the Yarden (Jordan) brought them to Yehoshua, and they made them into a monument (CEV)

Yehoshua had the men set up a memorial with the twelve stones that they had taken from the Yarden River and carried to Gilgal

4:20b

the twelve stones

  • the twelve stones they carried with them

  • those twelve stones

the twelve stones: The phrase the twelve stones refers to the twelve stones that Yehoshua (Joshua) told the men to take out of the Yarden River.

4:20c

they had taken from the Yarden (Jordan).

  • that they took from the Yarden River.

  • which they carried from the Yarden River.

they had taken from the Yarden: The word they refers to the twelve men whom Yehoshua chose to take the stones from the middle of the river.

General Comment on 4:20

In this verse the object (the stones) comes first and the subject (Yehoshua) comes after the verb. This is a device used in the Hebrew language to emphasize the stones. If possible, use the natural grammar of your language to give emphasis to the stones.

title: Joshua 4:21
content:
Section 4:1–5:1 The Israelis (Israelites) commemorated the crossing of the Yarden (Jordan) River

Twelve men from among the Israelis each took a stone from the middle of the Yarden River. With these stones Yehoshua (Joshua) built a monument to remind the Israeli (Israelite) people, and their descendants, about how God helped them cross the river.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Setting up memorial stones

Twelve memorial stones

A reminder that God brought them to the promised land

4:21a

Then Yehoshua said to the Israelis,

  • Then Yehoshua told the Israelis (Israelites):

  • Then he said to the Israelis:

Then Yehoshua (Joshua) said to the Israelis: Yehoshua spoke to all the people of Yisrael (Israel). Earlier in 4:6 he spoke only to the twelve chosen men.

4:21b

“In the future, when your children ask their fathers,

  • “The children of future generations may ask their parents,

  • “When your children ask you in the future

In the future, when your children ask their fathers: The word when creates a subordinate clause. In some languages, it may be more natural to use an independent clause. For example:

Years from now your children will ask you why these rocks are here. (CEV)

your children: The phrase your children refers to the present and future generations of Israeli (Israelite) children.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

your descendants

your children and grandchildren

ask their fathers: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as fathers can refer to both mothers and fathers.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

When your children ask their fathers (ESV)

When your children ask their parents (NRSV)

In the future your children will ask (NLT)

4:21c

‘What is the meaning of these stones?’

  • ‘Why are these rocks here?’

  • what these stones represent.

What is the meaning of these stones?: The children will ask the question What is the meaning of these stones? because they want to know why the stones are there. The children of future generations will see the stones and wonder why they are arranged as a memorial in that place.

title: Joshua 4:22
content:
Section 4:1–5:1 The Israelis (Israelites) commemorated the crossing of the Yarden (Jordan) River

Twelve men from among the Israelis each took a stone from the middle of the Yarden River. With these stones Yehoshua (Joshua) built a monument to remind the Israeli (Israelite) people, and their descendants, about how God helped them cross the river.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Setting up memorial stones

Twelve memorial stones

A reminder that God brought them to the promised land

4:22a

you are to tell them,

  • Then you must explain to them,

  • Then you must tell them this:

you are to tell them: The clause you are to tell them indicates that the parents of the children must explain to them the meaning of the stones.

In some languages, the quote formula between 4:22a-b may need to be made explicit. For example, you could say:

Then you should explain it to your children. Say to them…

4:22b

‘Yisrael (Israel) crossed the Yarden (Jordan) on dry ground.’

  • ‘The Israelis (Israelites) walked across the dry riverbed of the Yarden River.’

  • ‘The Yarden River dried up so that the nation of Yisrael could walk across it.’

Yisrael: The term Yisrael refers to all the Israeli (Israelite) people.

crossed: The word crossed means that the Israeli people walked across the Yarden River.

the Yarden: The phrase the Yarden refers to the Yarden River. This phrase is more literally “this Yarden.” The word “this” probably adds emphasis: “this very Yarden River that you see before your eyes.” In some languages it is not natural to include the word “this.” Try to find a natural way to add emphasis. If you can’t find a natural way to do this, then translate it as “the Yarden River.”

on dry ground: The phrase on dry ground refers to the riverbed of the Yarden. This was dry because Yahweh made the river stop flowing.

title: Joshua 4:23
content:
Section 4:1–5:1 The Israelis (Israelites) commemorated the crossing of the Yarden (Jordan) River

Twelve men from among the Israelis each took a stone from the middle of the Yarden River. With these stones Yehoshua (Joshua) built a monument to remind the Israeli (Israelite) people, and their descendants, about how God helped them cross the river.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Setting up memorial stones

Twelve memorial stones

A reminder that God brought them to the promised land

4:23a

For Yahweh your God dried up the waters of the Yarden before you

  • Yahweh your God made the Yarden (Jordan) River stop flowing so that

  • Yahweh your God made a dry path across the Yarden River in front of you

For Yahweh your God dried up the waters of the Yarden before you: It was Yahweh who made it possible for the people to cross the river. This theme of God’s deliverance continues throughout the book of Yehoshua (Joshua) as the Israelis (Israelites) move in to conquer the land.

dried up: The words dried up mean that Yahweh made the water stop flowing.

the waters of the Yarden: It may be more natural in some languages to translate the phrase the waters of the Yarden as “the Yarden River.”

4:23b

until you had crossed over,

  • you could walk across the river bed.

  • and kept it dry until you walked across on it.

until you had crossed over: The phrase crossed over means that they walked across the riverbed. God held back the water until they were all across on the west bank of the Yarden (Jordan).

4:23c

just as He did to the Red Sea,

  • He did this in the same way that he did when he parted the Red Sea.

  • This was like when Yahweh made a path through the Red Sea.

just as: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as just as introduces a comparison.

He did to the Red Sea: This is a comparison. Yahweh rescued the Israelis (Israelites) many years ago at the Red Sea. In a similar way, he has rescued Yisrael (Israel) once again at the Yarden River.

4:23d

which He dried up before us until we had crossed over.

  • He made a dry path for us to walk on until we crossed to the other side.

  • He dried up a path through the sea for us until we walked across.

which He dried up: God made a path for the Israelis to cross the Red Sea by making the waters stand like a wall on each side of the path. This story is told in Exodus 14:21–22.

before us: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as before us can also be translated as:

on our behalf

ahead of us (GW)

as we watched (NLT)

These three aspects of meaning all make sense in the context, and it is hard to know which meaning is more in focus. You should translate this phrase with the meaning that is most natural in your language.

until we had crossed over: The phrase until we had crossed over indicates that God held the water back until all the Israelis (Israelites) walked across to the other side of the Red Sea.

title: Joshua 4:24
content:
Section 4:1–5:1 The Israelis (Israelites) commemorated the crossing of the Yarden (Jordan) River

Twelve men from among the Israelis each took a stone from the middle of the Yarden River. With these stones Yehoshua (Joshua) built a monument to remind the Israeli (Israelite) people, and their descendants, about how God helped them cross the river.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Setting up memorial stones

Twelve memorial stones

A reminder that God brought them to the promised land

4:24a

He did this so that all the peoples of the earth may know

  • He did this so that every person in the whole world will know

  • Because he has done this, every nation on the earth will understand

so that all the peoples of the earth may know: There is some implied information here. Yahweh did this so that all the people will know. For example:

He has done this so that all the nations of the earth might recognize the Lord’s power (NET)

so that: The phrase so that indicates the reason why Yahweh dried up the Red Sea and the Yarden (Jordan) River.

all the peoples of the earth: The phrase all the peoples of the earth refers to all the nations that are in the world.

may know: The phrase may know indicates that everyone will know and understand that Yahweh is powerful.

4:24b

that the hand of Yahweh is mighty,

  • that Yahweh is powerful.

  • that he has mighty power.

that: The word that introduces the content of what all the peoples of the earth should know.

the hand of Yahweh is mighty: The phrase hand of Yahweh is mighty is a Hebrew idiom that to refers to Yahweh’s power. Translate this idiom in a way that is natural in your language. For example:

Yahweh is powerful

Yahweh has great power

4:24c

and so that you may always fear Yahweh your God.”

  • And so that you will respect Yahweh your God and worship him forever.”

  • He did this so that you will honor Yahweh your God forever.”

so that you may always fear Yahweh your God: There is implied information here. Yahweh did this so that you will fear him.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

Yahweh did this so that you would fear him forever

so that: The phrase so that expresses purpose. It could also be translated “that” or “in order that.”

fear Yahweh your God: The expression fear Yahweh implies loyalty, respect, or honor of Yahweh. It means to be in awe of God’s greatness.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

honor the Lord your God (GNT)

worship him (CEV)

always obey the Lord your God (NET)

General Comment on 4:21–24

These verses repeat the theme that was introduced in 4:6–7|. This repetition emphasizes the importance of this commemoration event, and the great deliverance performed by God. It also emphasizes the unity of the Israelis (Israelites) as a nation specially chosen by God.

title: Joshua 5:1
content:
Section 4:1–5:1 The Israelis (Israelites) commemorated the crossing of the Yarden (Jordan) River

Twelve men from among the Israelis each took a stone from the middle of the Yarden River. With these stones Yehoshua (Joshua) built a monument to remind the Israeli (Israelite) people, and their descendants, about how God helped them cross the river.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Setting up memorial stones

Twelve memorial stones

A reminder that God brought them to the promised land

Paragraph 5:1

This paragraph tells the reaction of the Israelis’s enemies when they heard about the things that God had done for the Israelis.

5:1a

Now when all the Amori (Amorite) kings west of the Yarden (Jordan)

  • ¶ All the Amori kings who ruled the regions that were west of the Yarden River

  • ¶ All the rulers of the Amor people who lived in the country west of the Yarden River

Now when all the Amori kings west of the Yarden: There is a contrast between the reaction of the Israelis (Israelites) and the reaction of their enemies, the Amorim (Amorites) and Kena’anim (Canaanites). When the Israelis saw what God had done, they respected and honored him, but their enemies were terrified. There may be a word or particle in your language that will help to emphasize that contrast.

Amori: The Amori people were people who lived in the hills in the land of Kena’an (Canaan) west of the Yarden River.

Here is another way to translate this name:

Amor people

kings: The word kings refers to the rulers of the small towns in the hills of Kena’an. Each “king” ruled one town and the villages around it.

Here are some other ways to translate this word:

rulers

leaders

west of the Yarden (Jordan): The phrase west of the Yarden refers to the land on the west side of the Yarden River.

5:1b

and all the Kena’ani (Canaanite) kings along the coast

  • and all the Kena’ani kings who ruled the places on the seacoast

  • and all the rulers of the Kena’an (Canaan) people who lived near the sea heard about this.

and all the Kena’ani kings: Here are some other ways to translate the word kings:

rulers

leaders

the Kena’ani: The Kena’ani people were people who lived in the land of Kena’an west of the Yarden (Jordan) River.

Here is another way to translate this word:

Kena’an people

along the coast: The phrase along the coast refers to the Mediterranean Sea.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

who lived along the coast of the sea

who lived near the Mediterranean Sea

5:1c

heard how Yahweh had dried up the waters of the Yarden (Jordan) before the Israelis (Israelites)

  • heard that Yahweh made the Yarden River stop flowing for the Israelis.

  • They heard that Yahweh made a dry path through the Yarden River.

heard: The Amori (Amorite) and Kena’ani (Canaanite) kings heard that the Israelis had crossed the Yarden River.

how Yahweh had dried up the waters of the Yarden: The main thing the kings heard was that Yahweh had dried up the waters of the Yarden. They understood the significance of this. Now that the Israelis had crossed the river they were a threat to their safety, especially because a powerful God was helping them.

before the Israelis: There are two ways to understand the phrase before the Israelis:

  1. God had acted on behalf of the people of Yisrael (Israel). For example:

    the Lord had dried up the waters of the Yarden for the people of Yisrael (ESV) (ESV, RSV, GNT, CEV, NLT)

  2. God had acted in the sight of the people of Yisrael. For example:

    the Lord had dried up the Yarden (Jordan) before the Israelis (Israelites) (NIV) (BSB, NIV, NET, KJV)

It is recommended that you follow interpretation (1). This is followed by many English versions and by many commentaries.

5:1d

until they had crossed over,

  • They heard that they walked across to the other side.

  • They heard that the Israelis walked over to the other side.

until they had crossed over: The phrase until they had crossed over indicates that God kept the Yarden River from flowing until the Israelis had walked across it.

they: There is a textual issue here.

  1. The Hebrew Masoretic text reads: “until they had crossed over.” For example:

    until they had crossed (NJB) (BSB, NJB, RSV, CEV, ESV, GW, NAB, NASB, NCV, NJPS, NLT, GNT)

  2. An alternate reading in the Hebrew Masoretic text reads: “until we had crossed over.” For example:

    until we had crossed over (NIV) (NIV)

It is recommended that you follow option (1). The standard Hebrew text, nearly all the English versions, and most commentaries follow option (1).

5:1e

their hearts melted

  • Then they became very afraid

  • Then they no longer had any courage

their hearts melted: The Hebrew phrase that the BSB translates as their hearts melted is an idiom. It means that the kings were afraid. There may be an idiom in your language that expresses this meaning in a vivid way.

5:1f

and their spirits failed

  • and lost their courage to fight the people of Yisrael (Israel)

  • and they were terrified

and their spirits failed: The Hebrew phrase that the BSB translates as and their spirits failed is an idiom. It means that the kings were afraid and lacked courage to fight against the Israelis (Israelites).

The two idioms “their hearts melted” and their spirits failed mean the same thing. The Hebrew text uses two phrases to describe their fear to add emphasis to how fearful they were. In some languages, it may be helpful to combine the two idioms into one emphatic statement. For example, you could say:

The kings were very frightened

Use a way that is natural in your language to emphasize their fear.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

The kings were very fearful and felt powerless to fight

5:1g

for fear of the Israelis.

  • because of what God did for the Israelis.

  • and were afraid to fight the Israelis (Israelites).

for fear of the Israelis: The phrase for fear of the Israelis indicates that they were fearful because of what God had done for the people of Yisrael (Israel). If this is not clear you might need to make this explicit. For example, you could say:

because of what God had done for the Israelis

title: Joshua 5:2
content:
Section 5:2–12 Yehoshua (Joshua) circumcised the men, and the Israelis (Israelites) observed Passover

Yehoshua circumcised the Israeli (Israelite) men, because they had not done this ceremony while they walked through the wilderness for forty years. Then the Israelis observed the Passover ceremony. They ate food from the land of Kena’an (Canaan), and God stopped sending them manna.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Circumcision of the next generation

Circumcision and the first Passover in the promised land

5:2a

At that time Yahweh said to Yehoshua,

  • ¶ Then Yahweh commanded Yehoshua:

  • ¶ While the Israelis (Israelites) were in their camp at Gilgal, Yahweh told Yehoshua (Joshua):

At that time: The phrase At that time refers to the time while the Israelis lived in their tents at Gilgal. This is the same time to which verse 5:1 refers.

Yahweh said: Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

Yahweh told them

Yahweh commanded them

5:2b

“Make flint knives and circumcise the sons of Yisrael (Israel) once again.”

  • “Make knives from flint stones and do another ceremony to circumcise the men of Yisrael.”

  • “Make stone knives and circumcise every man and boy who is not yet circumcised.”

Make flint knives and circumcise the sons of Yisrael: flint is a kind of stone that can be chipped until it forms a sharp edge. At this time humans were only just beginning to use iron, and flint knives were commonly used for cutting.

Here is another way to translate the term flint knives:

stone knives

circumcise: The verb circumcise means to cut off the foreskin of a man’s penis. This ceremony was first mentioned in Genesis 17:9–14 when Yahweh told Avraham (Abraham) to circumcise the men in his household. This was a sign, or a mark, of the covenant that God made with Avraham.

If you have translated the New Testament you should translate the word circumcise the same way you did there. For example, see Luke 1:59.

Consider whether you should use a euphemism or more general expression in your language to translate circumcise.

Here is another way to translate this word:

cutting ceremony

the sons of Yisrael (Israel): Only male people were circumcised. Normally, boys were circumcised when they were eight days old. It may be clearer to translate this as:

the men of Yisrael

the men and boys of Yisrael

once again: The phrase once again means that this is the second time that the nation of Yisrael had performed the ceremony of circumcision. The Israeli (Israelite) men who lived in Mitsrayim (Egypt) were circumcised as children, but that generation died while they walked through the wilderness. Now the men and boys who were born after the Israelis (Israelites) left Mitsrayim must be circumcised. Normally, boys were circumcised when they were eight days old.

title: Joshua 5:3
content:
Section 5:2–12 Yehoshua (Joshua) circumcised the men, and the Israelis (Israelites) observed Passover

Yehoshua circumcised the Israeli (Israelite) men, because they had not done this ceremony while they walked through the wilderness for forty years. Then the Israelis observed the Passover ceremony. They ate food from the land of Kena’an (Canaan), and God stopped sending them manna.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Circumcision of the next generation

Circumcision and the first Passover in the promised land

5:3a

So Yehoshua made flint knives

  • Then Yehoshua made stone knives,

  • So, Yehoshua (Joshua) did as Yahweh commanded.

So Yehoshua made flint knives: It may be more natural in some languages not to repeat the information contained in the previous verse.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

So Yehoshua did so

Then Yehoshua made the knives

5:3b

and circumcised the sons of Yisrael (Israel) at Givat-Ha’aralot (Gibeath-haaraloth).

  • and he circumcised the Israeli (Israelite) men and boys at Givat-Ha’aralot.

  • He circumcised them at the Hill of the Foreskins.

and circumcised the sons of Yisrael: The phrase the sons of Yisrael refers to the Israeli men who were not yet circumcised. Women were not circumcised.

at Givat-Ha’aralot: The phrase Givat-Ha’aralot is a Hebrew phrase meaning “hill of the foreskins.” It may be better to translate the meaning of this phrase. For example:

Circumcision Hill (GNT)

the hill of the foreskins (KJV)

If you transliterate the phrase Givat-Ha’aralot (Gibeath-haaraloth), a footnote may be helpful. Here is a sample footnote:

FOOTNOTE: Givat-Ha’aralot means “hill of the foreskins”

title: Joshua 5:4
content:
Section 5:2–12 Yehoshua (Joshua) circumcised the men, and the Israelis (Israelites) observed Passover

Yehoshua circumcised the Israeli (Israelite) men, because they had not done this ceremony while they walked through the wilderness for forty years. Then the Israelis observed the Passover ceremony. They ate food from the land of Kena’an (Canaan), and God stopped sending them manna.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Circumcision of the next generation

Circumcision and the first Passover in the promised land

5:4a

Now this is why Yehoshua circumcised them:

  • This is why Yehoshua circumcised the men:

  • Yehoshua (Joshua) had to circumcise them because

Now this is why Yehoshua circumcised them: The phrase this is why refers ahead to verses 5:5–7 and adds emphasis. Choose a word or phrase that naturally indicates emphasis in your language. For example:

Yehoshua had to circumcise them because (NLT)

this is why it was necessary to circumcise them

5:4b

All those who came out of Mitsrayim (Egypt)—all the men of war—

  • All the men who were soldiers when they left Mitsrayim

  • after the Israelis (Israelites) left Mitsrayim, all the men old enough to fight

All those who came out of Mitsrayim—all the men of war: The two phrases All those who came out of Mitsrayim and all the men of war refer to the same group of people and can be translated by one phrase. For example:

all the men old enough to serve in the army (NCV)

all the soldiers (GW)

all the men of military age (NIV)

who came out of Mitsrayim (Egypt): Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

After the Israelis left Mitsrayim, all the men old enough to serve in the army (NCV)

All the men who were old enough to fight in battle when they left Mitsrayim (NLT)

5:4c

had died on the journey in the wilderness after they had left Mitsrayim.

  • died in the wilderness after they left Mitsrayim.

  • died in the wilderness.

had died on the journey in the wilderness: The clause had died on the journey in the wilderness indicates that the men old enough to fight died while they walked through the wilderness.

after they had left Mitsrayim (Egypt): It may be redundant to translate this phrase in some languages because this information is already included in 5:4b.

title: Joshua 5:5
content:
Section 5:2–12 Yehoshua (Joshua) circumcised the men, and the Israelis (Israelites) observed Passover

Yehoshua circumcised the Israeli (Israelite) men, because they had not done this ceremony while they walked through the wilderness for forty years. Then the Israelis observed the Passover ceremony. They ate food from the land of Kena’an (Canaan), and God stopped sending them manna.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Circumcision of the next generation

Circumcision and the first Passover in the promised land

5:5a

Though all who had come out were circumcised,

  • Even though the men who left Mitsrayim (Egypt) were circumcised,

  • The men who came out of Mitsrayim were circumcised before they left Mitsrayim,

Though all who had come out were circumcised: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as Though is a connector to link verse 5a to 5b.

Here are some other ways to translate this word:

although

even though

even though the men who left Mitsrayim had been circumcised, the males born in the wilderness had not been circumcised

You should use the connector between these two clauses that is natural in your language.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

The men who left Mitsrayim (Egypt) had been circumcised. However, the men born later…were not circumcised (GW)

Those who left Mitsrayim had been circumcised. But none of those born after the Exodus…had been circumcised (NLT)

all: The word all refers to all the male people who had left Mitsrayim. It does not refer to women.

5:5b

none of those born in the wilderness on the journey

  • the men born later, on the way through the wilderness

  • but all the boys born on the journey through the wilderness

The Hebrew word that the BSB leaves untranslated but the many English versions translate as “but” contrasts the men and boys who left Mitsrayim (Egypt) with those who were born in the wilderness. Use a word that is natural in your language to show this contrast.

Here are some other ways to translate this word:

yet

however

none of those: The phrase none of those refers to all the boys who were born in the wilderness. It does not refer to the women. The word none refers to the males born after the Israeli (Israelite) people left Mitsrayim. If the reference is not clear, you may wish to make it explicit. For example:

The men who had come out of Mitsrayim had been circumcised, but none of those who were born in the desert on the trip from Mitsrayim had been circumcised. (NCV)

in the wilderness: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as wilderness refers to a place where no people live. Some English versions translate this word as “desert.”

on the journey: The phrase on the journey refers to the time that the Israelis (Israelites) wandered in the wilderness. These boys were born during that time.

5:5c

from Mitsrayim (Egypt) had been circumcised.

  • after they left Mitsrayim, never got circumcised.

  • were not circumcised.

from Mitsrayim had been circumcised: This phrase has been mentioned several times in previous verses, so it may be more natural to leave it implicit.

title: Joshua 5:6
content:
Section 5:2–12 Yehoshua (Joshua) circumcised the men, and the Israelis (Israelites) observed Passover

Yehoshua circumcised the Israeli (Israelite) men, because they had not done this ceremony while they walked through the wilderness for forty years. Then the Israelis observed the Passover ceremony. They ate food from the land of Kena’an (Canaan), and God stopped sending them manna.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Circumcision of the next generation

Circumcision and the first Passover in the promised land

5:6a

For the Israelis had wandered in the wilderness forty years,

  • The Israelis walked through the wilderness for forty years

  • The Israelis (Israelites) traveled in the wilderness for forty years.

For: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as For can also be translated as “because.” It connects verse 5 to verse 6, and it gives an explanation for what is stated in verse 5. Many English versions do not translate this word, and the function is implied. You should use a connecting word that is natural in your language to connect these two verses.

the Israelis had wandered in the wilderness forty years: The Israelis walked from place to place in the wilderness. It took the Israelis forty years to reach Kadesh Barnea. Deuteronomy 1:2 states that they could have walked this distance in eleven days. The Israelis walked for forty years because they disobeyed Yahweh.

in the wilderness: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as wilderness refers to a place where no people live.

5:6b

until all the nation’s men of war who had come out of Mitsrayim (Egypt) had died,

  • until all the soldiers who left Mitsrayim died

  • During that time all the men old enough to fight when they left Mitsrayim died.

until all the nation’s men of war: This phrase refers to men more than twenty years old and old enough to be soldiers.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

until all the nation, that is, the men of war (NASB)

In many languages it may be more natural to combine the two phrases or to delete all the nation’s. For example:

all their soldiers (GW)

all the men who were old enough to fight in battle (NLT)

the men in the army (CEV)

who had come out of Mitsrayim (Egypt): It was stated in the previous verse that they came out of Mitsrayim, so it may be more natural in some languages to leave this information implicit.

5:6c

since they did not obey Yahweh.

  • because they did not obey Yahweh.

  • They died because they disobeyed Yahweh.

since: The word since introduces the reason why all these men died in the wilderness.

they did not obey Yahweh: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as obey is literally “listen.” This is an idiom. It means “obey.”

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

they did not obey what Yahweh had commanded

General Comment on 5:6a-c

It may be more natural in some languages to state the reason at the beginning of the sentence instead of at the end. You can reorder the verse so that 5:6c starts the verse. For example:

6cThe Israelis (Israelites) did not obey Yahweh. Because they disobeyed him, 6athey had to walk in the wilderness for forty years 6buntil all of Yisrael’s (Israel’s) soldiers died.

5:6d

So Yahweh vowed

  • Because they disobeyed him, Yahweh made a solemn promise to them.

  • So, Yahweh vowed to them

So Yahweh vowed: The clause So Yahweh vowed means that Yahweh made a promise to them. It may be more natural in some languages to put the indirect object in its normal order. For example:

the Lord had sworn to them (NIV)

Use whatever order is most natural in your language.

5:6e

never to let them see the land

  • He said he will not let them enter the land

  • that they will not live long enough to see the land

never to let them see the land: The clause never to let them see the land indicates that Yahweh did not let them live long enough to enter the land of Kena’an (Canaan).

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

he would not let them enter the land of Kena’an

he would not let them live to see the land of Kena’an

5:6f

He had sworn to their fathers to give us,

  • which he promised their ancestors to give us,

  • he swore to give to them and to us.

He had sworn: The phrase He had sworn means that Yahweh made a vow or a promise.

to their fathers: The phrase to their fathers refers to their actual fathers and also their ancestors.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

to their ancestors

to their fathers and grandfathers

to give us: There is implied information. The phrase to give us can also be translated as:

to give to us(incl) Israelis (Israelites)

The writer of the book of Yehoshua (Joshua) wrote this many years later. When he said to give us he wrote about himself and the Israelis in his own time. He said that they also received what God had promised to their ancestors.5:6 Bratcher and Newman, p. 62.

Here is another way to translate this part of the verse:

Yahweh did not let them see the land which he promised to their ancestors, and which he said that he would give to them and to us(incl)

5:6g

a land flowing with milk and honey.

  • a rich and fertile land.

  • That land is a fertile land, and produces lots of crops.

a land flowing with milk and honey: The phrase a land flowing with milk and honey is a Hebrew idiom. In this idiom the rivers flow with milk and honey instead of water. It means that the land was fertile and produced abundant crops. If possible, use vivid language or an idiom which conveys the same meaning in your own language.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

a very fertile land

a land which produces lots of crops

General Comment on 5:4–6

The structure of 5:4–6 is complex. Some English versions reorder these verses. If you find these verses difficult to translate, you might want to consider reordering them. For example:

4bWhen the people of Yisrael (Israel) left Mitsrayim (Egypt), 5aall the males were already circumcised. 6aHowever, during the forty years the people spent crossing the desert, 5cnone of the baby boys had been circumcised. 6bAlso, by the end of that time all the men who were of fighting age when they left Mitsrayim had died 6cbecause they had disobeyed the Lord. 6dJust as he had sworn, 6ethey were not allowed to see 6gthe rich and fertile land 6fthat he had promised their ancestors. (GNT)

If you follow the GNT, you will need to look at how it translates 5:7. Verse 5:7 includes information that is implied at the beginning of the unit 5:4–6, specifically the statement about why these men had never been circumcised. Verse 5:7 in the GNT reads:

The sons of these men had never been circumcised, and it was this new generation that Yehoshua (Joshua) circumcised. (GNT)

You might also want to consider the CEV, which reorders 5:4–7.

acai.preferred_label: Land Flowing of Milk and Honey

title: Joshua 5:7
content:
Section 5:2–12 Yehoshua (Joshua) circumcised the men, and the Israelis (Israelites) observed Passover

Yehoshua circumcised the Israeli (Israelite) men, because they had not done this ceremony while they walked through the wilderness for forty years. Then the Israelis observed the Passover ceremony. They ate food from the land of Kena’an (Canaan), and God stopped sending them manna.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Circumcision of the next generation

Circumcision and the first Passover in the promised land

5:7a

And Yehoshua raised up their sons in their place,

  • Their sons were the people whom God chose to replace them.

  • So, Yehoshua (Joshua) circumcised their sons, those who grew up in place of their fathers.

And: Verse 7 is a summary of verses 5–6. The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as And is a connector word. It shows the relationship between this verse and the preceding verses.

Here are some other ways to translate this word:

That is why

In light of that

So, for that reason

You should translate this word with a connecting word or phrase that is most natural in your language.

Yehoshua (Joshua) raised up their sons in their place: The phrase raised up their sons in their place could mean that either God or Yehoshua allowed the sons of the men who had died to take their place. Although the BSB translates this clause as if Yehoshua raised up these people, most English versions follow the Hebrew and use the pronoun “he,” which can refer to either interpretation.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

he raised up their sons in their place (NIV)

he replaced them with their sons (NET)

their sons—those who had grown up to take their fathers’ places (NLT)

raised up their sons: The phrase their sons is the object of the sentence, and it is emphasized in the Hebrew text. The construction raised up their sons is a way of emphasizing their sons in English. You should choose a way that is natural in your language to emphasize this phrase.

their sons: The phrase their sons refers to the male children of the people who died in the wilderness because they disobeyed God. And their sons make up the same group of men as those referred to in verse 5:4a.

5:7b

and these were the ones he circumcised.

  • Yehoshua (Joshua) circumcised their sons

  • Yehoshua circumcised these sons,

these were the ones he circumcised: The clause these were the ones refers to the words “their sons” in verse 5:7a. Yehoshua circumcised the sons of the men who died in the wilderness. It may be more natural to reorder the verse. You could put the relative clause next to the noun it modifies. For example, you could say:

So, it was their children whom Yehoshua circumcised, those whom God had raised up instead of them

5:7c

Until this time they were still uncircumcised,

  • because they had not been circumcised before.

  • for they had not yet been circumcised

Until this time they were still uncircumcised: It may be more natural in some languages to leave this clause implicit and untranslated, because the meaning is included in 5:7d. Consider whether such repetition is natural in your language.

5:7d

since they had not been circumcised along the way.

  • No one was circumcised while Yisrael (Israel) walked through the wilderness.

  • in the wilderness.

since they had not been circumcised along the way: The phrase along the way refers to the time that the Israelis (Israelites) walked through the wilderness for forty years.

title: Joshua 5:8
content:
Section 5:2–12 Yehoshua (Joshua) circumcised the men, and the Israelis (Israelites) observed Passover

Yehoshua circumcised the Israeli (Israelite) men, because they had not done this ceremony while they walked through the wilderness for forty years. Then the Israelis observed the Passover ceremony. They ate food from the land of Kena’an (Canaan), and God stopped sending them manna.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Circumcision of the next generation

Circumcision and the first Passover in the promised land

5:8a

And after all the nation had been circumcised,

  • ¶ When all the men were circumcised

  • ¶ When they finished circumcising all the men,

And after all the nation had been circumcised: Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

When all the Israeli (Israelite) men had been circumcised

When they had finished circumcising all the men of Yisrael (Israel)

all the nation: The phrase the nation refers to all the Israeli men. It does not refer to women.

5:8b

they stayed there in the camp

  • they stayed in the camp

  • everyone stayed in the camp

they stayed there in the camp: The clause they stayed there in the camp indicates that all the Israeli (Israelite) males stayed in the place where they had set up their camp and did not go anywhere.

5:8c

until they were healed.

  • until they were healed.

  • until the men were well again.

until they were healed: The clause until they were healed means until their wounds from the cutting of circumcision were healed and they were no longer sore.

title: Joshua 5:9
content:
Section 5:2–12 Yehoshua (Joshua) circumcised the men, and the Israelis (Israelites) observed Passover

Yehoshua circumcised the Israeli (Israelite) men, because they had not done this ceremony while they walked through the wilderness for forty years. Then the Israelis observed the Passover ceremony. They ate food from the land of Kena’an (Canaan), and God stopped sending them manna.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Circumcision of the next generation

Circumcision and the first Passover in the promised land

5:9a

Then Yahweh said to Yehoshua,

  • Then Yahweh told Yehoshua:

  • Then Yahweh said to Yehoshua (Joshua):

Then: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as Then signals the next event in the storyline. Use a connecting word in your language that shows that the next event in the story line is taking place.

Yahweh said to Yehoshua: If it is necessary for this verb to have an explicit object, you can add “these words” or “this.” For example:

Yahweh said these words to Yehoshua

5:9b

“Today I have rolled away the reproach of Mitsrayim (Egypt) from you.”

  • “Today I have taken the disgrace of being slaves in Mitsrayim away from you.”

  • “It was shameful for you to be slaves in Mitsrayim. But now I have removed your shame.”

Today: The word Today means “this day” or “now.”

I have rolled away: The Hebrew phrase that the BSB translates as I have rolled away is a Hebrew idiom. It means “to remove” or “to take away.”

the reproach of Mitsrayim from you: The phrase the reproach of Mitsrayim refers to the shame the Israelis (Israelites) suffered while they were slaves in Mitsrayim. Being circumcised was the final step in their freedom from this shame.

The reproach does not mean that the Israelis could not be circumcised in Mitsrayim.5:9 See the footnote in NET at verse 5:9 about “disgrace of Mitsrayim.”

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

I have removed from you the disgrace of being slaves in Mitsrayim (GNT)

It was shameful for you to be slaves in Mitsrayim (Egypt). Now I have taken away your shame

5:9c

So that place has been called Gilgal to this day.

  • That is why they named that place Gilgal, the name it still has today.

  • Because of this, Yehoshua (Joshua) gave that place the name Gilgal, which it is still named today.

So: The word So can also be translated:

therefore

for this reason

that place has been called Gilgal: The Israelis (Israelites) called this place Gilgal when they made their camp there. It was not yet a town at that time. Later it became a center of worship.5:9 Rasmussen, p. 236. In some languages it may be more natural to say:

that place is called Gilgal

they named that place Gilgal

that place: The phrase that place refers to where the Israelis camped and were circumcised.

Gilgal: The name Gilgal sounds similar to the Hebrew word which means “to roll.” This is a pun on the idiom “I have rolled away the reproach of Mitsrayim (Egypt) from you.” If you have used the idiom “roll” in verse 9b you could include this information in a footnote. For example:

FOOTNOTE: The name Gilgal sounds like the Hebrew word “roll”

to this day: The phrase to this day means “until now” or “until today” and refers to the time when the author was writing the book of Yehoshua (Joshua).

title: Joshua 5:10
content:
Section 5:2–12 Yehoshua (Joshua) circumcised the men, and the Israelis (Israelites) observed Passover

Yehoshua circumcised the Israeli (Israelite) men, because they had not done this ceremony while they walked through the wilderness for forty years. Then the Israelis observed the Passover ceremony. They ate food from the land of Kena’an (Canaan), and God stopped sending them manna.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Circumcision of the next generation

Circumcision and the first Passover in the promised land

Paragraph 5:10–12

The Israelis celebrated Passover in Kena’an and they started to eat the food that grew there. The manna that God gave them in the wilderness for forty years stopped coming, because now God had brought them to the end of their journey.

5:10a

On the evening of the fourteenth day of the month,

  • On the evening of the fourteenth day of the first month,

  • On the evening of the fourteenth day of the first month,

On the evening: The Israelis (Israelites) considered the evening to be the beginning of a new day. The evening was the beginning of the fourteenth day.

of the fourteenth day of the month: The phrase the fourteenth day of the month refers to the fourteenth day of the first month in the Jewish calendar. They crossed the Yarden (Jordan) River was on the tenth day of the first month (see 4:19a). They celebrated the Passover four days after they crossed the river.

5:10b

while the Israelis were camped at Gilgal

  • ¶ while the Israelis were still in the camp at Gilgal,

  • ¶ the people of Yisrael (Israel) continued to camp at Gilgal,

while the Israelis were camped at Gilgal: The clause while the Israelis were camped at Gilgal can also be translated:

during the time that the Israelis set up their tents at Gilgal

5:10c

on the plains of Yeriho (Jericho),

  • in the plain in front of Yeriho City,

  • in the fields not far from Yeriho,

on the plains of Yeriho: The town of Yeriho was about ten kilometers west of the Yarden (Jordan) River on the plains, a level area of land. This land extended from Yeriho to the Yarden River. Gilgal was also on this plain, probably a few miles northeast of Yeriho.

5:10d

they kept the Passover.

  • they celebrated the Passover feast.

  • they ate the Passover feast.

they kept the Passover: The clause they kept the Passover indicates that the Israelis (Israelites) celebrated the Passover feast.

Passover: The Passover feast and the regulations about it are described in Exodus 12:1–20 and in Leviticus 23:4–8. This feast reminded the Israelis of the time when God delivered them from being slaves in Mitsrayim (Egypt).

If you have translated the New Testament, you should translate the term the Passover the same way here. For example, see Matthew 26:2.

title: Joshua 5:11
content:
Section 5:2–12 Yehoshua (Joshua) circumcised the men, and the Israelis (Israelites) observed Passover

Yehoshua circumcised the Israeli (Israelite) men, because they had not done this ceremony while they walked through the wilderness for forty years. Then the Israelis observed the Passover ceremony. They ate food from the land of Kena’an (Canaan), and God stopped sending them manna.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Circumcision of the next generation

Circumcision and the first Passover in the promised land

Paragraph 5:10–12

The Israelis celebrated Passover in Kena’an and they started to eat the food that grew there. The manna that God gave them in the wilderness for forty years stopped coming, because now God had brought them to the end of their journey.

5:11a

The day after the Passover,

  • The next morning, after they had celebrated the Passover,

  • The next day after they ate the Passover feast,

The Hebrew word that the BSB leaves untranslated but the many other English versions translate as “And” signals the next event in the storyline.

The day after: The phrase The day after refers to the morning after the Israelis (Israelites) had eaten the Passover feast.

the Passover: It may be more natural in some languages to translate this phrase as a clause. For example:

they ate the Passover feast

they celebrated the Passover

5:11b

on that very day, they ate unleavened bread and roasted grain from the produce of the land.

  • they began to eat the crops that grew in that land. They made bread without yeast and roasted grain.

  • on that same day, they ate food made from barley from the fields there, unleavened bread and grain roasted over a fire.

on that very day, they ate: The phrase on that very day emphasizes that now the Israelis (Israelites) could eat the crops that grew in the land of Kena’an (Canaan).

unleavened bread: The phrase unleavened bread refers to loaves of barley bread that they made without yeast.

and roasted grain: The phrase roasted grain refers to barley grain that they roasted over a fire.

from the produce of the land: The phrase the produce of the land refers to barley grain. Barley was ready to harvest at this time (see 3:15). The Israelis gathered barley from the fields belonging to the people of Yeriho (Jericho).

title: Joshua 5:12
content:
Section 5:2–12 Yehoshua (Joshua) circumcised the men, and the Israelis (Israelites) observed Passover

Yehoshua circumcised the Israeli (Israelite) men, because they had not done this ceremony while they walked through the wilderness for forty years. Then the Israelis observed the Passover ceremony. They ate food from the land of Kena’an (Canaan), and God stopped sending them manna.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Circumcision of the next generation

Circumcision and the first Passover in the promised land

Paragraph 5:10–12

The Israelis celebrated Passover in Kena’an and they started to eat the food that grew there. The manna that God gave them in the wilderness for forty years stopped coming, because now God had brought them to the end of their journey.

5:12a

And the day after they had eaten from the produce of the land,

  • Because they could eat things that grew in the land there,

  • That morning, since they had food to eat from the land,

  • After they started eating food from the land of Kena’an (Canaan)

And: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as And signals the next event in the storyline.

the day after: The phrase the day after refers to the morning after the Israelis (Israelites) celebrated the Passover feast. This was the day that the Israelis began to eat food from the land of Kena’an.

they had: The word had marks a transitional event. Yahweh stopped sending manna when they ate the produce from the land.

eaten from the produce of the land: The phrase produce of the land refers to the barley grain that the Israelis gathered to roast and to make into bread.

5:12b

the manna ceased.

  • God stopped sending manna.

  • God stopped sending them manna.

  • they stopped getting manna to eat.

the manna: The manna is the food that Yahweh gave to the Israelis (Israelites) every morning while they walked through the wilderness. It is described in Exodus 16:13–16.

ceased: The word ceased means “stopped.” The manna appeared on the ground every morning for forty years. Now it no longer appeared. There is implied information: Yahweh is the one who sent the manna, and who stopped sending it.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

Yahweh stopped sending the manna

5:12c

There was no more manna for the Israelis,

  • So, the Israelis no longer gathered manna to eat.

  • The manna that the Israelis ate for a long time came to an end.

There was no more manna for the Israelis (Israelites): The clause There was no more manna for the Israelis indicates that God no longer sent them manna from the sky.

5:12d

so that year they began to eat the crops of the land of Kena’an (Canaan).

  • That year they ate food gathered from what grew in the land of Kena’an.

  • From that time on, they ate food that grew in the land of Kena’an.

that year they began to eat the crops of the land of Kena’an: The clause the crops of the land of Kena’an has the same meaning as the clause “the produce of the land” in 12a.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

that year they ate things that grew in the land of Kena’an

The Israelis (Israelites) conquered Yeriho (Jericho), Ay (Ai), and many other towns in the southern part of the land of Kena’an. God helped them, and through these events they learned to depend on him.

title: Joshua 5:13
content:
Section 5:13–6:27 Yisrael (Israel) conquered Yeriho (Jericho) by God’s power

The Israelis (Israelites) followed God’s instructions and marched around the wall of Yeriho town. On the seventh day the wall of the town collapsed and they conquered the town. They killed everybody in it except for Rahav (Rahab) and her family.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The wall of Yeriho fell

The conquering of Yeriho

5:13a

Now when Yehoshua (Joshua) was near Yeriho,

  • ¶ While Yehoshua was near Yeriho,

  • ¶ One day, Yehoshua was near Yeriho (Jericho),

Now when: This sentence introduces a new section of the story. In many languages it is natural to start a new section with a time word.

Here is another way to translate this word:

One day…

Yehoshua was near Yeriho: The Hebrew preposition that the BSB translates as near means that Yehoshua was near the town of Yeriho. Perhaps he had come close to the town to spy on it and plan his strategy.

5:13b

he looked up and saw

  • he suddenly saw

  • and he was surprised to see

he looked up: The Hebrew clause that the BSB translates as he looked up is used to show that something unexpected is going to happen. It may not be natural in some languages to translate he looked up literally. Use an expression or grammatical device that shows that something surprising is going to happen. It is also possible to leave this phrase untranslated. For example:

While Yehoshua (Joshua) was near Yeriho (Jericho), he suddenly saw a man (GNT)

One day, Yehoshua was near Yeriho when he saw a man (CEV)

and saw: The Hebrew expression that the BSB translates as and saw is another way that the Hebrew language focuses attention on what is going to happen next. You may have a similar expression in your language. It is also possible to leave this phrase untranslated.

5:13c

a man standing in front of him with a drawn sword in His hand.

  • a man standing in front of him holding a sword.

  • a man who stood in front of him with his sword in his hand.

a man standing in front of him: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as man refers to a male person. Some commentators believe that this man was an angel. Others believe that this was Yahweh.

Here is another way to translate this clause:

a man stood in front of him

with a drawn sword in His hand: The phrase with a drawn sword means that he had taken the sword out of its sheath. It was in his hand and was ready to use.

5:13d

Yehoshua (Joshua) approached Him and asked,

  • So, Yehoshua walked up to him and asked him:

  • Then Yehoshua went near him and asked him:

and: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as and shows that this is the next event in the storyline.

Yehoshua approached Him and asked: The clause Yehoshua approached Him and asked can also be translated as:

Yehoshua approached the man and said

5:13e

“Are You for us or for our enemies?”

  • “Are you on our side, or are you against us?”

  • “Are you one of our friends, or are you an enemy?”

Are You for us or for our enemies?: Yehoshua (Joshua) asked this question to find out if the man would fight with the Israelis (Israelites) or against them. The word enemies means “adversaries.”

for us: With the phrase for us Yehoshua asked the man if he was a friend of the Israelis.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

one of our friends

somebody one our side

for our enemies: With the phrase our enemies Yehoshua asked the man if he was an enemy of the Israelis.

one of our enemies

somebody who is against us

title: Joshua 5:14
content:
Section 5:13–6:27 Yisrael (Israel) conquered Yeriho (Jericho) by God’s power

The Israelis (Israelites) followed God’s instructions and marched around the wall of Yeriho town. On the seventh day the wall of the town collapsed and they conquered the town. They killed everybody in it except for Rahav (Rahab) and her family.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The wall of Yeriho fell

The conquering of Yeriho

5:14a

“Neither,” He replied.

  • The man said: “I am not on your side and I am not against you.

  • Then that man answered Yehoshua (Joshua): “No, I am not either one.

Neither: The man answered Neither to indicate that he did not fit into either of the groups that Yehoshua named. He is not an Israeli (Israelite) soldier and he is not an enemy soldier. It may be helpful to repeat the information from Yehoshua’s question. For example, you could say:

No, I am not one of your friends, and I am not one of your enemies

He replied: The word He refers to the man who stood before Yehoshua.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

Then the man replied to Yehoshua

5:14b

“I have now come as Commander of Yahweh’s army.”

  • I have come as the commander of Yahweh’s army.”

  • I am here because I am the general of Yahweh’s army.”

I have now come as Commander of Yahweh’s army: The man who appeared before Yehoshua (Joshua) identified himself as the Commander of Yahweh’s army. Many commentators believe that this man was an angel. The phrase Yahweh’s army probably refers to the angels who help fight Yahweh’s battles. This commander came to take charge of the Israeli (Israelite) army. If Yehoshua and the Israelis (Israelites) obey the commander of Yahweh’s army, then they are also part Yahweh’s army, fighting on God’s side.

I have now come: The man told Yehoshua that he had come to Yeriho (Jericho) to carry out his duty as the commander of Yahweh’s army. He came to accomplish God’s plan, not Yisrael’s (Israel’s).

Commander: A Commander of an army is the person in charge of the army.

Here are some other ways to translate this word:

general

leader

5:14c

Then Yehoshua fell facedown in reverence

  • Then Yehoshua bowed down and put his face to the ground,

  • Yehoshua (Joshua) bowed down to the ground to show his respect.

Then Yehoshua fell facedown in reverence: The expression fell facedown means that Yehoshua bowed down and touched his forehead on the ground. He did this to show his respect for the leader of Yahweh’s army.

fell facedown in reverence: The action of bowing was a form of respect given to people, as well as to God. For example, in Genesis 23:7 Avraham (Abraham) bowed down out of respect to the Hitim (Hittites), the local inhabitants of Kena’an (Canaan).
