and a bar of gold: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as bar is literally “tongue.” The gold was probably in a lump similar in shape to the tongue. Use an expression for a large piece of gold that is natural in your language.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

a gold bar (CEV)

a wedge of gold (NIV)

weighing fifty shekels: The weight, fifty shekels, was a little over one pound or about one-half kilogram. Translate this weight using the standard measure for precious metals in your country.

7:21c

I coveted them and took them.

  • I wanted them very much, so I took them.

  • When I saw them, I wanted them so much that I stole them.

I coveted them: The phrase I coveted them means that Akan (Achan) wanted to have these things very much. The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as coveted is the same word used in the Ten Commandments in Exodus 20:17.

Here are some other ways to translate the word coveted:

I wanted these things very much for myself (NCV)

I wanted them so much (GNT)

I wanted them (NET)

and: The Hebrew prefix that the BSB translates as and indicates the next event in the storyline.

took them: The things that Akan took belonged to Yahweh. It may be more appropriate in some languages to translate the word took as “stole.” This is how Yahweh describes Akan’s action in 7:11d.

7:21d

They are hidden in the ground inside my tent,

  • I hid them in the ground underneath my tent,

  • I dug a hole in the ground underneath my tent and hid them in it.

The Hebrew word that the BSB leaves untranslated but some English versions translate as “behold” emphasizes the following word or clause. In this case, it adds emphasis to “They are hidden.” You may have a word or grammatical particle in your language that performs the same function. Many English versions leave this word untranslated.

They are hidden in the ground inside my tent: Akan (Achan) took the things and buried them in a hole in the ground under his tent. In some languages an active verb may be necessary. For example:

I dug a hole under my tent and hid the silver, the gold, and the robe. (CEV)

I hid them in the earth inside my tent

7:21e

with the silver underneath.”

  • and put the silver at the bottom of the hole with the other things on top of it.”

  • The silver is underneath the gold and the robe.”

with the silver underneath: Akan (Achan) buried the silver at the bottom of the hole, with the gold and the robe on top of it.

title: Joshua 7:22
content:
Section 7:1–26 Akan (Achan) sinned and God punished him

Akan disobeyed God. He took some of the things from Yeriho (Jericho) that God told them to destroy. Because of his sin, the Israelis (Israelites) lost the battle against the town of Ay (Ai). Yahweh showed the Israelis that Akan was the one who had sinned, and they punished Akan.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The defeat at Ay

Akan’s sin

Paragraph 7:22–26

Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis stoned and burned Akan and his family.

7:22a

So Yehoshua sent messengers

  • ¶ After Akan (Achan) confessed Yehoshua sent men to search Akan’s tent.

  • ¶ Then Yehoshua ordered some men to go and look for the things.

So: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as So introduces the result after Akan confessed his sin. It may be clearer to make the connection explicit. For example, you could say:

So, after Akan had confessed his sin, Yehoshua sent messengers

Yehoshua sent messengers: The word messengers refers to people whom Yehoshua told to go and search Akan’s tent.

7:22b

who ran to the tent,

  • These men ran to the tent,

  • The men hurried to the tent.

The Hebrew conjunction that the BSB leaves untranslated but some English versions translate as “and” indicates the next event in the storyline. Some other English versions do not translate this word. Translate it in a way that is natural in your language.

ran to the tent: The phrase ran to the tent indicates that it was urgent to resolve this serious problem.

7:22c

and there it all was, hidden in his tent, with the silver underneath.

  • and found the robe and the bar of gold with the silver underneath them.

  • The robe and the bar of gold were buried in the ground on top of the silver as Akan (Achan) said.

there: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as there emphasizes what happens next in the story. Some English versions do not translate this word, buy many English versions translate it as “behold.” You may have a particle or another way in your language that has the same function. Translate it in a way that is natural in your language.

was, hidden in his tent: The men Yehoshua (Joshua) sent found the things buried under his tent, as he said they were. The verb phrase was, hidden in his tent is passive. In some languages it may be necessary to translate with an active verb. For example, you could say:

Akan had hidden it in his tent

with the silver underneath: The silver was buried at the bottom of the hole. The robe and the bar of gold were on top of the silver.

title: Joshua 7:23
content:
Section 7:1–26 Akan (Achan) sinned and God punished him

Akan disobeyed God. He took some of the things from Yeriho (Jericho) that God told them to destroy. Because of his sin, the Israelis (Israelites) lost the battle against the town of Ay (Ai). Yahweh showed the Israelis that Akan was the one who had sinned, and they punished Akan.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The defeat at Ay

Akan’s sin

Paragraph 7:22–26

Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis stoned and burned Akan and his family.

7:23a

They took the things from inside the tent,

  • So they took the stolen things from Akan’s (Achan’s) tent

  • Then the men took the things out of the ground under his tent

The Hebrew word that the BSB leaves untranslated but some English versions translate as “and” indicates the next event in the storyline. Translate it in a way that is natural in your language.

They: The word They here refers to the men whom Yehoshua sent to search for the stolen things.

the things: The phrase the things refers to the three stolen things.

7:23b

brought them to Yehoshua (Joshua) and all the Israelis (Israelites),

  • and brought them to Yehoshua. All the Israelis were standing and watching near him.

  • and presented them to Yehoshua. All Israeli (Israelite) people were still gathered with him.

The Hebrew word that the BSB leaves untranslated but some English versions translate as “and” indicates the next event in the storyline. Translate it in a way that is natural in your language.

brought them to Yehoshua and all the Israelis: The pronoun them here refers to the stolen things which the messengers found buried in the tent. The men who searched Akan’s (Achan’s) tent brought the stolen things to Yehoshua and the people.

7:23c

and spread them out before Yahweh.

  • The men spread the things out in front of the Tent of Meeting.

  • The men spread out the things on the ground in the presence of Yahweh.

and: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as and indicates the next event in the storyline.

spread them out: The men spread out the stolen things on the ground before Yehoshua (Joshua), so that everyone could see them.

before Yahweh: The phrase before Yahweh means “in the presence of Yahweh.” The presence of Yahweh is represented by the ark of the covenant, which was in the Tent of Meeting. The men spread out the stolen things in front of the Tent of Meeting.

Here are some other ways to translate this part of the verse:

spread them out on the ground before the Lord (NCV)

they laid them on the ground in the presence of the Lord (NLT)

title: Joshua 7:24
content:
Section 7:1–26 Akan (Achan) sinned and God punished him

Akan disobeyed God. He took some of the things from Yeriho (Jericho) that God told them to destroy. Because of his sin, the Israelis (Israelites) lost the battle against the town of Ay (Ai). Yahweh showed the Israelis that Akan was the one who had sinned, and they punished Akan.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The defeat at Ay

Akan’s sin

Paragraph 7:22–26

Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis stoned and burned Akan and his family.

7:24a

Then Yehoshua, together with all Yisrael (Israel), took Akan son of Zerah,

  • Then Yehoshua, together with all the Israelis, led away Akan (Achan), whose father was Zerah.

  • Then Yehoshua and the Israeli (Israelite) people took Akan, Zerah’s son,

Then: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as Then indicates the next event in the storyline.

Yehoshua, together with all Yisrael, took Akan son of Zerah: The Israeli people, with Yehoshua as their leader, took Akan away to the place where he will be punished.

Akan son of Zerah: The phrase son of Zerah recalls the genealogy of Akan in 7:1. It emphasizes that the correct person will be punished. Some English versions leave out this phrase. Consider whether this phrase is natural in your language or not.

7:24b

the silver, the cloak, the bar of gold,

  • They brought along the silver and the robe and the bar of gold.

  • with the things Akan (Achan) stole from Yahweh.

the silver, the cloak, the bar of gold: These things were mentioned in 7:21. You should translate them the same way as you did there. If the repetition of the list is unnatural in your language, you can translate it as CEV has done:

the things he had stolen (CEV)

7:24c

his sons and daughters, his oxen and donkeys and sheep,

  • They also took his sons and daughters, and his oxen and donkeys and sheep.

  • They took him with his sons and daughters, and his oxen, donkeys, sheep, and goats,

his sons and daughters: The author specifies sons and daughters to indicate that Akan (Achan) will have no descendants. It may be more natural in some languages to begin a new sentence here.

his oxen and donkeys and sheep: oxen, donkeys and sheep were domestic animals. Listing the animals separately in Hebrew emphasizes that Akan did a serious thing. It may be more natural in some languages to use an inclusive term such as:

all his domestic animals

sheep: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as sheep refers to both goats and sheep. These are animals that they herded in flocks.

7:24d

his tent, and everything else he owned,

  • They took his tent and everything else that belonged to Akan,

  • and his tent, and all his other possessions.

his tent, and everything else he owned: Everything else that Akan (Achan) possessed was also brought with him to the Valley of Akor (Achor).

7:24e

and brought them to the Valley of Akor.

  • and brought them to the Valley of Trouble.

  • They brought them to Trouble Valley.

and: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as and introduces the next event in the storyline.

brought them: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as brought indicates that the Valley of Akor was on higher ground than the place where the Israelis (Israelites) camped. The Israelis went uphill to reach it. In some languages it is natural to use the phrase “brought up” to indicate this. Many English versions translate this phrase as:

took them

them: The word them here refers to all Akan’s (Achan’s) family as possessions that were mentioned earlier in the verse. In some languages it may be clearer to make this explicit.

to the Valley of Akor (Achor): We are not sure where the Valley of Akor was. Many scholars believe that it was a wilderness area eight miles north of Yeriho (Jericho). This means that Yehoshua (Joshua) took Akan far away from the Israeli (Israelite) camp.7:24 See, for example, Hess, p. 155.

Valley of Akor: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as Akor means “trouble.” There are two ways to translate the phrase Valley of Akor.

  1. Translate it as “Valley of Trouble” or “Trouble Valley.” For example:

    Valley of Disaster (NET) (NET, CEV, NCV, GNT)

  2. Translate it as “Valley of Akor.” For example:

    Valley of Akor (NIV) (BSB, NIV, RSV, ESV, NASB, NJB, NJPS, NLT, REB)

It is recommended that you follow option (1) and translate with a word meaning “trouble” or “disaster.” This will help readers to understand Yehoshua’s rhetorical question in 7:25.7:24 The term “Valley of Akor” also occurs in Isaiah 65:10 and Hosea 2:15.

If you choose option (2) it is recommended that you include a footnote explaining the meaning of Akor (Achor). For example:

FOOTNOTE: The name Akor means “trouble”

General Comment on 7:24

It is possible to break up this long Hebrew sentence into two or more shorter sentences. Some English versions also reorder the parts of this verse. For example:

24aThen Yehoshua (Joshua) and all the people led Akan (Achan) son of Zerah 24eto the Valley of Trouble. 24bThey also took the silver, the coat, the gold, 24cAkan’s sons, daughters, cattle, donkeys, sheep, 24dtent, and everything he owned. (NCV)

title: Joshua 7:25
content:
Section 7:1–26 Akan (Achan) sinned and God punished him

Akan disobeyed God. He took some of the things from Yeriho (Jericho) that God told them to destroy. Because of his sin, the Israelis (Israelites) lost the battle against the town of Ay (Ai). Yahweh showed the Israelis that Akan was the one who had sinned, and they punished Akan.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The defeat at Ay

Akan’s sin

Paragraph 7:22–26

Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis stoned and burned Akan and his family.

7:25a

“Why have you brought this trouble upon us?”

  • “Why have you brought so much trouble on us?”

  • “You have brought a lot of trouble for us,”

Why have you brought this trouble upon us?: This is a rhetorical question. It functions as a rebuke. Yehoshua rebuked Akan (Achan) because he stole the devoted things and caused the Israelis (Israelites) to lose the battle of Ay (Ai).

Here are two ways to translate this rebuke:

  • As a rhetorical question. For example:

    Why did you bring this disaster on us? (GW)

  • As a statement or exclamation. For example:

    You have brought a lot of trouble on us(excl)

    I don’t know why you caused so much trouble for us! (NCV)

Express this rebuke in a natural way in your language.

brought this trouble: The Hebrew verb that the BSB translates as brought…trouble is the same word that Yehoshua (Joshua) used in 6:18. You should use the same word to translate it here as you did in that verse.

The Hebrew word for brought…trouble sounds like “Akor (Achor)” the name of the valley.

7:25b

said Yehoshua.

  • Yehoshua asked.

  • Yehoshua said.

said Yehoshua: The Hebrew has this phrase at the beginning of 7:25a and begins with a word that many English versions translate as “and.” This word introduces the next event in the storyline. Indicate the next event in a way that is natural in your language.

In some languages it may be clearer to make the connection to the previous event explicit. For example:

When they arrived there, Yehoshua said

Yehoshua (Joshua) addressed Akan (Achan) with a rhetorical question in 7:25a. If you translate it as a question, you need to think about how to introduce a question in your language. In some languages it may be more natural to say:

Yehoshua asked

7:25c

“Today Yahweh will bring trouble upon you!”

  • “Now Yahweh will bring the same trouble on you.”

  • “Today Yahweh will bring trouble for you.”

Today Yahweh will bring trouble upon you: Because Akan took the things that belonged to Yahweh, Yahweh punished Akan.

7:25d

And all Yisrael (Israel) stoned him to death.

  • Then all the people of Yisrael threw stones at him so that he died.

  • Then all the Israelis (Israelites) threw stones at him until he died.

And: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as And indicates the next event in the storyline.

all Yisrael: The phrase all Yisrael means all the people of Yisrael.

stoned him to death: The phrase stoned him to death means that they threw stones at him until he died.7:25 Hess suggests that Akan’s (Achan’s) sons and daughters had to die with him so that Akan’s name will be forgotten. His sin was so grave that God did not allow him to have any descendants (Hess, p. 154). Butler suggests that “anyone who had come into contact with the goods was contaminated and had to be removed from the community to protect the community” (Butler, p. 86). Akan’s family came into contact with the stolen goods because he hid them inside his family tent.

7:25e

Then they stoned the others and burned their bodies.

  • They also threw stones at his family so that they died. Then they burned the bodies and their things.

  • They also killed his family by throwing stones at them. And they burned the bodies and the things that belonged to them.

Then they stoned the others: The stoning of Akan is mentioned first because he was the person who sinned. However, Akan’s family must die also.

The Hebrew clauses are not in chronological order. In some languages it may be clearer to rearrange them. First people stoned Akan, then they stoned his family, then they burned their bodies and their possessions.

and burned their bodies: There is disagreement among scholars as to whether their bodies refers to Akan’s possessions, or to the bodies of Akan and his family. Most English versions understand their bodies to refer to both the bodies and the possessions.

General Comment on 7:25d-e

These clauses can be reordered chronologically. It is also possible to include the implied information that Akan’s (Achan’s) possessions were with him.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

All the people then stoned Akan to death; they also stoned and burned his family and possessions (GNT)

And all the Israelis (Israelites) stoned Akan and his family and burned their bodies (NLT)

title: Joshua 7:26
content:
Section 7:1–26 Akan (Achan) sinned and God punished him

Akan disobeyed God. He took some of the things from Yeriho (Jericho) that God told them to destroy. Because of his sin, the Israelis (Israelites) lost the battle against the town of Ay (Ai). Yahweh showed the Israelis that Akan was the one who had sinned, and they punished Akan.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The defeat at Ay

Akan’s sin

Paragraph 7:22–26

Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis stoned and burned Akan and his family.

7:26a

And they heaped over Akan a large pile of rocks

  • Then they covered Akan’s (Achan’s) body with a big pile of rocks.

  • Then the Israelis (Israelites) piled up rocks to completely cover Akan’s body.

And: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as And introduces the next event in the storyline.

they heaped over Akan a large pile of rocks: This phrase indicates that the people of Yisrael (Israel) took stones and piled them over him until his body was hidden.

7:26b

that remains to this day.

  • That pile of rocks is still here today.

  • The heap of rocks has stood here until this time.

that remains to this day: This phrase indicates that the pile of stones was still there when the author wrote the book of Yehoshua (Joshua).

7:26c

So Yahweh turned from His burning anger.

  • After that, Yahweh stopped being angry with the Israelis (Israelites).

  • Then Yahweh was no longer angry.

So: The Hebrew prefix that the BSB translates as So introduces the next event in the storyline. Introduce the next event in a way that is natural in your language.

Yahweh turned from His burning anger: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as turned from is more literally “turned back.” It indicates that Yahweh stopped being angry.

His burning anger: The Hebrew phrase that the BSB translates as His burning anger is more literally “the burning of his anger.” This is an idiom. It means that Yahweh was angry at the Israelis. However, they obeyed him by destroying the devoted things, and so Yahweh was no longer angry.

7:26d

Therefore that place is called the Valley of Akor (Achor) to this day.

  • That is why the place where Akan (Achan) was stoned is called the Valley of Trouble.

  • Because of this, the name of that place is still called Trouble Valley.

Therefore: The Hebrew connector that the BSB translates as Therefore introduces the reason why the place is called Akor.

that place is called the Valley of Akor: The word Akor in Hebrew means “trouble.” You should translate it as you did in 7:24e. It is recommended that you translate it as “Trouble Valley.”

to this day: This phrase this day refers to the time that the book of Yehoshua (Joshua) was written.

title: Joshua 8:1
content:
Section 8:1–29 Yisrael (Israel) defeated Ay (Ai).

In chapter 7, Yisrael attacked Ay and the soldiers of Ay defeated them. They were discouraged but they repented of their sin. In chapter 8, God told Yehoshua (Joshua) to attack Ay again. This time, the Israelis (Israelites) were victorious and defeated Ay.

Verses 8:1–9 describe Yehoshua’s preparations to attack Ay, with details about the ambush. The soldiers in the ambush left by night ahead of the other soldiers. Verses 8:10–27 describe the movement of the soldiers, and the defeat of Ay. Verses 8:28–29 is a summary of the story.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The fall and destruction of Ay

Yisrael conquered Ay

8:1a

Then Yahweh said to Yehoshua,

  • ¶ Then Yahweh said to Yehoshua:

  • ¶ Yahweh told Yehoshua (Joshua):

Then Yahweh said to Yehoshua: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as Then introduces the next event in the storyline. Some English versions use a different word to mark the next event. Some do not use any word. For example:

And the Lord said to Yehoshua (RSV)

The Lord said to Yehoshua (GNT)

Use a natural way in your language to introduce the next event in the storyline.

8:1b

“Do not be afraid or discouraged.

  • “Don’t(sing) be afraid and don’t give up.

  • “Do not be afraid at all.

Do not be afraid or discouraged: The two Hebrew words that the BSB translates as afraid and discouraged are imperative commands. The repetition of two synonyms makes this command emphatic. Yehoshua (Joshua) should not be afraid at all.

Translate this as an emphatic command. It is not necessary to use two verbs unless it is natural to do so. An adverb or an emphatic particle may be a more natural way to express this idea. Some languages have an idiom with this meaning.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged (NIV)

Don’t be afraid or give up (NCV)

It may be helpful to add implicit information to make clear why Yehoshua might be afraid, as in the CEV:

Don’t be afraid, and don’t be discouraged by what happened at the town of Ay (Ai) (CEV)

8:1c

Take the whole army with you,

  • Take(sing) all the soldiers with you(sing)

  • Take the whole army with you

Take the whole army with you: The phrase whole army refers to the Israeli (Israelite) soldiers.

8:1d

and go up and attack Ay.

  • and go up to Ay (Ai).

  • and attack Ay.

and go up and attack Ay: The Hebrew that the BSB translates as go up and attack is more literally “arise, go up.” The command “arise” is used to introduce a command. The command is “go up.” Translate this command in a way that is natural in your language. For example:

go on up to Ay (GNT)

attack: As mentioned in the previous note, the Hebrew word that the BSB translates as attack is more literally “go up.” The town of Ay was at a higher elevation than Gilgal, where the Israelis (Israelites) camped. The Israelis went uphill to go from Gilgal to Ay. If your language does not keep track of elevation in this way, you can translate it as:

fight against Ay

Lead all your fighting men to Ay (NCV)

Ay (Ai): The town of Ay was mentioned in 7:2. You should translate it in the same way in both places.

8:1e

See, I have delivered into your hand the king of Ay,

  • I will help you(sing) to defeat the king of Ay.

  • I will give the king of Ay,

See, I have delivered into your hand the king of Ay: It is recommended that you begin a new sentence here.

See: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as See is an emphatic word. It shows the importance of what Yahweh told Yehoshua (Joshua). There may be another word or a grammatical particle in some languages to add emphasis. Some versions do not mark emphasis here. Use a word or a grammatical marker that is natural in your language.

I have delivered into your hand: The phrase I have delivered into your hand is a Hebrew idiom. It means that Yahweh will help Yehoshua and the Israelis (Israelites) to defeat the king of Ay.

your: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as your is singular. God is speaking to Yehoshua. It may be more natural in some languages to translate this as a plural. For example:

I will give the king of Ay (Ai) into your hands

I will help you(plur) to defeat the king of Ay

8:1f

his people, his city, and his land.

  • You will defeat the people in Ay and conquer his land.

  • and his people, and his city, and his land to you.

his people, his city, and his land: The word his refers to the king of Ay.

The phrase his people, his city, and his land emphasizes that Yahweh will give Yehoshua (Joshua) complete victory over every part of Ay (Ai). This includes its citizens and all the land that is under the power of the king.

title: Joshua 8:2
content:
Section 8:1–29 Yisrael (Israel) defeated Ay (Ai).

In chapter 7, Yisrael attacked Ay and the soldiers of Ay defeated them. They were discouraged but they repented of their sin. In chapter 8, God told Yehoshua (Joshua) to attack Ay again. This time, the Israelis (Israelites) were victorious and defeated Ay.

Verses 8:1–9 describe Yehoshua’s preparations to attack Ay, with details about the ambush. The soldiers in the ambush left by night ahead of the other soldiers. Verses 8:10–27 describe the movement of the soldiers, and the defeat of Ay. Verses 8:28–29 is a summary of the story.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The fall and destruction of Ay

Yisrael conquered Ay

8:2a

And you shall do to Ay and its king as you did to Yeriho (Jericho) and its king,

  • You will do the same thing to Ay and its king that you did to Yeriho and its king.

  • In the same way that you destroyed Yeriho and its king, you must destroy Ay (Ai) and its king.

And you shall do to Ay and its king: It is recommended that you begin a new sentence here. The command you shall do refers to what the Israelis (Israelites) did in Yeriho. In some languages it may be more natural to make explicit what Yehoshua (Joshua) and the army must do. They must kill the people of Ay, as they killed the people of Yeriho. For example:

Destroy Ay and kill its king as you did at Yeriho (CEV)

as you did to Yeriho and its king: Verse 6:21 said that the Israelis killed the men and women in Yeriho with their swords. This is what they must also do to the king of Ay and the citizens.

8:2b

except that you may carry off their plunder and livestock for yourselves.

  • However, you may take the things in the city and the domestic animals for yourselves.

  • But you may take the things there for yourselves, including the cattle and the sheep.

except: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as except expresses contrast with what God commanded Yisrael (Israel) previously regarding Yeriho (Jericho). Show contrast in a way that is natural in your language.

Here are some other ways to translate this word:

but

however

you may carry off for yourselves: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as carry off for yourselves is more literally the simple verb “take.” In Yeriho all the things belonged to God and the Israelis (Israelites) could not take them. But in Ay (Ai) the Israelis can take these things for their own use.

Here are some other ways to translate this verb:

you may keep (these things) for yourselves (GNT)

you may carry off (these things) for yourselves (NIV)

their plunder and livestock: The Hebrew puts the phrase their plunder and livestock before “you may carry off for yourselves” in the sentence to show emphasis. You should emphasize this phrase in a way that is natural in your language.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

you may keep the livestock and everything else you want (CEV)

you may take its loot and livestock for yourselves (GW)

their plunder: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as plunder refers to things of value in the town that the Israelis (Israelites) could take.

livestock: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as livestock refers to domesticated animals. It can also include sheep and goats.

8:2c

Set up an ambush behind the city.”

  • Get ready to attack the city by surprise from behind.”

  • Tell some of your soldiers to go hide west of the city, so that they can attack it by surprise.”

It is recommended that you begin a new sentence here.

Set up an ambush behind the city: The phrase Set up an ambush indicates that some of the Israeli (Israelite) soldiers hid so that they could attack Ay (Ai) by surprise.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

set an ambush behind the city (NET)

prepare to attack the city by surprise from the rear (GNT)

behind the city: The phrase behind the city indicates that the purpose of the “ambush” is to attack the town. In 8:9 it is clear that behind the city indicates the direction west of the town.

title: Joshua 8:3
content:
Section 8:1–29 Yisrael (Israel) defeated Ay (Ai).

In chapter 7, Yisrael attacked Ay and the soldiers of Ay defeated them. They were discouraged but they repented of their sin. In chapter 8, God told Yehoshua (Joshua) to attack Ay again. This time, the Israelis (Israelites) were victorious and defeated Ay.

Verses 8:1–9 describe Yehoshua’s preparations to attack Ay, with details about the ambush. The soldiers in the ambush left by night ahead of the other soldiers. Verses 8:10–27 describe the movement of the soldiers, and the defeat of Ay. Verses 8:28–29 is a summary of the story.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The fall and destruction of Ay

Yisrael conquered Ay

8:3a

So Yehoshua and the whole army set out to attack Ay.

  • ¶ So Yehoshua and all the soldiers started to go up to Ay.

  • ¶ So Yehoshua (Joshua) and all his soldiers got ready to go to Ay (Ai).

So Yehoshua and the whole army set out: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as set out shows that a new action is beginning. This verb does not mean that Yehoshua was lying down.8:3 Bratcher and Newman, p. 105.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

Yehoshua and all the fighting men set out to go up against Ay (NRSV)

Yehoshua and all the fighting men started to go up to Ay

and the whole army: The phrase the whole army refers to all the soldiers of Yisrael (Israel).

to attack Ay: The Hebrew verb that the BSB translates as to attack literally means “ascend.” Ay was at a higher elevation than the Israeli (Israelite) camp, and the Hebrew language keeps track of elevation. If your language does not keep track of elevation in this way you can translate it as:

to go to Ay

to go and attack Ay (Ai)

8:3b

Yehoshua (Joshua) chose 30,000 mighty men of valor

  • Yehoshua picked out thirty thousand strong and brave soldiers

  • And Yehoshua chose thirty thousand soldiers who were strong and brave

It is recommended that you begin a new sentence here.

Yehoshua chose 30,000 mighty men of valor: In 4:13 it says that there were forty thousand Israeli (Israelite) soldiers in total. Thirty thousand of them went to hide behind the town, and ten thousand of them stayed with Yehoshua.

mighty men of valor: The phrase mighty men of valor indicates that the soldiers Yehoshua chose were strong and brave.

8:3c

and sent them out at night

  • and sent them out at night.

  • and told them to march to Ay (Ai) during the night.

and sent them out at night: The clause sent them out at night indicates that the soldiers whom Yehoshua (Joshua) chose went during the night. They went at night so that the people of Ay would not see them.

title: Joshua 8:4
content:
Section 8:1–29 Yisrael (Israel) defeated Ay (Ai).

In chapter 7, Yisrael attacked Ay and the soldiers of Ay defeated them. They were discouraged but they repented of their sin. In chapter 8, God told Yehoshua (Joshua) to attack Ay again. This time, the Israelis (Israelites) were victorious and defeated Ay.

Verses 8:1–9 describe Yehoshua’s preparations to attack Ay, with details about the ambush. The soldiers in the ambush left by night ahead of the other soldiers. Verses 8:10–27 describe the movement of the soldiers, and the defeat of Ay. Verses 8:28–29 is a summary of the story.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The fall and destruction of Ay

Yisrael conquered Ay

8:4a

with these orders:

  • Yehoshua gave them these orders:

  • Before they left, Yehoshua (Joshua) commanded them:

The Hebrew connector that the BSB leaves untranslated but many English versions translate as “And” introduces the next event in the storyline.

with these orders: Before they began to walk towards Ay (Ai), Yehoshua explained to them what they must do when they reached the town.

8:4b

“Pay attention. You are to lie in ambush behind the city,

  • “Listen carefully. You must hide yourselves behind the city.

  • “Pay attention. Hide yourselves west of the city.

Pay attention: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as Pay attention is literally “see.” It shows that what Yehoshua is about to say is important and that the soldiers should listen carefully. You may have a grammatical particle or another way to mark the importance of a command.

Here are some other ways to translate this word:

listen carefully (NIV)

pay attention

lie in ambush behind the city: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as lie in ambush indicates that the soldiers hid in order to attack the town by surprise.

behind the city: The soldiers are to hide on the far side of the town. From 8:12 it is clear that behind the city indicates the direction to the west of the town.

8:4c

not too far from it. All of you must be ready.

  • Do not hide far away from it. Be ready to attack it.

  • Stay close to the city and be prepared to attack it.

not too far from it: This indicates that the soldiers must hide themselves close to the town.

All of you must be ready: The soldiers must be ready to attack at any time.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

be ready to attack (GNT)

title: Joshua 8:5
content:
Section 8:1–29 Yisrael (Israel) defeated Ay (Ai).

In chapter 7, Yisrael attacked Ay and the soldiers of Ay defeated them. They were discouraged but they repented of their sin. In chapter 8, God told Yehoshua (Joshua) to attack Ay again. This time, the Israelis (Israelites) were victorious and defeated Ay.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The fall and destruction of Ay

Yisrael conquered Ay

8:5a

Then I and all the troops with me will advance on the city.

  • I and all the people who are with me will march to the city.

  • My men and I will all approach the city,

Then I and all the troops with me: The phrase all the troops with me refers to the ten thousand Israeli (Israelite) soldiers who stayed with Yehoshua (Joshua) and who did not hide behind Ay (Ai).

will advance on the city: The phrase will advance on the city indicates that Yehoshua and the soldiers with him will move toward the town as if they are going to attack it.

8:5b

When they come out against us as they did the first time,

  • When the Ay soldiers come out against us(excl), as they did before,

  • and they will come out to fight us as they did the first time.

When: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as When introduces the next event in the storyline.

they come out against us: The clause they come out against us indicates that the soldiers of Ay will come out of the town gate to attack the Israeli soldiers.

us: The word us is exclusive. Yehoshua spoke to the soldiers who were not with him.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

when they come out of the town to attack us(excl)

as they did the first time: The phrase as they did the first time refers to the first time that the Israelis (Israelites) tried to capture Ay (Ai) in 7:4–5. Some English versions place this phrase at the end of verse 5c. For example:

When the men of Ay come out against us, we will turn and run, just as we did the first time. (GNT)

8:5c

we will flee from them.

  • we(excl) will turn and run away.

  • Then we will run away from them.

we will flee from them: The clause we will flee from them indicates that the soldiers who are with Yehoshua (Joshua) will run away from the soldiers of Ay.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

we(excl) will run away from them

title: Joshua 8:6
content:
Section 8:1–29 Yisrael (Israel) defeated Ay (Ai).

In chapter 7, Yisrael attacked Ay and the soldiers of Ay defeated them. They were discouraged but they repented of their sin. In chapter 8, God told Yehoshua (Joshua) to attack Ay again. This time, the Israelis (Israelites) were victorious and defeated Ay.

Verses 8:1–9 describe Yehoshua’s preparations to attack Ay, with details about the ambush. The soldiers in the ambush left by night ahead of the other soldiers. Verses 8:10–27 describe the movement of the soldiers, and the defeat of Ay. Verses 8:28–29 is a summary of the story.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The fall and destruction of Ay

Yisrael conquered Ay

8:6a

They will pursue us

  • They will come out of the city and chase us(excl)

  • Then they will come out and run after us

It is recommended that you begin a new sentence here.

They will pursue us: The clause They will pursue us indicates that the soldiers of Ay (Ai) will come out of their town and chase the Israelis (Israelites) when they run away.

8:6b

until we have drawn them away from the city,

  • until we lead them far away from the city.

  • and we will trick them into going away from the city.

until we have drawn them away from the city: The clause until we have drawn them away from the city indicates that the Israeli (Israelite) soldiers continued to run away until the soldiers of Ay were far from their town.

until: The English word until can also be spelled “till” as in most English versions.

have drawn them away: The expression drawn them away indicates that they lured them or enticed them to leave.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

we will trick them into going far from their town

8:6c

for they will say, ‘The Israelis (Israelites) are running away from us as they did before.’

  • They will say: ‘They are running away from us as they did before.’

  • They will think we are running away from them, as we did the first time.

for: The word for introduces the reason why the citizens of Ay (Ai) left the town in 8:6a-b. Use a natural way in your language to indicate reason. It is recommended that you begin a new sentence here.

they will say, ‘The Israelis are running away from us as they did before.’: The clause they will say introduces what the soldiers of Ay would think and say to each other. In some languages it might be more natural to use an indirect quote. For example:

They will pursue us until we have led them away from the city. They will think that we are running from them, as we did before. (GNT)

as they did before: The citizens of Ay assumed that the Israelis would act the same way that they did the first time.

8:6d

So as we flee from them,

  • When we run away from them

  • While we are running

So as we flee from them: The clause So as we flee from them repeats information that Yehoshua (Joshua) stated in verse 8:5c. Even though this phrase is at the end of a verse, it is the beginning of a new sentence. For example:

6dSo when we flee from them, 7ayou are to rise up from ambush and take the town, (NIV)

title: Joshua 8:7
content:
Section 8:1–29 Yisrael (Israel) defeated Ay (Ai).

In chapter 7, Yisrael attacked Ay and the soldiers of Ay defeated them. They were discouraged but they repented of their sin. In chapter 8, God told Yehoshua (Joshua) to attack Ay again. This time, the Israelis (Israelites) were victorious and defeated Ay.

Verses 8:1–9 describe Yehoshua’s preparations to attack Ay, with details about the ambush. The soldiers in the ambush left by night ahead of the other soldiers. Verses 8:10–27 describe the movement of the soldiers, and the defeat of Ay. Verses 8:28–29 is a summary of the story.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The fall and destruction of Ay

Yisrael conquered Ay

8:7a

you are to rise from the ambush and seize the city,

  • then you(plur) must come out from where you are hiding and take the city.

  • you should come out from behind the city and capture it.

you are to rise from the ambush: This clause indicates the next step in Yehoshua’s (Joshua’s) plan. First the Israeli (Israelite) soldiers with Yehoshua will lead the Ay (Ai) soldiers away from the town. Then the soldiers who are hiding will attack the town.

and seize the city: The phrase seize the city indicates that the Israelis (Israelites) would defeat the people who remained in the town and capture it.

8:7b

for Yahweh your God will deliver it into your hand.

  • Yahweh your(plur) God will give it to you.

  • Yahweh your God will help you to take it.

for: The word for introduces the reason for Yisrael’s (Israel’s) success.

Yahweh your God will deliver it into your hand: Yahweh will enable the Israeli soldiers to defeat the town. The Israelis captured the town because of the power of Yahweh, and not because of their own cleverness or strength.

deliver it into your hand: The expression deliver it into your hand is a Hebrew idiom. It means that Yahweh will help Yehoshua and the Israelis to defeat the king of Ay.

Here are some other ways to translate this idiom:

The Lord your God will give you the power to win. (NCV)

The Lord our God will help you capture the town. (CEV)

title: Joshua 8:8
content:
Section 8:1–29 Yisrael (Israel) defeated Ay (Ai).

In chapter 7, Yisrael attacked Ay and the soldiers of Ay defeated them. They were discouraged but they repented of their sin. In chapter 8, God told Yehoshua (Joshua) to attack Ay again. This time, the Israelis (Israelites) were victorious and defeated Ay.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The fall and destruction of Ay

Yisrael conquered Ay

8:8a

And when you have taken the city,

  • After you(plur) have taken the city,

  • After you defeat the city and its people,

And: The Hebrew connector that the BSB translates as And is the normal way to indicate the next event of the story. Use a connecting word that is natural in your language.

when you have taken the city: The clause when you have taken the city refers to the time after the Israeli (Israelite) soldiers have captured the town. For example:

After you have taken the city (GNT)

8:8b

set it on fire. Do as Yahweh has commanded!

  • you(plur) must set it on fire. This is what Yahweh says.

  • burn the city, as Yahweh commanded.

set it on fire: Yehoshua (Joshua) commanded the Israelis (Israelites) to burn the buildings and other flammable objects in the town.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

light the town on fire

burn the town

Do as Yahweh has commanded: Yehoshua told the Israeli (Israelite) soldiers that this was the command of Yahweh.

8:8c

See, I have given you orders.”

  • I am telling you(plur) his commands.”

  • This is the command I am giving you.”

See: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as See emphasizes the importance of the command. You may have some other word or grammatical marker to emphasize that this command is important.

I have given you orders: The clause I have given you orders refers to the instructions that Yehoshua (Joshua) gave the soldiers. As Yahweh’s spokesperson, Yehoshua gave the soldiers Yahweh’s commands.

title: Joshua 8:9
content:
Section 8:1–29 Yisrael (Israel) defeated Ay (Ai).

In chapter 7, Yisrael attacked Ay and the soldiers of Ay defeated them. They were discouraged but they repented of their sin. In chapter 8, God told Yehoshua (Joshua) to attack Ay again. This time, the Israelis (Israelites) were victorious and defeated Ay.

Verses 8:1–9 describe Yehoshua’s preparations to attack Ay, with details about the ambush. The soldiers in the ambush left by night ahead of the other soldiers. Verses 8:10–27 describe the movement of the soldiers, and the defeat of Ay. Verses 8:28–29 is a summary of the story.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The fall and destruction of Ay

Yisrael conquered Ay

Paragraph 8:9

In verses 8:4–8 Yehoshua gave instructions to the thirty thousand soldiers who will carry out the ambush. In 8:9 those soldiers started to go to their hiding place west of Ay.

8:9a

So Yehoshua sent them out,

  • ¶ So Yehoshua (Joshua) sent them out

  • ¶ Then Yehoshua sent the thirty thousand soldiers on their way

So Yehoshua sent them out: The clause Yehoshua sent them out indicates that Yehoshua ordered the soldiers who were to hide behind Ay (Ai) to begin to move towards the town.

8:9b

and they went to the place of ambush

  • and they went to their hiding place.

  • and they went to a place where they could hide.

and they went to the place of ambush: The soldiers walked to the place where they hid until the time came to attack the town.

8:9c

and lay in wait between Beyt-El (Bethel) and Ay, to the west of Ay.

  • And they stayed there on the west side of Ay, between Ay and Beyt-El.

  • They hid on the west side of Ay (Ai), between Ay and Beyt-El, and waited to attack.

and lay in wait between Beyt-El and Ay: The soldiers found a place to hide between the towns of Beyt-El and Ay. They hid and waited there until the rest of the Israeli (Israelite) soldiers came to Ay the next day.

lay in wait: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as lay is more literally “stayed” or “remained.” The soldiers stayed there overnight and probably many of them lay down to sleep.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

they stayed between Beyt-El and Ay

they hid between Beyt-El and Ay

to the west of Ay: The place where the soldiers hid was west of Ay. The town of Beyt-El (Bethel) was further west of their hiding place.

8:9d

But Yehoshua (Joshua) spent that night among the people.

  • But Yehoshua stayed that night in the camp with the rest of the army.

  • But Yehoshua spent the night in the camp.

But Yehoshua spent that night among the people: The clause Yehoshua spent that night among the people indicates that Yehoshua stayed with the rest of the Israeli (Israelite) soldiers in the camp. For example:

Yehoshua spent the night with the rest of the troops (NJPS)

title: Joshua 8:10
content:
Section 8:1–29 Yisrael (Israel) defeated Ay (Ai).

In chapter 7, Yisrael attacked Ay and the soldiers of Ay defeated them. They were discouraged but they repented of their sin. In chapter 8, God told Yehoshua (Joshua) to attack Ay again. This time, the Israelis (Israelites) were victorious and defeated Ay.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The fall and destruction of Ay

Yisrael conquered Ay

8:10a

Yehoshua got up early the next morning and mobilized his men,

  • ¶ Yehoshua got up early the next morning and gathered the people together.

  • ¶ Early the next morning Yehoshua (Joshua) assembled the soldiers.

The Hebrew connector that the BSB leaves untranslated but many English versions translate as “and” indicates the next event of the storyline.

Yehoshua got up early the next morning: This indicates that Yehoshua woke up early.

and mobilized his men: The clause mobilized his men indicates that Yehoshua assembled the rest of his army and got them ready to go to Ay (Ai).

mobilized: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as mobilized can also be translated as:

assembled

gathered together

8:10b

and he and the elders of Yisrael (Israel) marched before them up to Ay.

  • He and the leaders of Yisrael led the soldiers up to Ay.

  • Then he and the other leaders of Yisrael marched in front of the army to Ay.

and he and the elders of Yisrael marched before them up to Ay (Ai): Yehoshua (Joshua) and the elders of Yisrael led the way as the army went up to Ay.

the elders of Yisrael: the elders of Yisrael were the leaders of the Israeli (Israelite) community. They were heads of tribes and families.

marched before them up: The Hebrew text says marched…up because Ay was higher than the Israeli camp. If your language does not keep track of elevation in the same way that Hebrew does, you can translate this as:

went

title: Joshua 8:11
content:
Section 8:1–29 Yisrael (Israel) defeated Ay (Ai).

In chapter 7, Yisrael attacked Ay and the soldiers of Ay defeated them. They were discouraged but they repented of their sin. In chapter 8, God told Yehoshua (Joshua) to attack Ay again. This time, the Israelis (Israelites) were victorious and defeated Ay.

Verses 8:1–9 describe Yehoshua’s preparations to attack Ay, with details about the ambush. The soldiers in the ambush left by night ahead of the other soldiers. Verses 8:10–27 describe the movement of the soldiers, and the defeat of Ay. Verses 8:28–29 is a summary of the story.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The fall and destruction of Ay

Yisrael conquered Ay

8:11a

Then all the troops who were with him marched up

  • All the soldiers who were with him walked up

  • The soldiers who were with him went

Then: The Hebrew connector that the BSB translates as Then indicates the next event of the storyline.

all the troops who were with him: The phrase all the troops refers to the Israeli (Israelite) soldiers who were with Yehoshua (Joshua). The word him refers to Yehoshua, who was the commander of the army.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

all the soldiers who were with Yehoshua

marched up: The Hebrew text says marched up because Ay (Ai) was higher than the Israeli camp. If your language does not keep track of elevation in the same way that Hebrew does, you can translate this as:

went

8:11b

and approached the city. They arrived in front of Ay

  • until they got near Ay city.

  • to Ay.

and approached the city: The clause approached the city indicates that the soldiers walked until they were close to the town of Ay.

8:11c

and camped to the north of it, with the valley between them and the city.

  • They camped north of Ay (Ai) with the valley between them and Ay.

  • They set up camp on the north side of the city, with a valley between themselves and Ay.

and camped to the north of it: The clause camped to the north of it indicates that the soldiers set up their tents on the northern side of the town of Ay. It may be clearer in some languages if you begin a new sentence here. For example:

They set up camp north of Ay (NIV)

with the valley between them and the city: The Israeli (Israelite) soldiers made their camp north of the town, with a valley separating them from the town of Ay.

General Comment on 8:11

Because the information contained in 11a-b is already stated in 8:10, it may be more natural in some languages to leave this information implicit, as the CEV does:

They set up camp in full view of the town, across the valley to the north. (CEV)

title: Joshua 8:12
content:
Section 8:1–29 Yisrael (Israel) defeated Ay (Ai).

In chapter 7, Yisrael attacked Ay and the soldiers of Ay defeated them. They were discouraged but they repented of their sin. In chapter 8, God told Yehoshua (Joshua) to attack Ay again. This time, the Israelis (Israelites) were victorious and defeated Ay.

Verses 8:1–9 describe Yehoshua’s preparations to attack Ay, with details about the ambush. The soldiers in the ambush left by night ahead of the other soldiers. Verses 8:10–27 describe the movement of the soldiers, and the defeat of Ay. Verses 8:28–29 is a summary of the story.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The fall and destruction of Ay

Yisrael conquered Ay

8:12a

Now Yehoshua had taken about five thousand men

  • Then Yehoshua ordered about five thousand soldiers

  • And Yehoshua (Joshua) chose about five thousand men

Now Yehoshua had taken about five thousand men: This clause indicates that Yehoshua gave orders to about five thousand soldiers.

In verse 8:3 it says that thirty thousand men were part of the ambush. In this verse it says there were five thousand men. The commentaries do not suggest any good way to reconcile these different numbers. It is recommended that you translate them literally.

had taken: There are two ways to interpret the meaning of the verb had taken.

  1. The form of the verb indicates the next event in the story. For example:

    He took five thousand men (NET) (NET, RSV, ESV, NJPS, GNT, NLT, KJV)

  2. The form of the verb indicates an event that has already happened. For example:

    Yehoshua had taken about five thousand men (NIV) (BSB, NIV, CEV, GW)

It is recommended that you follow interpretation (1). This is the interpretation followed by many English versions and by many commentaries.

8:12b

and set up an ambush between Beyt-El (Bethel) and Ay (Ai), to the west of the city.

  • to hide and be ready to attack on the west side of Ay, between Ay and the city of Beyt-El.

  • and sent them west of the city between Beyt-El and Ay. He told them to hide there and be ready to attack.

and set up an ambush: The clause set up an ambush indicates that Yehoshua (Joshua) told them to hide and wait to attack Ay.

between Beyt-El and Ay, to the west of the city: Beyt-El was three kilometers west of Ay.8:12 Bratcher and Newman, p. 110. The soldiers hid themselves Beyt-El and Ay.

title: Joshua 8:13
content:
Section 8:1–29 Yisrael (Israel) defeated Ay (Ai).

In chapter 7, Yisrael attacked Ay and the soldiers of Ay defeated them. They were discouraged but they repented of their sin. In chapter 8, God told Yehoshua (Joshua) to attack Ay again. This time, the Israelis (Israelites) were victorious and defeated Ay.

Verses 8:1–9 describe Yehoshua’s preparations to attack Ay, with details about the ambush. The soldiers in the ambush left by night ahead of the other soldiers. Verses 8:10–27 describe the movement of the soldiers, and the defeat of Ay. Verses 8:28–29 is a summary of the story.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The fall and destruction of Ay

Yisrael conquered Ay

8:13a

So the forces were stationed

  • And Yehoshua and the leaders put the soldiers in their places.

  • So the soldiers went to the right positions.

So: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as So introduces the next event in the storyline. Often this word is translated as “and.”

the forces were stationed: The clause the forces were stationed indicates that Yehoshua (Joshua) and the leaders of Yisrael (Israel) arranged the army in their places to attack the soldiers of Ay (Ai).

8:13b

with the main camp to the north of the city and the rear guard to the west of the city.

  • The main camp was north of Ay and the rest of the soldiers went to the west.

  • The main army was north of Ay, and the other soldiers hid west of the city.

with the main camp to the north of the city: It may be clearer to begin a new sentence here. The main group of soldiers was in their camp north of Ay.

and the rear guard to the west of the city: The rear guard refers to the soldiers who hid west of Ay so that they could attack by surprise.

8:13c

And that night Yehoshua went into the valley.

  • But Yehoshua (Joshua) spent that night in the valley.

  • But that night Yehoshua stayed in the valley that was between the army and Ay (Ai).

And that night Yehoshua went into the valley: The phrase into the valley refers to the valley mentioned in 8:11c that was between the Israeli (Israelite) camp and the town of Ay. Yehoshua may have gone down into the valley so that he would know the best way to conduct the battle the next morning.8:13 Boling, p. 239.

title: Joshua 8:14
content:
Section 8:1–29 Yisrael (Israel) defeated Ay (Ai).

In chapter 7, Yisrael attacked Ay and the soldiers of Ay defeated them. They were discouraged but they repented of their sin. In chapter 8, God told Yehoshua (Joshua) to attack Ay again. This time, the Israelis (Israelites) were victorious and defeated Ay.

Verses 8:1–9 describe Yehoshua’s preparations to attack Ay, with details about the ambush. The soldiers in the ambush left by night ahead of the other soldiers. Verses 8:10–27 describe the movement of the soldiers, and the defeat of Ay. Verses 8:28–29 is a summary of the story.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The fall and destruction of Ay

Yisrael conquered Ay

8:14a

When the king of Ay saw the Israelis,

  • ¶ When the King of Ay saw the Israeli (Israelite) army,

  • ¶ But the king of Ay (Ai) saw Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis (Israelites).

When the king of Ay saw the Israelis: The King of Ay saw Yehoshua’s main army in its place north of the town, ready to attack the town.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

When the king of Ay saw the Israeli army

8:14b

he hurried out early in the morning with the men of the city

  • he and the people of his city got up early in the morning, and hurried out.

  • So he and his army went out early

he hurried out early in the morning with the men of the city: The phrases he and the men of the city refer to the same group of fighting men in Ay (Ai). They can be translated as one phrase. For example:

he and all the men of the town hurried (NIV)

he hurried out: The phrase he hurried out indicates that they went quickly.

8:14c

to engage them in battle at an appointed place overlooking the Aravah (Arabah).

  • They went to a place near the valley of the Yarden (Jordan) River, to attack the Israelis (Israelites).

  • to meet the Israelis at a place near the valley of the Yarden River and fight them there.

to engage them in battle: The phrase to engage them in battle indicates that the king of Ay intended to fight as he had done the day before.

at an appointed place overlooking the Aravah: The Hebrew text is more literally “at the meeting place near the Aravah.”

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

to the meeting place near the Aravah (NET)

to meet…at a certain place overlooking the Aravah (NIV)

toward the Yarden (Jordan) Valley to fight…at the same place as before (GNT)

The army of Ay (Ai) went toward the valley of the Yarden River. Some English versions include the implied information that the place was on the downhill slope toward the Yarden River. For example:

to the descent toward the Aravah (Arabah) (RSV)

on the slope facing the Aravah (NJB)

the Aravah: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as the Aravah refers to the valley of the Yarden River. This was east of the town of Ay. For example:

at a place overlooking the Yarden Valley (NLT)

8:14d

But he did not know that an ambush had been set up against him behind the city.

  • But the king did not know that there were more soldiers hiding behind the city.

  • But he didn’t realize that there were Israeli (Israelite) soldiers behind the city.

But he did not know that an ambush had been set up against him behind the city: The clause an ambush had been set up against him refers to the Israeli soldiers who hid to attack the town by surprise. The king of Ay (Ai) did not know about these soldiers.

behind the city: The phrase behind the city indicates the direction west of the town.

content:

Here are some other possible section headings:

The fall and destruction of Ay

Yisrael conquered Ay

8:15a

Yehoshua and all Yisrael let themselves be beaten back before them,

  • Yehoshua and his soldiers pretended to run away

  • Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israeli (Israelite) army ran away as if they were defeated.

The Hebrew connector that the BSB leaves untranslated but many English versions translate as “And” indicates the next event in the story.

Yehoshua and all Yisrael (Israel) let themselves be beaten back before them: Yehoshua and the Israeli soldiers pretended that the soldiers of Ay (Ai) were winning the battle by running away from them.

all Yisrael: The phrase all Yisrael refers to the Israeli soldiers.

8:15b

and they fled toward the wilderness.

  • toward the wilderness.

  • They ran toward the wilderness.

and they fled toward the wilderness: The word fled means “ran away.” The Israeli (Israelite) soldiers ran away towards the wilderness.

the wilderness: The wilderness refers to the uninhabited land east of Ay, between Ay and the Yarden (Jordan) River valley. Only a little vegetation grows in this area. Although some English versions use the word “desert,” this area is not sand. It is a rocky area that leads down to the Yarden River valley.

  • So the king of Ay called all his soldiers together to chase the Israelis.

  • So all the men of Ay (Ai) gathered together to chase the Israelis (Israelites).

Then all the men of Ay: The phrase all the men of Ay refers to the fighting men of Ay.

were summoned to pursue them: The phrase were summoned is a passive.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

the king called them together

they all gathered together

and they followed Yehoshua (Joshua) and were drawn away from the city.

  • As they chased Yehoshua, they were lured away from the city.

  • Yehoshua’s army kept running so that they could lead them further away from Ay (Ai).

and they followed Yehoshua: The phrase they followed Yehoshua implies that the soldiers of Ay chased the Israeli (Israelite) soldiers. It may be clearer to make this information explicit in some languages.

For example:

and as the army of Ay pursued Yehoshua and his army

were drawn away from the city: The Israeli army kept running away from the town so that the soldiers of Ay would go far away from it.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

they were lured away from the city (NIV)

they kept getting farther away from the city (GNT)

they were deceived into going far from the town

title: Joshua 8:17
content:
Section 8:1–29 Yisrael (Israel) defeated Ay (Ai).

Yisrael conquered Ay

8:17a

Not a man was left in Ay or Beyt-El (Bethel) who did not go out after Yisrael,

  • Not even one man was left in Ay or Beyt-El; they all ran out after Yisrael.

  • Every single fighting man in Ay (Ai) and Beyt-El went to chase the Israeli (Israelite) army.

Not a man was left in Ay or Beyt-El who did not go out after Yisrael (Israel): The clause Not a man was left refers to the men who were able to fight. Every fighting man went out.

Not a man was left…who did not go out: This use of Not and not is an example of a double negative in English. These two negative words together have an emphatic positive sense. In other words, every man went after Yisrael.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

every man in Ay went (GNT)

not a man stayed (NCV)

in Ay or Beyt-El (Bethel): The word Beyt-El is in the Hebrew text and in most English versions. Some versions omit the word Beyt-El because this town was not mentioned in the preceding verses.

It is recommended that you include the word Beyt-El. The towns of Ay and Beyt-El were close together. The people of Beyt-El went to help the men of their neighboring town.8:17 Hess, p. 166.

8:17b

leaving the city wide open while they pursued Yisrael.

  • The city was wide open; and they chased after Yisrael (Israel).

  • They left the city gates open when they left it to run after the Israelis (Israelites).

leaving the city wide open while they pursued Yisrael: The soldiers of Ay (Ai) ran out of the town gates and left them open, so that anyone could enter.

content:

Then Yahweh said to Yehoshua,

  • ¶ Then Yahweh told Yehoshua:

  • ¶ Then Yahweh commanded Yehoshua (Joshua):

Then: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as Then introduces a new event in the storyline.

Yahweh said to Yehoshua: The words that Yahweh told Yehoshua are a command.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

Yahweh told Yehoshua

Yahweh commanded Yehoshua

8:18b

“Hold out your battle lance toward Ay (Ai),

  • “Point your(sing) sword toward Ay,

  • “Stretch out your arm and point the spear that you are holding towards Ay.

Hold out your battle lance toward Ay: The clause Hold out your battle lance toward Ay indicates that Yehoshua (Joshua) must extend his arm to its full length with the javelin pointing towards Ay.

battle lance: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as battle lance refers to either a short sword used for thrusting and hunting, or a curved, crescent-shaped sword.8:18 Holladay, p. 156. These are some other ways that English versions have translated it:

sword (NRSV)

curved sword (NET)

spear (GNT)

You should choose a word that is similar in meaning to one of these terms and will be understood by your readers.

8:18c

for into your hand I will deliver the city.”

  • because I am going to help you(sing) defeat it.”

  • I will give you power to conquer it.”

8:18d

So Yehoshua held out his battle lance toward Ay,

  • So Yehoshua pointed his sword toward Ay.

  • Yehoshua did what Yahweh commanded him to do.

So: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as So introduces a new event in the storyline.

Yehoshua held out his battle lance toward Ay: Yehoshua obeyed the command that Yahweh gave him. If this repetition is not natural in your language, you can translate the meaning in another way. For example:

Yehoshua did as he was told (GNT)

So Yehoshua (Joshua) held out his spear (GW)

So Yehoshua did what Yahweh commanded him

content:
Section 8:1–29 Yisrael (Israel) defeated Ay (Ai).

Here are some other possible section headings:

The fall and destruction of Ay

Yisrael conquered Ay

8:19a-b

Scholars disagree about whether Yehoshua pointed his javelin toward Ay as a signal to the men who were hiding, or as a symbol of God’s action in defeating the town. It seems likely that it served both functions. It signaled the troops to advance, and it symbolized God’s power and victory over Ay. In 8:19 the focus is on the signal to the soldiers, but 8:26 shows that the outstretched arm is also a symbol of God’s victory.

8:19a

and as soon as he did so,

  • When Yehoshua (Joshua) stretched out his hand,

  • As soon as Yehoshua raised his hand,

and as soon as he did so: When Yehoshua stretched out his hand with the lance, it was a signal to the troops to attack. Some English versions make this explicit. For example:

When the Israelis (Israelites) who were in ambush saw this (NCV)

As soon as he did this, the men in the ambush rose quickly (NIV)

as soon as he lifted his hand, the men who had been hiding got up quickly (GNT)

8:19b

the men in ambush rose quickly from their position.

  • the soldiers who were hiding quickly got up.

  • the soldiers behind the city quickly came out from where they were hiding.

the men in ambush rose quickly from their position: This clause indicates that the soldiers who were hiding got up from their hiding places. They knew that the time had come to attack the town.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

the men who had been hiding got up quickly (GNT)

General Comment on 8:19a-b

In some languages it is more natural to change the order of 19a and b to reflect the order in the original language. For example:

19bThe soldiers rose quickly from where they were hiding 19aas soon as Yehoshua (Joshua) stretched out his hand

8:19c

They rushed forward, entered the city, captured it,

  • They ran into the city and captured it.

  • They entered the city through the open gates and captured it,

They rushed forward, entered the city, captured it: The soldiers ran through the open gates and captured the town.

8:19d

and immediately set it on fire.

  • Immediately they set the city on fire.

  • and they quickly set it on fire.

and immediately set it on fire: The soldiers quickly set fire to the houses and other things in the town.

Yisrael conquered Ay

8:20a

When the men of Ay turned and looked back,

  • When the soldiers of Ay looked behind them

  • Then the men of Ay (Ai) turned around and looked back toward Ay

When the men of Ay turned and looked back: The soldiers of Ay were chasing the Israeli (Israelite) soldiers. At some point, they turned around and looked back towards their town. The story does not say why they looked back. Perhaps they heard noise coming from the direction of the town.

8:20b

the smoke of the city was rising into the sky.

  • they saw that the sky was filled with smoke.

  • and saw smoke rising to the sky because the city was burning.

The Hebrew word that the BSB leaves untranslated but some English versions translate as “behold” is used to emphasize what happens next. You may have a word or particle in your language that is used for emphasis. Many English versions do not translate this word. It may be more natural to leave this word implicit.

the smoke of the city was rising into the sky: The clause the smoke of the city was rising into the sky indicates that the sky was filled with smoke because the town was burning.

8:20c

They could not escape in any direction,

  • But there was nowhere that they could run and escape

  • None of them had the courage to run away

They could not escape in any direction: The clause They could not escape in any direction indicates that the soldiers of Ay (Ai) were surrounded, and so could not escape. They were caught between the two parts of the Israeli (Israelite) army.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

There was no way for them to escape (GNT)

they had no chance to escape in any direction (NIV)

they had nowhere to go (NLT)

They could not escape: The Hebrew phrase that the BSB translates as They could not implies a loss of courage. Some English versions make this explicit. For example:

None of them had the courage to run (NJB)

were so shocked they were unable to flee (NET)

and the troops who had fled to the wilderness now became the pursuers.

  • because the Israelis (Israelites) who led them to the wilderness turned back on them.

  • because the Israelis who ran away toward the wilderness now turned around to attack them.

and the troops who had fled to the wilderness now became the pursuers: The clause and the troops who had fled to the wilderness refers to Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israeli (Israelite) soldiers who had pretended to run away. These are the same people referred to in 8:15.

now became the pursuers: The phrase that the BSB translates as became the pursuers is translated as “turned back against the pursuers” in most English versions. With either interpretation, the Israeli soldiers who had run away from the town now turned around and fought with the soldiers of Ay (Ai).

the pursuers: According to the BSB interpretation, the phrase the pursuers refers to Yehoshua and the Israeli soldiers who had pretended to run away. However, most English versions indicate that the pursuers refers to the soldiers of Ay.

title: Joshua 8:21
content:

The fall and destruction of Ay

Yisrael conquered Ay

8:21a

When Yehoshua and all Yisrael saw that the men in ambush had captured the city

  • Yehoshua and the Israeli (Israelite) army saw that the soldiers in hiding had taken the city

  • Yehoshua (Joshua) and his men saw that the other soldiers had captured the city

When The Hebrew conjunction that the BSB translates as When is used to give prominence to Yehoshua and his men and what they saw. You should translate the word with a connecting word that is most natural in your language. In some languages it may be most natural to omit them.

Yehoshua and all Yisrael (Israel) saw that the men in ambush had captured the city: The phrase Yehoshua and all Yisrael refers to Yehoshua and the soldiers who were with him.

the men in ambush: The phrase the men in ambush refers to the men who were hiding behind Ay (Ai).

had captured the city: The clause had captured the city indicates that the soldiers who were in hiding had attacked the town and defeated Ay.

8:21b

and that smoke was rising from it,

  • and that the sky was full of smoke because the city was burning.

  • and that smoke was rising from the city.

and that smoke was rising from it: The clause that smoke was rising from it indicates that the town was burning. The smoke was the visible signal of this for them.

8:21c

they turned around and struck down the men of Ay.

  • So they turned and attacked the soldiers of Ay (Ai).

  • Then they turned back towards the city and attacked the people of Ay.

they turned around: The clause they turned around indicates that Yehoshua (Joshua) and the soldiers with him stopped running away. They turned around to face the soldiers of Ay.

and struck down the men of Ay: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as struck is more literally “hit.” This is an idiom. It means that the Israeli (Israelite) soldiers attacked them.

title: Joshua 8:22
content:
Section 8:1–29 Yisrael (Israel) defeated Ay (Ai).

The fall and destruction of Ay

Yisrael conquered Ay

8:22a

Meanwhile, those in the ambush came out of the city against them,

  • The other Israeli (Israelite) soldiers came out of the city to help attack them.

  • The Israelis (Israelites) soldiers from the city also came to attack the Ay (Ai) soldiers.

Meanwhile: The Hebrew conjunction that the BSB translates as Meanwhile is used to add emphasis to what happens next. Use a connecting word that is most natural in your language. It may be most natural to leave the word implicit.

those in the ambush came out of the city against them: This clause indicates that the Israeli soldiers who captured the town now came out of it to help Yehoshua (Joshua) and the rest of the army attack the soldiers of Ay.

8:22b

and the men of Ay were trapped between the Israeli forces on both sides.

  • The men of Ay were caught between the armies of Yisrael (Israel).

  • So the Israeli army surrounded the army of Ay on both sides.

and the men of Ay were trapped between the Israeli (Israelite) forces on both sides: The clause were trapped between the Israeli forces on both sides indicates that the soldiers of Ay were surrounded by the Israeli army. It may be more natural to begin a new sentence here.

on both sides: This indicates that the Israeli army were on both sides of the men of Ay (Ai).

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

the soldiers of Ay were caught between the two groups of Israeli soldiers

the Israeli soldiers were around them in front and behind

the Israeli soldiers surrounded the soldiers of Ay

8:22c

So Yisrael (Israel) struck them down

  • The Israeli (Israelite) army attacked them

  • Then the Israeli soldiers killed them

So: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as So introduces the next event in the storyline. It may be clearer in some languages to begin another sentence here.

Yisrael struck them down: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as struck…down is more literally “hit.” This is an idiom. It means that the Israelis (Israelites) attacked them and killed them.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

Yisrael smote them (RSV)

Yisrael cut them down (NIV)

Yisrael (Israel) attacked them (NLT)

8:22d

until no survivor or fugitive remained.

  • and none of the men of Ay (Ai) was left alive. None of them escaped.

  • and all the Ay soldiers died. Not one of them escaped

until no survivor or fugitive remained: This clause indicates that the Israeli (Israelite) army killed all the soldiers of Ay. The Israelis (Israelites) did not let any of them escape and run away. They killed them all. For example:

until no one was left who survived or escaped (NRSV)

title: Joshua 8:23
content:
Section 8:1–29 Yisrael (Israel) defeated Ay (Ai).

Yisrael conquered Ay

8:23

But they took the king of Ay alive and brought him to Yehoshua.

  • But they did not kill the king of Ay. They captured him and brought him to Yehoshua.

  • except the king of Ay (Ai). They captured him and took him to Yehoshua (Joshua).

But they took the king of Ay alive and brought him to Yehoshua: The Israeli (Israelite) soldiers killed all the soldiers of Ay, but they did not kill the king. Instead they captured him and brought him to Yehoshua.

In Hebrew the object of the sentence, the king of Ay, comes first for emphasis. It may be more natural in some languages to move it to its normal place in the clause. For example:

But they took alive the king of Ay (NASB)

Another way to translate the sentence is by using a passive construction. This may allow you to put the king of Ay at the front of the sentence. For example:

But the king of Ay was taken alive (NRSV)

title: Joshua 8:24
content:
Section 8:1–29 Yisrael (Israel) defeated Ay (Ai).

In chapter 7, Yisrael attacked Ay and the soldiers of Ay defeated them. They were discouraged but they repented of their sin. In chapter 8, God told Yehoshua (Joshua) to attack Ay again. This time, the Israelis (Israelites) were victorious and defeated Ay.
