8:24a

When Yisrael had finished killing all the men of Ay

  • ¶ The Israeli (Israelite) soldiers killed all the Ay soldiers

  • ¶ The Israeli army finished killing all the fighting men of Ay (Ai)

When Yisrael (Israel): The word Yisrael refers to the Israeli army.

had finished killing: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as killing means that the Israeli army killed all the soldiers of Ay.

all the men of Ay: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as men refers to the men of Ay who had come out to fight the Israelis (Israelites).

8:24b

who had pursued them into the field and wilderness,

  • in the wilderness where they chased them.

  • in the wilderness to which the Israelis led them.

who had pursued them into the field and wilderness: In 8:15 Yehoshua (Joshua) and his army pretended to be afraid and ran away into the wilderness between Ay (Ai) and the Yarden (Jordan) River Valley. In 8:20 the soldiers of Ay chased them there. In this verse the roles are reversed. Yisrael chased the soldiers of Ay and killed them. This change of roles adds dramatic impact to this turning point in the story.

who had pursued them: Scholars and English versions differ on who who and them refer to.

  1. The word them refers to the Israeli (Israelite) soldiers and who refers to the soldiers of Ay. For example:

    When the Israeli army finished chasing and killing all the men of Ay in the open fields (NLT) (BSB, NLT, RSV, NIV, NASB, NCV, NJB, REB, GNT, CEV, KJV)

  2. The word them refers to the soldiers of Ay and who refers to the Israeli soldiers. For example:

    When Yisrael (Israel) had finished killing all the men of Ay who had chased them toward the desert (NET) (NET, GW, NJPS)

The Hebrew text is not clear on this issue. It is recommended that you follow option (1) along with the majority of English versions. As noted above, option (1) adds impact to this climactic turn of events where Yisrael is now the victor.

into the field and wilderness: The phrase the field and wilderness refers to the barren, uninhabited country that was mentioned in 8:15.

8:24c

and when every last one of them had fallen by the sword,

  • They killed them all. Not one of them lived.

  • They killed every single one of them.

and when every last one of them: The phrase every last one of them refers to the fighting men of Ay (Ai). This phrase indicates that not one of the soldiers of Ay was left. They were all dead.

had fallen by the sword: The Hebrew clause that the BSB translates as had fallen by the sword is more literally “had fallen by the mouth of the sword.” This is a Hebrew idiom. It means that the Israeli (Israelite) soldiers killed them.

This is a passive clause. The Israelis (Israelites) are the implied subject. The Israeli soldiers killed the men of Ay.

Here are some other ways to translate this Hebrew idiom:

they had been put to the sword (NIV)

they put them all to death (GW)

The Israelis killed every one of the enemy (GNT)

8:24d

all the Israelis returned to Ay (Ai) and put it to the sword as well.

  • Then the Israelis went back to Ay and killed everyone left there with their swords.

  • Then the Israeli (Israelite) army returned to Ay and killed everyone who was still alive in the city.

all the Israelis (Israelites) returned to Ay and put it to the sword as well: This clause indicates that the Israeli army killed the people who were still left in the town of Ay, the women and children.

A total of twelve thousand men and women fell that day—all the people of Ay.

  • All the people of Ay died that day. There were twelve thousand men and women.

  • Twelve thousand men and women from Ay (Ai) died that day. All the people of Ay died.

A total of twelve thousand men and women fell that day—all the people of Ay: This verse is a summary of the outcome of the battle between the Israelis (Israelites) and the citizens of Ay. The summary statement as introduced in Hebrew with the words “and it was.” The NLT introduces this summary statement with the word:

So (NLT)

Translate the summary statement in a way that is natural in your language.

A total of twelve thousand…all the people of Ay: The total population of Ay, including men and women, numbered twelve thousand people. All of these people died.

men and women fell that day: The phrase men and women fell that day refers to the people who died that day.

men and women: The phrase men and women refers to the men who had gone out to battle and the women who had stayed in the town.

  • Yehoshua kept holding out his sword

  • Yehoshua (Joshua) kept his arm stretched out with the spear in his hand pointed toward Ay (Ai)

The Hebrew conjunction that BSB leaves untranslated but many English versions translate as “For” introduces the reason why the Israelis (Israelites) could destroy Ay. You should indicate reason in a natural way in your language. It some languages it may be most natural to use no connecting word, as in many English versions.

Yehoshua did not draw back the hand: This clause indicates that Yehoshua continued to stretch out his arm.

that held his battle lance: Yehoshua stretched out his arm while he held the battle lance in his hand, and pointed the lance towards Ay.

battle lance: Translate the phrase battle lance the same way as you did in 8:18.

It was important that Yehoshua keep his arm stretched out and point the battle lance towards Ay until all the people of Ay were dead. This was what Yahweh commanded him to do. This was a symbol that it was Yahweh who won the victory over Ay and not the Israelis themselves.

8:26b

until he had devoted to destruction all who lived in Ay.

  • until they killed all the people of Ay.

  • until the Israeli (Israelite) army killed every person in the city.

until he had devoted to destruction all who lived in Ay (Ai): It may be necessary to make explicit the implied information that Yehoshua (Joshua) did not kill the people himself. The Israeli soldiers followed his orders and killed every Ay person. For example, you could say:

until the Israeli soldiers destroyed all the inhabitants of Ay

Many English versions use a passive verb. For example:

until all who lived in Ay had been destroyed (REB)

Translate this in a way that is natural in your language.

title: Joshua 8:27
content:
Section 8:1–29 Yisrael (Israel) defeated Ay (Ai).

In chapter 7, Yisrael attacked Ay and the soldiers of Ay defeated them. They were discouraged but they repented of their sin. In chapter 8, God told Yehoshua (Joshua) to attack Ay again. This time, the Israelis (Israelites) were victorious and defeated Ay.

Verses 8:1–9 describe Yehoshua’s preparations to attack Ay, with details about the ambush. The soldiers in the ambush left by night ahead of the other soldiers. Verses 8:10–27 describe the movement of the soldiers, and the defeat of Ay. Verses 8:28–29 is a summary of the story.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The fall and destruction of Ay

Yisrael conquered Ay

8:27a

Yisrael took for themselves only the cattle and plunder of that city,

  • But the Israelis took for themselves the livestock and the goods in the city,

  • But the Israelis (Israelites) kept the animals and other things from Ay (Ai),

Yisrael (Israel) took for themselves only the cattle and plunder of that city: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as only marks a contrast. They killed the people of Ay, but they took the cattle. Another way to mark this contrast is with the word “but.” For example:

But the Israelis took the animals and other possessions of the people of Ay (CEV)

Yisrael: The word Yisrael refers to the soldiers of Yisrael.

took for themselves: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as took for themselves is more literally “take.”

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

The Israelis kept for themselves the livestock and goods (GNT)

Yisrael did carry off for themselves the livestock and plunder (NIV)

the cattle: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as cattle is more literally “livestock.” It refer to cattle and to other domestic animals such as sheep and goats.

Here are some other ways to translate this word:

animals

domestic animals

plunder: The word plunder refers to the things in the town that were not burned when the army set fire to the town.

8:27b

as Yahweh had commanded Yehoshua (Joshua).

  • as Yahweh told Yehoshua.

  • because this is what Yahweh told Yehoshua they could do.

as Yahweh had commanded Yehoshua: This clause is a reminder about verse 8:2. At that time Yahweh told Yehoshua that the Israelis (Israelites) could take the goods and animals of Ay (Ai) for themselves.

title: Joshua 8:28
content:
Section 8:1–29 Yisrael (Israel) defeated Ay (Ai).

In chapter 7, Yisrael attacked Ay and the soldiers of Ay defeated them. They were discouraged but they repented of their sin. In chapter 8, God told Yehoshua (Joshua) to attack Ay again. This time, the Israelis (Israelites) were victorious and defeated Ay.

Verses 8:1–9 describe Yehoshua’s preparations to attack Ay, with details about the ambush. The soldiers in the ambush left by night ahead of the other soldiers. Verses 8:10–27 describe the movement of the soldiers, and the defeat of Ay. Verses 8:28–29 is a summary of the story.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The fall and destruction of Ay

Yisrael conquered Ay

8:28a

So Yehoshua burned Ay

  • So Yehoshua’s army burned the city of Ay.

  • Then Yehoshua (Joshua) and his army burned Ay (Ai)

So Yehoshua burned Ay: This indicates that Yehoshua gave orders to his soldiers to burn the town of Ay. He did not burn the town himself.

8:28b

and made it a permanent heap of ruins, a desolation to this day.

  • It has remained a pile of ruins, up to today.

  • and made it a heap of ruins. It is still like that now.

and made it a permanent heap of ruins: The Israelis (Israelites) burned the buildings and everything in Ay so that it was a pile of rubble. The name “Ay” in Hebrew means ruins. It is recommended that you add a footnote to explain that this is a word play. For example:

FOOTNOTE: The name Ay means “ruins”

a desolation to this day: The phrase this day refers to the time that the author wrote the book of Yehoshua (Joshua). At that time it was still a heap of ruins

General Comment on 8:28

Verse 8:28 is a summary statement about the battle of Ay (Ai). The burning of Ay is mentioned three times in this chapter. The first mention, in 8:8, is part of God’s command to Yisrael (Israel). The next mention, in 8:19, reports that the soldiers burned the town. The final mention in this verse is the summary of what Yisrael did to Ay. The Israelis burned Ay only once. Make sure that is clear in your translation.

title: Joshua 8:29
content:
Section 8:1–29 Yisrael (Israel) defeated Ay (Ai).

In chapter 7, Yisrael attacked Ay and the soldiers of Ay defeated them. They were discouraged but they repented of their sin. In chapter 8, God told Yehoshua (Joshua) to attack Ay again. This time, the Israelis (Israelites) were victorious and defeated Ay.

Verses 8:1–9 describe Yehoshua’s preparations to attack Ay, with details about the ambush. The soldiers in the ambush left by night ahead of the other soldiers. Verses 8:10–27 describe the movement of the soldiers, and the defeat of Ay. Verses 8:28–29 is a summary of the story.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The fall and destruction of Ay

Yisrael conquered Ay

8:29a

He hung the king of Ay on a tree until evening,

  • Yehoshua hung the king of Ay’s dead body on a pole and left him there until evening.

  • Yehoshua (Joshua) ordered his soldiers to kill the king of Ay (Ai) and hang his dead body on a tree.

He hung the king of Ay on a tree until evening: It is most likely that Yehoshua ordered his soldiers to kill the king. Then his dead body was hung on a tree. This was a common practice in the Ancient Near East.8:29 Hess, p. 170. The bodies of defeated enemies were hung up as an example to others of what might happen to them.

until evening: The phrase until evening means until the sun went down.

8:29b

and at sunset Yehoshua commanded that

  • When the sun went down, Yehoshua gave the order

  • At sunset, Yehoshua commanded his soldiers

and at sunset: It may be more natural to begin a new sentence here. For example:

When the sun was setting

Yehoshua (Joshua) commanded: It may be necessary to make explicit to whom Yehoshua gave the command. He commanded some of his soldiers. For example:

Yehoshua told his soldiers

8:29c

they take down the body from the tree

  • to take the king’s dead body down from the tree.

  • to take his body down.

that they take down the body from the tree: The Israeli (Israelite) soldiers took the dead body of the king down from the tree on which it was hanging.

8:29d

and throw it down at the entrance of the city gate.

  • They threw it in the entrance of the city

  • He told them to throw it down near the city gate.

and throw it down: The phrase throw it indicates that the soldiers threw down the corpse of the king.

at the entrance of the city gate: The phrase at the entrance of the city gate indicates a place in front of the town gates. A wall enclosed the town and people entered and left the town through the town gate.

8:29e

And over it they raised a large pile of rocks, which remains to this day.

  • and made a large pile of stones over it. That pile is still there today.

  • Then they piled large stones in a mound over it. The pile of stones is still there now.

And over it they raised a large pile of rocks: The clause over it they raised a large pile of rocks indicates that the Israeli (Israelite) soldiers piled stones over the king’s dead body so that it was covered up.

which remains to this day: The pile of stones was still there in front of Ay (Ai) at the time that the author wrote the book of Yehoshua (Joshua).

title: Joshua 8:30
content:
Section 8:30–35 Yehoshua (Joshua) read the law of Mosheh (Moses) to the Israelis (Israelites).

In this section the people of Yisrael (Israel) built an altar to Yahweh and made sacrifices to him. Yehoshua had them write the law of Mosheh on stone tablets. Then all the people assembled at Mount Eyval (Ebal) and Mount Gerazim while Yehoshua read the law aloud to them. He read all of its blessings and its curses.

Before they crossed the Yarden (Jordan) River, Mosheh foretold this event. He gave them detailed instructions for how they should do this in Deuteronomy 27:1–13. Now that the Israelis were well established in the land of Kena’an (Canaan) they followed the instructions of Mosheh.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Reading the law at Mount Eyval and Mount Gerazim

Yehoshua reads the blessings and the curses to the people

8:30a

At that time Yehoshua built an altar on Mount Eyval

  • ¶ Then Yehoshua built an altar on Mount Eyval

  • ¶ Some time later, Yehoshua (Joshua) told the Israelis (Israelites) to build an altar on Mount Eyval (Ebal)

At that time Yehoshua built an altar on Mount Eyval: There was probably a period of several days between the fight against Ay (Ai), and the time when Yehoshua built the altar to Yahweh.8:30 Bratcher and Newman, p. 119. If the phrase At that time suggests that this happened immediately after Ay, it may be better to add a phrase such as:

some time later

on another day

Yehoshua: The Hebrew text says that Yehoshua built the altar. It is most likely that he told some of the Israelis to build the altar for him. You may want to make this explicit. For example:

he told some of his men, “Build an altar for offering sacrifices to the Lord” (CEV)

built an altar: This altar was made by piling up stones. It is different from the altar of burnt offering that was inside the tent of meeting. That altar was made of acacia wood overlaid with bronze. See Exodus 38:1–7.

Verse 8:31 says that the altar was made of stones that were not cut with a tool. Do not use a word for built in your language which implies that tools were used.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

made an altar

piled stones up as an altar

on Mount Eyval (Ebal): The altar was on the top of Mount Eyval. It was not buried inside it. The Hebrew preposition that the BSB translates as on is translated that way by most English versions. Use a preposition that is appropriate in your language.

Mount Eyval: Mount Eyval is about 32 kilometers north of Ay (Ai).8:30 Boling, p. 247.

8:30b

to Yahweh, the God of Yisrael (Israel),

  • to Yahweh, the God of Yisrael.

to Yahweh, the God of Yisrael: They built the altar so that they could make sacrifices to Yahweh on it. Yahweh is given this extended title for emphasis. You should translate this phrase consistently with the decisions you have made about translating the name of God throughout the Old Testament.

title: Joshua 8:31
content:
Section 8:30–35 Yehoshua (Joshua) read the law of Mosheh (Moses) to the Israelis (Israelites).

In this section the people of Yisrael (Israel) built an altar to Yahweh and made sacrifices to him. Yehoshua had them write the law of Mosheh on stone tablets. Then all the people assembled at Mount Eyval (Ebal) and Mount Gerazim while Yehoshua read the law aloud to them. He read all of its blessings and its curses.

Before they crossed the Yarden (Jordan) River, Mosheh foretold this event. He gave them detailed instructions for how they should do this in Deuteronomy 27:1–13. Now that the Israelis were well established in the land of Kena’an (Canaan) they followed the instructions of Mosheh.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Reading the law at Mount Eyval and Mount Gerazim

Yehoshua reads the blessings and the curses to the people

8:31a

just as Mosheh the servant of Yahweh had commanded the Israelis.

  • This was what Mosheh, Yahweh’s servant, commanded the Israelis.

  • He followed the instructions that Mosheh (Moses), the servant of Yahweh, gave the Israelis (Israelites)

just as Mosheh the servant of Yahweh had commanded the Israelis: Mosheh gave the Israelis this command in Deuteronomy 27:1–13. It may be clearer to translate this dependent clause as an independent sentence. For example, you could say:

This is what Mosheh, the servant of Yahweh, commanded the Israelis to do

Mosheh the servant of Yahweh: Translate the title servant of Yahweh as you did in 1:1.

8:31b

He built it according to what is written in the Book of the Law of Mosheh:

  • Yehoshua (Joshua) obeyed these instructions from the book of Mosheh’s teachings which say:

  • in the law of Mosheh. It says there:

He built it according to what is written in the Book of the Law of Mosheh (Moses): The phrase the Book of the Law of Mosheh refers to Deuteronomy, where these instructions were written down.

the Book of the Law of Mosheh: The phrase Law of Mosheh refers to the teachings, or instructions, of Mosheh.

8:31c

“an altar of uncut stones on which no iron tool has been used.”

  • “The altar must be made from stones that have not been cut or shaped by an iron tool.”

  • “Make an altar from stones that are uncut and that nobody has touched with iron tools.”

an altar of uncut stones on which no iron tool has been used: There is implied information. Yehoshua (Joshua) made an altar of unhewn stones. It may be more natural to state this information as an independent sentence. For example:

Yehoshua built an altar out of stones that had not been cut with an iron tool

uncut stones: The phrase uncut stones can also be translated as “unhewn stones.” It indicates that no one used any tool to chisel the stones or cut them up. An “altar of uncut stones” is mentioned in Exodus 20:25 and in Deuteronomy 27:5.

no iron tool has been used: The clause no iron tool has been used indicates that no person used a tool to cut or shape the stones.

8:31d

And on it they offered burnt offerings to Yahweh,

  • On the altar they offered to Yahweh burnt offerings

  • Then the Israelis (Israelites) made sacrifices that are completely burnt on the altar to Yahweh,

And on it they offered burnt offerings to Yahweh: Probably the priests offered the sacrifices on behalf of the Israelis. It may be more natural in some languages to make this explicit. For example:

and the priests offered burnt offerings to Yahweh on the altar

burnt offerings: The phrase burnt offerings refers to animals that were totally burned up as an atonement for sins. See Leviticus 1:1–17 for more information about burnt offerings.

8:31e

and they sacrificed peace offerings.

  • and fellowship offerings.

  • and they made sacrifices of fellowship with Yahweh.

and they sacrificed peace offerings: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as sacrificed describes the same action as “offered burnt offerings” in 8:31d. It may be clearer in some languages to use the same verb to refer to both sacrifices.

peace offerings: The phrase peace offerings refers to sacrifices in which only part of the animal was burned. The rest of the animal was eaten by the worshipers.8:31 Bratcher and Newman, p. 119. Many English versions refer to these offerings as “fellowship offerings.” The person who ate the animal had fellowship with Yahweh. See Leviticus 3:1–17 for more information about peace offerings.

title: Joshua 8:32
content:
Section 8:30–35 Yehoshua (Joshua) read the law of Mosheh (Moses) to the Israelis (Israelites).

In this section the people of Yisrael (Israel) built an altar to Yahweh and made sacrifices to him. Yehoshua had them write the law of Mosheh on stone tablets. Then all the people assembled at Mount Eyval (Ebal) and Mount Gerazim while Yehoshua read the law aloud to them. He read all of its blessings and its curses.

Before they crossed the Yarden (Jordan) River, Mosheh foretold this event. He gave them detailed instructions for how they should do this in Deuteronomy 27:1–13. Now that the Israelis were well established in the land of Kena’an (Canaan) they followed the instructions of Mosheh.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Reading the law at Mount Eyval and Mount Gerazim

Yehoshua reads the blessings and the curses to the people

8:32a

And there in the presence of the Israelis,

  • There on Mount Eyval, while the Israelis watched,

  • At that place, while the Israelis (Israelites) were there,

And there: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as there refers to the site of the altar on Mount Eyval (Ebal). The ceremony at this place represents a climax for Yisrael (Israel) because it fulfilled Mosheh’s (Moses’) command in Deuteronomy 27.

in the presence of the Israelis: The phrase in the presence of the Israelis indicates that Yehoshua (Joshua) wrote a copy of the law while all the Israelis watched him.

8:32b

Yehoshua inscribed on the stones a copy of the law of Mosheh,

  • he wrote a copy of the law on some flat stones.

  • Yehoshua wrote on stones a copy of the teachings of Mosheh.

Yehoshua inscribed on the stones a copy of the law of Mosheh: The word that the BSB translates as Yehoshua is literally the pronoun “he.” Use the word that would be most natural in your language.

the stones: In Deuteronomy 27:2–4 Mosheh told Yehoshua to write the law of Mosheh on large stones which they should first coat with plaster. The term the stones does not refer to the stones used to build the altar.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

he wrote on some flat stones

he chose some flat stones and wrote on them

a copy of the law of Mosheh (Moses): The stones were not large enough for the entire law of Mosheh, which is Genesis through Deuteronomy. Yehoshua (Joshua) copied some part of the law of Mosheh onto the stones, perhaps the Ten Commandments.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

he copied parts of the book of the Law of Mosheh onto the stones (CEV)

8:32c

which he had written.

  • This was the law which Mosheh wrote for them.

  • These are the teachings that Mosheh gave them.

which he had written: It is not clear in the Hebrew text whether the pronoun he refers to Yehoshua or to Mosheh. It is recommended that you translate the pronoun he as referring to Mosheh, as in the NET, NJB, NJPS, NLT, and GNT.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

which Mosheh (Moses) had written (GNT)

the instructions Mosheh had given them (NLT)

title: Joshua 8:33
content:
Section 8:30–35 Yehoshua (Joshua) read the law of Mosheh (Moses) to the Israelis (Israelites).

In this section the people of Yisrael (Israel) built an altar to Yahweh and made sacrifices to him. Yehoshua had them write the law of Mosheh on stone tablets. Then all the people assembled at Mount Eyval (Ebal) and Mount Gerazim while Yehoshua read the law aloud to them. He read all of its blessings and its curses.

Before they crossed the Yarden (Jordan) River, Mosheh foretold this event. He gave them detailed instructions for how they should do this in Deuteronomy 27:1–13. Now that the Israelis were well established in the land of Kena’an (Canaan) they followed the instructions of Mosheh.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Reading the law at Mount Eyval and Mount Gerazim

Yehoshua reads the blessings and the curses to the people

8:33a

All Yisrael, foreigners and citizens alike, with their elders, officers, and judges,

  • All the Israelis, foreigners and native-born, together with their leaders and officers and judges,

  • Then all the Israelis (Israelites), those who had Israeli (Israelite) parents and those who were foreigners living among them, along with the elders, officers, and judges,

The Hebrew connector that the BSB leaves untranslated but many English versions translate as “and” indicates the next event of the story.

All Yisrael (Israel), foreigners and citizens alike: The phrase All Yisrael indicates that every Israeli was present at the ceremony.

foreigners and citizens alike: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as foreigners refers to foreigners who lived in the Israeli community.8:33 Howard, p. 216.

The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as citizens refers to Israelis who were descendants of Avraham (Abraham), Yitshak (Isaac) and Ya’akov (Jacob).

Here are some other ways to translate these two words:

resident foreigners and native Israelis (NET)

aliens and citizens (NIV)

foreigners and native-born (NLT)

with their elders, officers, and judges: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as elders refers to the leaders of tribes and families who represented their tribe on special occasions.8:33 Woudstra, p. 139.

officers: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as officers refers to people who had both military and administrative responsibilities.8:33 Woudstra, p. 64, footnote 1.

Here are some other ways to translate this term:

leaders (NET)

officials (NIV)

judges: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as judges refers to people who judged disputes between Israelis (Israelites). See Exodus 18:17–26 where Mosheh (Moses) first appointed judges.

8:33b

stood on both sides of the ark of the covenant of Yahweh facing the Levitical priests

  • stood in two groups. One group stood on each side of the ark facing the priests, the Levites.

  • were divided into two groups. Each group faced inward toward the ark.They were facing the priests,

stood on both sides of the ark of the covenant of Yahweh: The clause stood on both sides of the ark indicates that the Israelis stood in two groups facing each other. The ark was in-between them.

the ark of the covenant of Yahweh: The ark was a wooden box that was a sign of God’s presence. The term ark has different descriptive phrases attached to it in different contexts. In this verse it is called ark of the covenant of Yahweh. This emphasizes that inside it were the stone tablets on which Mosheh wrote the Ten commandments, the symbol of Yahweh’s covenant with Yisrael (Israel).

facing the Levitical priests: Two Levitical priests stood at each end of the ark, carrying it on poles over their shoulders. The two groups of Israelis faced the ark and the priests who carried it.

Levitical priests: The Hebrew phrase that the BSB translates as Levitical priests is literally “the priests, the Levites.” The priests were descendants of Levi, and belonged to the tribe of Levi.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

the priests, the Levites

the priests of the Levi tribe

It is also possible to say just “the priests,” and put the literal translation in a footnote. See how you translated this term in Joshua 3:3.

priests: The priests were people who offered sacrifices to God on behalf of the people. You should translate this the same way you do in the New Testament. See, for example, Mark 1:44.

8:33c

who carried it.

  • The priests were carrying the ark of Yahweh’s covenant.

  • the Levites who held the ark of the covenant of Yahweh.

who carried it: It was the responsibility of the priests to carry the ark of the covenant.

8:33d

Half of the people stood in front of Mount Gerizim and half of them in front of Mount Eyval (Ebal),

  • Half of the people stood on the slope of Mount Gerizim and the other half on the slope of Mount Eyval.

  • Half of the people stood in front of Mount Gerizim and half stood in front of Mount Eyval.

Half of the people stood in front of Mount Gerizim and half of them in front of Mount Eyval: The phrase half of them indicates that the Israelis (Israelites) were divided into two large groups.

in front of Mount Gerizim and…in front of Mount Eyval: The Israelis stood in the Valley of Shekem (Shechem), which was between the two mountains, Mount Gerizim and Mount Eyval. One group stood facing Mount Gerizim and the other group stood facing Mount Eyval.

In Deuteronomy 27:12–13 Mosheh (Moses) told the people to stand “on” Mount Gerizim and Mount Eyval, whereas this verse uses the words in front of. Because the Israelis followed the commands that Mosheh gave them, it may be that they stood on the slopes of the two mountains, facing in the direction of the opposite mountain. For example:

on the upper slopes of Mount Gerizim and Mount Eyval (NJB)

8:33e

as Mosheh the servant of Yahweh had commanded earlier,

  • This was what Mosheh, the servant of Yahweh originally commanded them.

  • This was done according to the instructions that Mosheh, Yahweh’s servant, previously gave them.

as Mosheh the servant of Yahweh had commanded earlier: This indicates that the Israelis (Israelites) obeyed the instructions that Mosheh gave them before he died.

earlier: The word earlier refers to the time when Mosheh gave the Israelis this command in Deuteronomy 27:12–13. For example:

the Lord’s servant Mosheh (Moses) had earlier commanded the people (NCV)

General Comment on 8:33

This is a long and complicated verse, and you will have to think about it carefully. It is recommended that you begin a new sentence at 8:33d.

8:33f

to bless the people of Yisrael (Israel).

  • Mosheh told Yehoshua (Joshua) and the priests to bless the Israelis.

  • This was the way that they should bless the Israelis.

title: Joshua 8:34
content:
Section 8:30–35 Yehoshua (Joshua) read the law of Mosheh (Moses) to the Israelis (Israelites).

In this section the people of Yisrael (Israel) built an altar to Yahweh and made sacrifices to him. Yehoshua had them write the law of Mosheh on stone tablets. Then all the people assembled at Mount Eyval (Ebal) and Mount Gerazim while Yehoshua read the law aloud to them. He read all of its blessings and its curses.

Before they crossed the Yarden (Jordan) River, Mosheh foretold this event. He gave them detailed instructions for how they should do this in Deuteronomy 27:1–13. Now that the Israelis were well established in the land of Kena’an (Canaan) they followed the instructions of Mosheh.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Reading the law at Mount Eyval and Mount Gerazim

Yehoshua reads the blessings and the curses to the people

8:34a

Afterward, Yehoshua read aloud all the words of the law—the blessings and the curses—

  • Then Yehoshua read the whole Law of Mosheh, including the blessings and the curses

  • Then Yehoshua (Joshua) read out loud the entire teachings of Mosheh (Moses), including the blessings and the curses

Afterward: The word Afterward refers to the time after the people arranged themselves in the two groups. Many English versions use the word “then” to signal this next event. Use the connecting word that is most natural in your language to indicate this.

Yehoshua read aloud all the words of the law: The clause Yehoshua read aloud all the words of the law indicates that Yehoshua read aloud the entire teachings of Mosheh.

the blessings and the curses: The phrase the blessings and the curses refers to the words of Mosheh in Deuteronomy 27:12–28:68. Mosheh said that they would receive blessings if they obeyed Yahweh, but they would experience curses if they did not obey him.

8:34b

according to all that is written in the Book of the Law.

  • as Mosheh wrote them down.

  • as they are written in the book of the law.

according to all that is written in the Book of the Law: The phrase according to all that is written in the Book of the Law repeats 8:34a in different words. The information that Yehoshua (Joshua) read the entire Book of the Law is repeated to emphasize its importance. Find a way to emphasize the reading of the law that is natural in your language.

title: Joshua 8:35
content:
Section 8:30–35 Yehoshua (Joshua) read the law of Mosheh (Moses) to the Israelis (Israelites).

In this section the people of Yisrael (Israel) built an altar to Yahweh and made sacrifices to him. Yehoshua had them write the law of Mosheh on stone tablets. Then all the people assembled at Mount Eyval (Ebal) and Mount Gerazim while Yehoshua read the law aloud to them. He read all of its blessings and its curses.

Before they crossed the Yarden (Jordan) River, Mosheh foretold this event. He gave them detailed instructions for how they should do this in Deuteronomy 27:1–13. Now that the Israelis were well established in the land of Kena’an (Canaan) they followed the instructions of Mosheh.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Reading the law at Mount Eyval and Mount Gerazim

Yehoshua reads the blessings and the curses to the people

8:35a

There was not a word of all that Mosheh had commanded

  • There was not one of the words of Mosheh

  • Yehoshua (Joshua) read every one of Mosheh’s (Moses’) commandments

There was not a word of all that Mosheh had commanded: The phrase not a word of all that Mosheh had commanded emphasizes again that Yehoshua read all Mosheh’s teaching for the Israelis (Israelites). This information is given again in this verse to emphasize how important the reading of the law was.

8:35b

that Yehoshua failed to read before the whole assembly of Yisrael (Israel),

  • which Yehoshua did not read to all the people of Yisrael.

  • while the entire population of the Israelis listened.

that Yehoshua failed to read before the whole assembly of Yisrael: In the previous verse, the information that Yehoshua read the entire law is stated in a positive manner. Now it is restated using a double negative for extra emphasis. In some languages a double negative may convey a wrong meaning. Use a natural means to emphasize that Yehoshua read the entire law to the Israelis. For example, the GNT states 8:35a-b in a positive way:

Every one of the commandments of Mosheh was read by Yehoshua to the whole gathering (GNT)

before the whole assembly of Yisrael: The phrase before the whole assembly of Yisrael indicates that Yehoshua (Joshua) read Mosheh’s (Moses’) teachings while all the Israelis stood and listened.

8:35c

including the women, the little ones, and the foreigners who lived among them.

  • All the people listened, including the women and the children and the foreigners who lived with them.

  • This included the women and children, as well as the foreigners living among them.

including the women, the little ones: The phrase including the women, the little ones indicates that women and children were present and listened while Yehoshua read the law. Women and children were not present at every gathering. The author includes this information to show that the entire population of Yisrael (Israel) listened while Yehoshua read aloud the law.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

including the women and the children

and the foreigners who lived among them: The foreigners were foreigners who lived with the Israelis (Israelites). They were not Israelis by birth.8:35 Howard, p. 216–217.

General Comment on verse 8:35

It may be more natural in some languages to reorder the parts of this verse so that 8:35c is first, as in the NCV:

35bAll the Israelis were gathered together--35cmen, women and children, along with the non-Israelites who lived among them. 35aYehoshua (Joshua) read every command that Mosheh (Moses) had given. (NCV)

title: Joshua 9:1
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

Paragraph 9:1–2

This paragraph forms an introduction to the story of this chapter. It tells how a group of kings from the nearby towns decided to fight together against the Israelis. Their action contrasts with how the Givonim deceived the Israelis.

9:1a

Now when news of this reached all the kings west of the Yarden (Jordan)—

  • ¶ All the kings who ruled the cities west of the Yarden River heard about the Israelis (Israelites).

  • ¶ When all the kings west of the Yarden River heard that the Israelis lost a battle at Ay (Ai)

Now when news of this reached: The words of this are not included in the Hebrew text. The Hebrew text says only, “When all the kings heard.” In some languages it may be clearer to add words about what the kings heard.

These kings heard something that made them decide to join forces and attack the Israelis. Probably they heard how Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis were defeated in the first battle of Ay. Because they saw that it was possible for the Israelis to lose a battle, they decided to attack them.9:1 Howard, p. 218; Hess, p. 175.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

When the kings heard about the Israelis they gathered together

When the kings heard that the Israelis lost a battle against Ay, they gathered together

all the kings west of the Yarden (Jordan): The phrase the kings west of the Yarden refers to the kings who ruled towns on the west side of the Yarden River. It may be clearer to add the implied information in this clause. For example:

the kings of the towns beyond the Yarden River

the kings of the towns west of the Yarden River

west of the Yarden: The phrase west of the Yarden refers to the region west of the Yarden River.

9:1b

those in the hill country, the foothills, and all along the coast of the Great Sea toward Levanon (Lebanon)

  • They are the kings in the mountains and the lower slopes and on the Mediterranean seacoast northwards toward Levanon,

  • (they are the kings in the mountain country, the foothills to the west, and on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea up north towards Levanon,

those in the hill country: The term hill country refers to the central mountain range of Palestine.

the foothills: The term foothills refers to the western side of the central mountain range. It is a rocky plateau that is higher than the land near the Mediterranean Sea, but lower than the hill country.

Here are some other ways to translate this word:

western foothills (NIV)

the lowland (RSV)

and all along the coast of the Great Sea: The phrase Great Sea refers to the Mediterranean Sea.

toward Levanon (Lebanon): Levanon was a small but powerful kingdom to the north of Palestine. The phrase toward Levanon indicates that some of these kings were from the north, near the kingdom of Levanon.

9:1c

(the Hitim (Hittites), Amorim (Amorites), Kena’anim (Canaanites), Perizim (Perizzites), Hivim (Hivites), and Yevusim (Jebusites))—

  • namely, the kings of the Hitim, Amorim, Kena’anim, Perizim, Hivim, and Yevusim.

  • the kings who ruled the Het (Heth) people, the Amor people, the Kena’an (Canaan) people, the Periz people, the Hiw people, and the Yabus people),

the Hitim, Amorim, Kena’anim, Perizim, Hivim, and Yevusim: These six groups of people were mentioned in 3:10. You should translate them the same way you did there. These people are inhabitants of the land of Kena’an. In Deuteronomy 20:16–18 Yahweh told the Israelis (Israelites) to destroy these nations with his help.

General Comment on 9:1

This is a long sentence with a long and complicated subject. It may be clearer to break it into two sentences. For example:

1aThere were many people who lived on the west side of the Yarden (Jordan) River, 1bin the hill country, and in the foothills, and along the coast of the Mediterranean Sea and up north toward Levanon. 1cThe kings of the Hitti people, the Amor people, the Kena’an people, the Periz people, the Hiw people, and the Yabus people 1aheard about the Israelis.

title: Joshua 9:2
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

Paragraph 9:1–2

This paragraph forms an introduction to the story of this chapter. It tells how a group of kings from the nearby towns decided to fight together against the Israelis. Their action contrasts with how the Givonim deceived the Israelis.

9:2

they came together to wage war against Yehoshua and Yisrael (Israel).

  • Then they agreed to join together in fighting Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israeli (Israelite) army.

  • they got together and agreed to fight against Yehoshua and the Israelis (Israelites).

they came together: The clause they came together indicates that the kings and their armies joined as one group to fight the Israelis.

together: The Hebrew phrase that the BSB translates as together is more literally “one mouth.” This means that all the kings agreed to do this.

to wage war against Yehoshua and Yisrael: The clause to wage war against Yehoshua and Yisrael indicates that the kings agreed that they and their armies would fight against Yehoshua and his army, the Israelis.

title: Joshua 9:3
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:3a

But the people of Giveon, having heard

  • ¶ But when the people in the city of Giveon heard the news

  • ¶ The people of Giveon City heard

But: The Hebrew conjunction that the BSB translates as But shows that there is a contrast between what the six kings did and what the Givonim (Gibeonites) did. Show this contrast in a natural way in your language.

the people of Giveon (Gibeon), having heard: The phrase people of Giveon refers to the people who lived in the town of Giveon. They are also referred to as “Givonim.” Giveon town was about twenty kilometers west of Ay (Ai) town.9:3 Howard, p. 223.

9:3b

what Yehoshua (Joshua) had done to Yeriho (Jericho) and Ay,

  • that Yehoshua and the Israelis (Israelites) defeated the cities of Yeriho and Ay,

  • how Yehoshua defeated Yeriho and Ay.

what Yehoshua had done to Yeriho and Ay: The clause what Yehoshua had done to Yeriho and Ay refers to Yehoshua’s victories over these two towns. The Israeli (Israelite) army, with Yehoshua as their leader, defeated the armies of both Yeriho and Ay.

title: Joshua 9:4
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:4a-b

acted deceptively and set out as envoys: There is a Hebrew phrase near the beginning of this verse, which the BSB leaves implicit, that can be translated as “also they.” This phrase contrasts the Givonim with the kings mentioned in 9:1–2. Translate this phrase with whatever lexical or grammatical means is most natural to show this contrast.

9:4a

acted deceptively

  • they decided to deceive the Israelis (Israelites).

  • So they used a deception.

acted deceptively: The phrase acted deceptively indicates that the Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

they deceived the Israelis

they did a trick/deception/scheme

9:4b

and set out as envoys,

  • They packed up food for a journey

  • They got together some food

set out as envoys: There is a textual issue with the phrase set out as envoys.

  1. Some Hebrew manuscripts have a verb that means “made ready provisions.” For example:

    they provided themselves with supplies (NJB) (NJB, RSV, NRSV, ESV, NAB, NCV, NET, GNT)

  2. The Hebrew Masoretic Text uses a verb that occurs only here. Some scholars think this verb means “to act as an ambassador,” but the meaning is uncertain. The NIV is an example of an English version that follows this interpretation:

    they went as a delegation (NIV) (BSB, NIV, CEV, GW, NASB, NLT, BSB)

It is recommended that you follow option (1) along with a majority of English versions.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

they packed food to take on a journey

They went and got some food (GNT)

9:4c

carrying on their donkeys worn-out sacks

  • and put it in old sacks for their donkeys to carry,

  • and used old bags to put it in on their donkeys.

carrying on their donkeys: The phrase on their donkeys means that they carried the sacks on the backs of their donkeys.

donkeys: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as donkeys is translated “asses” in some English versions. The word “ass” is from old English.9:4 The word “ass” can have vulgar connotations in English.

worn-out sacks: The phrase worn-out sacks indicates that they used old sacks to carry things on their donkeys. The sacks were worn thin from much use.

9:4d

and old wineskins, cracked and mended.

  • They put wine in old wineskins that were torn and mended.

  • Their leather bags for wine were old and torn and mended.

and old wineskins, cracked and mended: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as wineskins refers to leather bags that were used to carry wine. The wineskins, like the sacks, were old and in poor condition.

title: Joshua 9:5
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:5a

They put worn, patched sandals on their feet and threadbare clothing on their bodies,

  • They put worn and patched sandals on their feet and wore worn-out clothes.

  • They wore sandals that were old and patched, and clothes that were worn-out.

They put worn, patched sandals on their feet and threadbare clothing on their bodies: It may be more natural in some languages to translate this as an independent sentence. For example:

They put on ragged clothes and worn-out sandals that had been mended (GNT)

The men put worn and patched sandals on their feet and wore old clothes (NIV)

9:5b

and their whole supply of bread was dry and moldy.

  • All their bread was dried out and hard.

  • Their bread was dry and crumbly.

and their whole supply of bread was dry and moldy: The phrase their whole supply of bread refers to the bread they took with them to eat.

moldy: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as moldy is rarely used. Bible scholars and the English versions disagree about its meaning.

  1. It means crumbly or hard rather than moldy. This seems likely because mold requires moisture for growth, and the climate in Palestine is very dry.9:5 Howard, p. 223. For example:

    And all their provisions were dry and crumbly. (ESV) (ESV, GW, NAB, NASB, NET, NJB, NJPS, REB, CEV)

  2. It means moldy. For example:

    All the bread of their food supply was dry and moldy. (NIV) (BSB, NIV, RSV, NCV, NLT, GNT)

It is difficult to know the meaning of this word because it is rare. It occurs only three times in the Old Testament (Joshua 9:5, 12, and I Kings 13:4). Both options are used by English versions. Even though Palestine generally had a dry climate, there was also a wet season and old bread could get moldy. Either option is acceptable.

title: Joshua 9:6
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:6a

They went to Yehoshua in the camp at Gilgal

  • ¶ Then they went to meet Yehoshua in the Israeli (Israelite) camp at Gilgal,

  • ¶ When the Givonim (Gibeonites) arrived at the Israeli camp at Gilgal,

They went to Yehoshua (Joshua) in the camp at Gilgal: After the Givoni (Gibeonite) men got their things together, they traveled to the Israeli camp at Gilgal to talk to Yehoshua.

Gilgal: Gilgal was first mentioned in 4:19. You should translate it the same way you did there.

9:6b

and said to him and the men of Yisrael (Israel),

  • and said to Yehoshua and the Israeli leaders:

  • they spoke to Yehoshua and the Israeli leaders and said:

and said to him and the men of Yisrael: The Givoni men met with Yehoshua and the Israelis (Israelites). The Hebrew phrase that the BSB translates as men of Yisrael is more literally “man of Yisrael.” This is a collective term that is frequently used for the Israeli (Israelite) army.9:6 Howard, p. 224. The phrase men of Yisrael probably refers to the leaders of the Israelis, rather than to all the male Israelis.

9:6c

“We have come from a distant land; please make a treaty with us.”

  • “We(excl) have come from a country that is far from here. Please make(plur) a peace treaty with us(excl).”

  • “We have come from a distant land. We want you to make a treaty with us.”

We have come from a distant land: The Givonim (Gibeonites) claimed that they had traveled a long distance and lived far away from the land of Kena’an (Canaan).

We: The word We is exclusive. It refers to the Givonim and not to the Israelis.

please make a treaty with us: The clause make a treaty with us is a request for the Israelis to make a treaty or agreement of friendship with them. A treaty is a formal agreement between two people or groups of people.

title: Joshua 9:7
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:7a

But the men of Yisrael (Israel) said to the Hivim (Hivites),

  • The Israelis said to the Hivim:

  • But the Israelis (Israelites) said to the Givonim (Gibeonites), who were also called Hivim:

But the men of Yisrael: The Hebrew phrase that the BSB translates as men of Yisrael is more literally “man of Yisrael.” This is a collective term that is frequently used for the Israeli (Israelite) army. The phrase men of Yisrael probably refers to the leaders of the Israelis.

said to the Hivim: The Givonim were one part of the “Hivi (Hivite)” nation. God ordered Yisrael to destroy this nation in 3:10. This group of people was also mentioned in 9:1. You should translate the word Hivim the same way you translated it earlier.

9:7b

“Perhaps you dwell near us. How can we make a treaty with you?”

  • “Perhaps you really live near to us. If that is so, we cannot make a treaty with you.”

  • “We want to know for sure that you really live far from us. We cannot make a treaty with anyone who lives in the land of Kena’an (Canaan).”

Perhaps you dwell near us. How can we make a treaty with you?: In Deuteronomy 7:1–7 Yahweh told the Israelis that they must not make any treaties with the people who lived in the land of Kena’an. This question shows that the Israelis were suspicious of the Givonim’s statement that they came from a far away country. The Israelis wanted to make sure it was true. It may be more natural in some languages to translate this question as a statement. For example:

But maybe you really live near us. We can’t make a peace treaty with you if you live nearby. (CEV)

We(excl) want to know for sure that you(plur) do not live near us. We cannot make a treaty with any one who lives in the land of Kena’an.

title: Joshua 9:8
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:8a

“We are your servants,” they said to Yehoshua.

  • But they said to Yehoshua: “We are willing to be your servants.”

  • The Givonim (Gibeonites) told Yehoshua (Joshua): “We acknowledge your authority.”

We are your servants: The sentence We are your servants indicates that the Givonim wanted to accept Yehoshua as their leader and to become part of the Israeli (Israelite) nation.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

we are willing to be your subjects (NET)

we acknowledge you as our masters

they said to Yehoshua: The word they refers to the Givonim. It may be helpful to make this explicit.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

the Givonim said to Yehoshua

9:8b

Then Yehoshua (Joshua) asked them, “Who are you and where have you come from?”

  • Then Yehoshua asked them: “What nationality are you? Where exactly do you come from?”

  • Yehoshua said to them: “I must know for sure what city and nation you come from.”

Then: The word Then indicates the next event in the storyline. Indicate this in a natural way in your language.

Who are you and where have you come from?: The question Who are you…? indicates that Yehoshua wanted to know their nationality. The question where have you come from? indicates that Yehoshua wanted to know where the Givonim (Gibeonites) lived. These two questions together emphasize that Yehoshua wanted to be sure about who these men were. It may be more natural in some languages to combine these two questions in a way that shows this emphasis. For example:

Tell me from exactly from where you have come.

I must know for sure from what town and nation you have come.

title: Joshua 9:9
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:9a

“Your servants have come from a very distant land,” they replied,

  • They told Yehoshua: “Your servants have come from a very far away land

  • The Givonim (Gibeonites) answered: “We are your servants. We have come from a very far country

Your servants have come from a very distant land: The Givonim lied to Yehoshua (Joshua) so that they could make a treaty with the Israelis (Israelites). The phrase from a very distant land is placed at the beginning of the sentence in the Hebrew text to emphasize it. If a location phrase at the beginning of the sentence is not natural, you should use some other means in your language to show this emphasis.

they replied: In some languages it may be more natural to translate the word replied as “answered.”

9:9b

“because of the fame of Yahweh your God.

  • because we heard of the fame of Yahweh your God.

  • because of the reputation of your God, Yahweh.

because of the fame of Yahweh your God: The phrase the fame of Yahweh your God refers to the reputation, or name, that Yahweh had because of the miracles he did for the Israelis. He made it possible for them to leave Mitsrayim (Egypt) and then to defeat the kings of the Amorim (Amorites).

9:9c

For we have heard the reports about Him: all that He did in Mitsrayim,

  • We have heard about what he has done and how he helped you to escape from Mitsrayim.

  • We heard about everything he did in Mitsrayim.

For we have heard the reports about Him: The clause we have heard the reports about Him indicates that the news about Yahweh had spread among the people in the surrounding area.

all that He did in Mitsrayim: The clause all that He did in Mitsrayim indicates that the Givonim (Gibeonites) heard about the miracles Yahweh did when he helped the Israelis (Israelites) escape from Mitsrayim. These events are described in Exodus chapters 5–14.

title: Joshua 9:10
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:10a

and all that He did to the two kings of the Amorim (Amorites) beyond the Yarden (Jordan)—

  • We have heard how he defeated the two Amori (Amorite) kings on the east of the Yarden River,

  • And we heard that he defeated the two kings of the Amorim from the east side of the Yarden River.

and all that He did to the two kings of the Amorim beyond the Yarden: The phrase all that He did refers to the victories that the Israelis (Israelites) won over the two Amori kings. These events are described in Numbers 21:21–35.

beyond the Yarden: The phrase beyond the Yarden indicates that these two Amori kings ruled territories east of the Yarden River.

9:10b

Sihon king of Heshbon and Og king of Bashan, who reigned in Ashtarot (Ashtaroth).

  • King Sihon of Heshbon, and King Og of Bashan who lived in Ashtarot.

  • He defeated King Sihon the king of Heshbon Country, and King Og the king of Bashan Country, who ruled in Ashtarot City.

Sihon king of Heshbon: Sihon was the name of one of the Amori (Amorite) kings.

Heshbon: The town of Heshbon was the capital town of King Sihon’s kingdom.

and Og king of Bashan, who reigned in Ashtarot: Og was the name of the other Amori king.

Bashan: Bashan was an area east and northeast of the Sea of Galil (Galilee). The Yarden (Jordan) River Valley forms its western boundary. Mount Hermon is its northern boundary, and the area of Gilead is the southern boundary. In modern times this is the Golan Heights.

Here are some other ways to translate this name:

Bashan Country

Bashan Region

Ashtarot (Ashtaroth): The town of Ashtarot was the capital town of Bashan, and was the town where King Og lived.9:10 Rasmussen, p. 227–228.

title: Joshua 9:11
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:11a

So the elders and inhabitants of our land told us,

  • So our elders and all the people who live in our land told us,

  • Our leaders and all our people told us

So the elders: The term elders refers to the leaders of the Givonim (Gibeonites). Unlike the other towns in the region of Kena’an (Canaan), the Givonim were ruled by leaders but had no king.9:11 Woudstra, p. 159.

and inhabitants of our land told us: The phrase inhabitants of our land refers to the people who lived in the region of the Givonim. Giveon (Gibeon) was actually a town, but it had power over the other nearby towns.

Here are some other ways to translate the term land:

area

region

9:11b

‘Take provisions for your journey;

  • ‘Take food for your journey

  • to get some food ready for the journey

Take provisions for your journey: The clause Take provisions for your journey indicates that the people took food to eat. They put the food in sacks which their donkeys carried. They did not carry the food in their hands.

for your journey: The phrase for your journey refers to the trip that the Givonim (Gibeonites) took from their own town to the Israeli (Israelite) camp.

9:11c

go to meet them and say to them:

  • Travel to the Israeli camp and tell their leaders:

  • and to come and meet you Israelis (Israelites). They wanted us to tell you:

go to meet them and say to them: The clause go to meet them indicates that the Givonim should travel to the Israeli camp and introduce themselves to Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis leaders.

General Comment on 9:11a-c

The Givonim report this as a direct quote of what the elders told them to do. In some languages it may be more natural to translate this as an indirect quote. For example:

Our leaders and all the people that live in our land told us to get some food ready for a trip and to go and meet you. (GNT)

9:11d

We are your servants. Please make a treaty with us.’

  • “We are willing to be your servants. Make a treaty with us.”

  • “We acknowledge your authority. Please make a treaty with us.”

We are your servants: The clause We are your servants indicates that the Givonim (Gibeonites) were willing to become subject to the Israelis (Israelites) and submit to them. You should translate the phrase your servants in the same way as in 9:8a.

Please: The word Please is a way to make a polite request. You should use whatever word or grammatical means is appropriate to make a polite request in your language.

make a treaty with us: The clause make a treaty with us indicates that the Givonim wanted the Israelis to make a peace treaty with them.

title: Joshua 9:12
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:12a

This bread of ours

  • Look at our bread.

  • Do you see this bread?

This bread of ours: The Givonim (Gibeonites) said This bread of ours to call attention to the old bread they brought with them. In some languages it may be better to translate this as an imperative command, or as a rhetorical question. For example:

Look, see what our bread is like!

See this dry, crumbly bread of ours? (CEV)

9:12b

was warm when we packed it at home on the day we left to come to you.

  • On the day we left our houses to come to you it was still warm out of the oven.

  • It was still warm from being cooked when we packed our food for the journey and left home.

was warm when we packed it at home: The clause was warm indicates that they had just finished baking the bread. It was warm because they took it out of the oven. If people are not familiar with making bread, it may be necessary to make this information explicit. For example:

it was hot out of the oven on the day we packed the food when we left our homes (CEV)

we had just baked this bread and it was still warm when we took it from our houses

on the day we left to come to you: The phrase on the day we left to come to you refers to the day that the Givonim (Gibeonites) started their trip to the Israeli (Israelite) camp.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

on the day we left our houses

The phrase on the day we left to come to you may be incorporated into the first verse part, as in CEV above. It may also be left as implicit information and not translated, as in NCV:

Look at our bread. On the day we left home to come to you it was warm and fresh (NCV)

9:12c

But take a look, it is now dry and moldy.

  • But now it is dried out and hard.

  • But now, look and see how dry and crumbly it is.

But take a look: The phrase But take a look calls attention to something important. It emphasizes that the journey was long because the bread is all dried up. Show this emphasis in a way that is natural in your language.

it is now dry and moldy: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as moldy is used only three times in the Old Testament. The meaning is uncertain. You should translate it the same way you did in 9:5b.

title: Joshua 9:13
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:13a

These wineskins were new when we filled them, but look, they are cracked.

  • When we put wine in these wineskins they were new. Now they are torn.

  • These leather wine bags were new when we filled them with wine. But look, now they are split open.

These wineskins were new when we filled them: The term wineskins refers to the leather bags or pouches in which people carried their wine. Translate it the same way you did in 9:4.

but look: The word look calls attention to something important and emphasizes it. Use whatever means is appropriate in your language to show importance or emphasis.

they are cracked: The clause they are cracked means that the wineskins were so old that there were cracks in the leather.

9:13b

And these clothes and sandals are worn out from our very long journey.”

  • Our clothes and our sandals are worn out from the very long trip.”

  • Our clothes and our sandals are worn out because we came from so far away.”

And these clothes: The word clothes refers to the clothes the men were wearing.

and sandals are worn out from our very long journey: The phrase worn out from our very long journey emphasizes that the Givonim (Gibeonites) have come a long way and that they do not live near the Israelis (Israelites).

sandals: The sandals that people wore in those times were open, with a sole under the foot and straps around the top. In some languages it may be more natural to call them:

shoes

General Comment on 9:11–13

When the Givonim said this they were telling lies to the Israelis. They were trying to deceive them. Translate this in a way that sounds like people who are telling convincing lies.

title: Joshua 9:14
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:14a

Then the men of Yisrael (Israel) sampled their provisions,

  • ¶ The Israelis examined their things.

  • ¶ So the Israelis (Israelites) looked at the food that the Givonim (Gibeonites) showed them and believed what they said.

Then the men of Yisrael sampled their provisions: The word men refers to the Israeli (Israelite) leaders. The term their provisions refers to the food that the Givonim brought with them.

sampled their provisions: There are three ways to interpret the meaning of the Hebrew clause that the BSB translates as sampled their provisions.

  1. The Hebrew clause means that the Israeli leaders examined the food and accepted it as evidence that the Givonim had traveled from a distant place. For example:

    the Israelis examined their food (NLT) (NLT, NET, GW, NJPS)

  2. The Hebrew clause means that the Israeli leaders ate some of the food. For example:

    the men of Yisrael (Israel) sampled their provisions (NIV) (BSB, NIV, RSV, GNT, CEV, NABRE, KJV)

  3. The Hebrew clause means that the Israeli leaders ate some of the food as part of a covenant ceremony. Some commentaries follow this interpretation, including the UBS Handbook, but no English version follows this interpretation.

It is recommended that you follow option (1). This seems most likely in the context. The Givonim (Gibeonites) provided evidence, and the Israelis (Israelites) examined the evidence and believed it.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

the men believed the evidence they were shown (GW)

sampled: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as sampled is more literally “took.”

9:14b

but did not seek the counsel of Yahweh.

  • And they did not ask Yahweh what he wanted them to do.

  • But they did not ask for help from Yahweh.

but did not seek the counsel of Yahweh: The clause did not seek the counsel of Yahweh means that the Israeli (Israelite) leaders did not ask Yahweh to show them what to do. They decided what to do without listening to Yahweh.

This is an important point in the story. In the Hebrew text it is emphasized by a change of word order. Look for a natural way to emphasize it in your language. It might be clearer in some languages to translate this as an independent sentence with the subject made explicit: For example:

But the Israeli leaders did not ask Yahweh what they should do.

title: Joshua 9:15
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:15a

And Yehoshua made a treaty of peace with them to let them live,

  • And Yehoshua made a peace treaty with the Givonim. He made an agreement that they will not kill them.

  • So Yehoshua (Joshua) made a treaty of friendship with the Givonim (Gibeonites). He agreed to let them live.

And: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as And indicates the next action in the storyline. Indicate this in a natural way in your language.

Yehoshua made a treaty of peace with them: The Hebrew that the BSB and many English versions collapse into one clause, Yehoshua made a treaty of peace with them, is literally two clauses, “Yehoshua made peace with them, and he made a covenant for them.” Making a covenant, or a treaty, showed that there will be peace between the two groups of people. For example:

So Yehoshua made peace with them by making a treaty (GW)

to let them live: The terms of the peace treaty allowed the Givonim to live as subjects, under the rule of the Israelis (Israelites). The Israelis promised not to kill the Givonim as they did the other inhabitants of Kena’an (Canaan).

9:15b

and the leaders of the congregation swore an oath to them.

  • And Yisrael’s (Israel’s) leaders swore that Yisrael will do according to the treaty.

  • And the leaders of the Israelis promised to keep this treaty.

and the leaders of the congregation swore an oath to them: The phrase the leaders of the congregation refers to the leaders of the whole Israeli (Israelite) community.

congregation: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as congregation refers to a meeting of free Israeli men who were eligible for military service.9:15 Boling and Wright, p. 268.

Here are some other ways to translate this word:

the leaders of the assembly (NIV)

the leaders of the community (NET, NABRE)

Some English versions leave this word implicit. For example:

the Israeli leaders (NLT)

their leaders (GNT)

swore an oath to them: The clause swore an oath to them means that the Israeli (Israelite) leaders swore an oath, or made a solemn promise, that they will keep the agreement that they made with the Givonim (Gibeonites).

title: Joshua 9:16
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:16a

Three days after they had made the treaty with the Givonim,

  • ¶ Three days after they made a treaty with the Givonim,

  • ¶ On the third day after they made the peace agreement,
