Three days: In Hebrew, part of a day was counted as one day when reckoning time. For example, if the treaty was made on a Monday, these events were probably on the Wednesday evening. Translate this reference to Three days in a natural way in your language.

after they had made the treaty with the Givonim (Gibeonites): It may be necessary in some languages to make the subject and the object explicit, For example, you could say:

three days after the Israelis (Israelites) made a covenant with the Givonim

9:16b

the Israelis learned that they were neighbors, living among them.

  • the Israelis learned that the Givonim lived nearby; that they were neighbors.

  • they found out that the Givonim lived near them, not far from them.

the Israelis learned that they were neighbors: This indicates that the Israelis heard that the Givonim were their neighbors. In some languages it may be clearer to make either the subject or the object explicit. For example:

the Israelis learned that these people did indeed live nearby (GNT)

the Israelis (Israelites) learned that the Givonim (Gibeonites) lived nearby (NCV)

living among them: The clause living among them is another way to say that the Givonim lived in a nearby town. It emphasizes that the Givonim lived close by, not far away, as they had claimed. Use whatever lexical or grammatical means is natural to show this emphasis.

title: Joshua 9:17
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:17a

So the Israelis set out and on the third day arrived at their cities—

  • So the Israelis went to see them, and on the third day they got to their cities.

  • Then the Israelis (Israelites) walked to where the Givonim (Gibeonites) lived, and reached their cities in three days.

So: The Hebrew connector that the BSB translates as So introduces the next event in the narrative.

the Israelis set out: The clause the Israelis set out indicates that the Israelis left their camp to walk to where the Givonim lived and to confront them.

and on the third day: In Hebrew, part of a day was counted as one day when reckoning time. For example, if they started to walk on a Thursday, then they probably arrived on a Saturday. Translate this time reference in a natural way in your language.

arrived at their cities: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as arrived at means “reached.”

their cities: The Givonim lived in a group of at least four towns. These towns are named in the next part of this verse.

9:17b

Giveon (Gibeon), Kefirah (Chephirah), Be’erot (Beeroth), and Kiryat-Yearim (Kiriath-jearim).

  • The cities were Giveon, Kefirah, Be’erot, and Kiryat (Kiriath) Jearim.

  • The names of the cities were Giveon, Kefirah, Be’erot, and Kiryat-Yearim.

Giveon, Kefirah, Be’erot, and Kiryat-Yearim: In some languages it may be clearer to make it explicit that these are names of towns. For example:

the names of their towns were Giveon, Kefirah, Be’erot, and Kiryat-Yearim

title: Joshua 9:18
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:18a

But the Israelis did not attack them,

  • But the Israelis did not attack them

  • But the people of Yisrael (Israel) did not attack them,

But: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as But indicates contrast. Contrary to what one would expect, the Israelis (Israelites) did not attack these enemies.

the Israelis did not attack them: The term the Israelis refers to the people of Yisrael who went to visit the Givonim (Gibeonites).

attack: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as attack can be translated in two different ways.

  1. It is translated “did not attack them.” For example:

    the people of Yisrael did not attack them (ESV) (BSB, ESV, NIV, NRSV, NASB, NCV, NET, NJB, NAB, NJPS, NLT, REB, CEV, KJV)

  2. It is translated “did not kill them.” For example:

    the Israelis could not kill them (GNT) (GNT, RSV, GW)

It is recommended that you follow option (1). This is the more accurate way to translate the Hebrew word. However, option (2) is may be used if you consider this to be implied information. If the Israelis (Israelites) “attacked” the Givonim, then they would probably kill them.

9:18b

because the leaders of the congregation had sworn an oath to them by Yahweh, the God of Yisrael (Israel).

  • because the leaders of the community swore to a treaty of friendship with them in the name of Yahweh, the God of Yisrael.

  • because the leaders of their assembly made a solemn promise in the name of Yahweh, the God of Yisrael to spare the Givonim (Gibeonites).

because the leaders of the congregation: The word congregation refers to a meeting of free Israeli (Israelite) men who were eligible for military service. You should translate this the same way you did in 9:15.

had sworn an oath to them by Yahweh, the God of Yisrael: The clause sworn an oath to them by Yahweh, the God of Yisrael indicates that the leaders made a promise to the Givonim in the name of Yahweh. The full name of God is used to emphasize the solemnity of this vow.

9:18c

And the whole congregation grumbled against the leaders.

  • Then all the community of Israelis (Israelites) criticized the leaders.

  • Then all the assembly were not satisfied and grumbled about the leaders’ decision.

And the whole congregation: The phrase the whole congregation refers to all the members of the assembly of Israeli men. It is the same group of people as in 9:18b.

grumbled against the leaders: The clause grumbled against the leaders indicates that the Israeli men were not satisfied with the leaders’ decision and complained about it. They wanted to attack the Givonim (Gibeonites), as is made clear in 9:26.9:18 Howard, p. 229.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

the whole community criticized the leaders (NET)

the whole assembly grumbled against the leaders (NIV)

title: Joshua 9:19
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:19a

All the leaders answered,

  • But all the leaders said to them:

  • But they all said:

All the leaders answered: The subject and the object of this sentence are repeated in the Hebrew text for emphasis. In some languages it may be more natural to use pronouns. For example:

But they answered (GNT)

But the leaders said to them

9:19b

“We have sworn an oath to them by Yahweh, the God of Yisrael (Israel),

  • “We swore an oath to them in the name of Yahweh, the God of Yisrael.

  • “We made a solemn promise to them before Yahweh, the God of Yisrael,

We have sworn an oath to them by Yahweh, the God of Yisrael: It may be more natural in some languages to introduce this clause with a word which shows it is the reason for the action. For example:

Since we have sworn an oath in the presence of the Lord, the God of Yisrael, we cannot touch them (NLT)

9:19c

and now we cannot touch them.

  • Now we cannot harm them.

  • so now we can not attack them.

and now we cannot touch them: The clause we cannot touch them indicates that the Israelis (Israelites) could not attack the Givonim (Gibeonites) or harm them. This was because they made a vow to them in the name of Yahweh and this vow was binding.

General Comment on 9:19b-c

It may be more natural in some languages to switch the order of 19b and 19c, and put the reason for the action at the end of the sentence. For example:

19cWe must not harm them in any way, 19bbecause we have made a promise to them in the name of Yahweh, the God of Yisrael (Israel).

title: Joshua 9:20
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:20a

This is how we will treat them: We will let them live,

  • This is what we will do. We will let them live.

  • We must let them live

This is how we will treat them: We will let them live: The clause This is how we will treat them is a way to emphasize the second clause, We will let them live. The Israelis (Israelites) intend to let the Givonim (Gibeonites) live.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

This is what we will do to them: we will let them live (NIV)

This we will do to them: let them live (ESV)

We must let them live (NET)

9:20b

so that no wrath will fall on us because of the oath we swore to them.”

  • If we don’t let them live God will punish us, because we made an oath to them.”

  • because we promised we will not hurt them. God will be angry with us if we break this promise.

so that no wrath will fall on us: The clause so that no wrath will fall on us indicates that Yahweh would be angry and punish the Israelis (Israelites) if they broke their vow and harmed the Givonim (Gibeonites).

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

so that God’s wrath will not fall on us (NIV11)

otherwise God will be angry at us

because of the oath we swore to them: The phrase the oath we swore to them states the reason that God would be angry with the Israelis. They made an oath to the Givonim in God’s name. God will be angry if they break that oath.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

for breaking the oath we swore to them (NIV)

It may be clearer to combine these two clauses:

If we break our promise, God will punish us (CEV)

divine anger would come upon us if we broke our oath (NLT)

title: Joshua 9:21
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:21a

They continued, “Let them live,

  • The leaders repeated: “We must let them live.”

  • So we must let them live.”

They continued: Verse 21 continues the answer that the Israeli (Israelite) leaders gave to those who wanted to attack the Givonim (Gibeonites). The clause They continued may not be necessary in some languages. It may not be natural to repeat a quote margin in the middle of continuous speech. For example, the NLT deletes the quote margin:

Let them live. (NLT)

The ESV follows the Hebrew with a long form of the quote margin:

And the leaders said to them, “Let them live” (ESV)

Let them live: The clause Let them live indicates that the Israelis (Israelites) will not kill the Givonim.

The words Let them live are a repetition of what the leaders said in 20a. In some languages it may be clearer to use the word “repeated” in the quote margin. For example:

They repeated, “Let them live”

9:21b

but let them be woodcutters and water carriers for the whole congregation.”

  • So they became servants for the whole community and cut the firewood and drew water from the wells,

  • And so the Givonim (Gibeonites) cut firewood and drew water from the wells for all the Yisrael (Israel) people.

but let them be woodcutters and water carriers for the whole congregation: There are two ways to interpret the use of this phrase:

  1. These words are not part of the quotation that started in 21a. Instead, this phrase shows the result of the Israelis’s (Israelites’) decision. For example:

    21a“Let them live.” 21bSo they became woodcutters and water carriers for the whole community. (NET) (NET, RSV, ESV, NJPS, NLT, NASB)

  2. These words are part of the quotation that started in 21a. For example:

    21a“Let them live, 21bbut let them be woodcutters and water carriers for the entire community.” (NIV) (BSB, NIV, NABRE, GNT, KJV)

It is recommended that you follow option (1). This is followed by several English versions and several commentaries.

woodcutters: The word woodcutters indicates that the Givonim (Gibeonites) cut firewood for the Israelis.

water carriers: The phrase water carriers indicates that the Givonim drew water from the wells and carried it for the Israelis.

the whole congregation: The phrase the whole congregation indicates that the Givonim performed these tasks for the whole Israeli (Israelite) community, including the leaders and their families.

9:21c

So the leaders kept their promise.

  • which was what the leaders decided.

  • This is what the Israeli leaders said they should do.

So the leaders kept their promise: The clause So the leaders kept their promise emphasizes the decision of the leaders about the Givonim. It was the leaders who made the decisions.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

So they became hewers of wood and drawers of water for all the congregation, as the leaders had decided concerning them (NRSV)

So they made them woodcutters and water carriers for the entire community, as the Israeli (Israelite) leaders directed (NLT)

Use a way that is natural in your language to emphasize this decision of the leaders.

title: Joshua 9:22
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:22a

Then Yehoshua summoned the Givonim and said,

  • ¶ Yehoshua sent for the Givoni leaders and asked them:

  • ¶ Yehoshua (Joshua) called together the Givoni (Gibeonite) leaders and said:

Then Yehoshua summoned the Givonim (Gibeonites): The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as summoned indicates that Yehoshua ordered the Givonim to come see him. He wanted to tell them how the Israelis (Israelites) would respond to their trickery.

the Givonim: The phrase the Givonim refers to the leaders or representatives of the Givonim, not to the whole group of Givonim.

and said: Some English versions translate the word said as “asked” because it introduces a rhetorical question. For example:

Yehoshua ordered the people of Giveon (Gibeon) to be brought to him, and he asked them (GNT)

9:22b

“Why did you deceive us by telling us

  • “Why did you lie to us when you said,

  • “You lied to us. You told us

Why did you deceive us by telling us: This is the beginning of a rhetorical question. It functions as a strong statement that the Givonim (Gibeonites) should not have tricked the Israelis (Israelites).

Here are two ways to translate this statement:

  • Use a rhetorical question. For example:

    Why did you trick us? (NET)

  • Use a strong statement. For example:

    you should not have deceived us

    you lied to us

Translate this strong statement in a way that is natural in your language.

9:22c

you live far away from us, when in fact you live among us?

  • ‘We live far away,’ but actually you live very close by.

  • that you live far away, but actually you live nearby.

you live far away from us: The clause you live far away from us is Yehoshua’s (Joshua’s) paraphrase of what the Givonim (Gibeonites) told the Israelis (Israelites).

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

We live in a far country

when in fact you live among us: The clause when…you live among us indicates that the Givonim lived nearby.

General Comment on 22b-c

Some other ways to translate the statements in 22b-c are:

You actually live close to us. Why did you lie and tell us that you live far away?

You lied to us and said that you live far away. But actually you live nearby.

Why did you deceive us and tell us that you were from far away, when you live right here? (GNT)

title: Joshua 9:23
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:23a-b

Now therefore you are under a curse and will perpetually serve as woodcutters and water carriers for the house of my God: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as Now therefore can be translated in two different ways:

  1. It means therefore, or because of this, or for that reason. For example:

    Because you did this, God has condemned you. (GNT) (BSB, GNT, RSV, ESV, NAB, NASB, NJPS, KJV)

  2. It is a temporal marker now. For example:

    You are now under a curse (NIV) (NIV, NABRE, GW, NCV, NET, NJB, REB, CEV)

It is recommended that you follow option (1) and make the reason relation explicit. But option (2) is acceptable if the reason relation is implied by the context in your translation.

will perpetually serve as woodcutters and water carriers: The Hebrew words are more literally “not he will be cut off from you a slave.” There are two ways to interpret what this means.

  1. This means that all the Givonim (Gibeonites) became slaves. For example:

    every one of you shall always be a slave (NABRE) (BSB, NABRE, NASB, NIV, NET, GNT, GW, NAB, NCV, NJB, NJPS, NLT, KJV)

  2. This means that some of the Givonim became slaves. For example:

    some of you shall never be anything by servants (ESV) (ESV, RSV, REB, CEV)

It is recommended that you follow interpretation (1). God’s curse was on the whole Givoni (Gibeonite) nation. It is not clear from the Hebrew that we can translate this as only “some” of the Givonim.

9:23a

Now therefore you are under a curse and will perpetually serve

  • Because you did this there is a curse on you. You will always be our slaves.

  • Therefore, God has condemned you. For all time you will be slaves.

you are under a curse: The phrase you are under a curse means that God considered them to be guilty and condemned them.

will perpetually serve: The phrase will perpetually serve indicates the Givonim (Gibeonites) will live in submission to the Israelis (Israelites).

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

shall always be slaves (RSV)

shall never be anything but servants (ESV)

perpetual servitude (NET)

9:23b

as woodcutters and water carriers for the house of my God.”

  • You will cut firewood and draw water for the house of my God.”

  • You will have to cut wood and draw water from the wells for the tabernacle of my God.”

woodcutters: The word woodcutters indicates that they will cut firewood.

and water carriers: The phrase water carriers indicates that they will draw water from the wells and carry it.

for the house of my God: The phrase for the house of my God indicates that the Givonim (Gibeonites) will provide wood and water for the place of worship. During the time of Yehoshua (Joshua), the house of my God in which the Israelis (Israelites) worshiped was a tent, not a permanent house. In 9:27 it is clear that the Givonim served both the place of worship and also the broader community in this way.

my God: The word my refers to Yehoshua. Yehoshua referred to Yahweh as his God.

title: Joshua 9:24
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:24a

The Givonim answered,

  • ¶ The Givonim answered Yehoshua:

  • ¶ The Givonim (Gibeonites) leaders replied to Yehoshua (Joshua):

The Givonim answered: The phrase The Givonim refers to the Givoni (Gibeonite) leaders who met with Yehoshua. It may be necessary to make this clear in your translation.

9:24b

“Your servants were told clearly

  • “We did it because people told us for sure

  • “We lied to you because they told us how certain is it

Your servants were told clearly: The phrase were told is passive. In some languages it may be clearer to make this an active phrase.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

we learned (GNT)

We heard (NCV)

people told us

Your servants: The Givonim (Gibeonites) called themselves Your servants to show respect to Yehoshua (Joshua). Many languages have pronouns or other vocabulary for showing respect. Use whatever means is natural to indicate this.

were told clearly: The phrase told clearly translates an emphatic form of the Hebrew verb “told.” The Givonim emphasized that they heard a sure and certain report that the God of the Israelis (Israelites) was powerful. Use whatever means is natural to show that there is no doubt that the Givonim heard these things.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

your servants were clearly told (NIV)

we learned that it was really true (GNT)

9:24c

that Yahweh your God had commanded His servant Mosheh (Moses) to give you all the land

  • that Yahweh your God commanded his servant Mosheh to give you all of this land.

  • that Yahweh your God told his servant Mosheh to help you conquer this land.

that Yahweh your God had commanded His servant Mosheh to give you all the land: It may be more natural to divided this long clause into two or more clauses. For example:

we heard that Yahweh your God had made a promise to his servant Mosheh. Yahweh promised Mosheh that he would help the Israelis (Israelites) conquer this land

we heard about the promise that Yahweh your God gave to Mosheh, who served him. Yahweh told Mosheh that the Israelis would take this land

9:24d

and wipe out all its inhabitants before you.

  • Yahweh promised Mosheh (Moses) that he will help the Israelis kill all the people as you move into the land.

  • We heard that you will kill all the people in the land.

and wipe out all its inhabitants: It may be more natural in some languages to begin a new sentence. For example:

We heard that they will kill all the people who live in the land

before you: The phrase before you indicates that the Israelis (Israelites) will advance into the land, and kill the people living there wherever they find them.

9:24e

So we greatly feared for our lives because of you, and that is why we have done this.

  • We were afraid that you will kill us, and so we lied to you.

  • This is why we tricked you into making a peace treaty. We were afraid you will kill us.

So we greatly feared for our lives because of you: The clause we greatly feared for our lives indicates that the Givonim (Gibeonites) were afraid the Israelis would kill them.

and that is why we have done this: The word this refers to the lie that the Givonim told the Israelis.

General Comment on 9:24

It may be more natural in some languages to rearrange the parts of this verse of the Givonim’s answer to Yehoshua (Joshua).9:24 Bratcher and Newman, p. 134. For example:

24aThey answered, 24e“We did it, sir, 24bbecause we learned that it was really true 24cthat the Lord your God had commanded his servant Mosheh (Moses) to give you the whole land 24dand to kill the people living in it as you advanced. 24eWe did it because we were terrified of you; we were in fear of our lives. (GNT)

title: Joshua 9:25
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:25a

Now we are in your hands.

  • We know that you are more powerful than we are.

  • Now look, you have the strength to do anything you want.

Now: The word Now calls attention to what the Givonim (Gibeonites) said next. It is a way to emphasize it. Use whatever means is natural to show this emphasis.

we are in your hands: The clause we are in your hands is an idiom. It indicates that the Givonim know the Israelis (Israelites) are stronger than them and can do whatever they want to them.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

we are in your power (NET)

you are strong enough to do anything to us that you want (CEV)

9:25b

Do to us whatever seems good and right to you.”

  • So treat us in whatever way seems just to you.”

  • Do to us whatever you think is right.”

Do to us whatever seems good and right to you: The phrase Do to us whatever seems good and right to you indicates that the Givonim (Gibeonites) asked the Israelis (Israelites) to treat them in whatever way seemed just to the Israelis.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

do to us what you think is good and appropriate (NET)

do to us whatever you think is right (NLT)

title: Joshua 9:26
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:26a

So Yehoshua did this and delivered them from the hands of the Israelis,

  • ¶ So Yehoshua saved them from the Israelis,

  • ¶ So Yehoshua (Joshua) rescued the Givonim (Gibeonites) from them

So Yehoshua did this and delivered them: The two clauses Yehoshua did this and delivered them indicate that Yehoshua decided to save the lives of the Givonim. These clauses can be combined as one clause, for example,

So Yehoshua saved them from the Israelis (Israelites). (NIV)

So Yehoshua rescued them (GW)

from the hands of the Israelis: The phrase from the hands of the Israelis indicates that Yehoshua did not allow the Israelis to kill the Givonim.

9:26b

and they did not kill the Givonim.

  • and they did not kill them.

  • and the Israelis did not kill them.

and they did not kill the Givonim (Gibeonites): The clause they did not kill the Givonim states the same meaning as 26a in different words. Yehoshua (Joshua) kept the Israelis (Israelites) from killing the Givonim, and the Israelis did not kill them.

title: Joshua 9:27
content:
Section 9:1–27 The Givonim (Gibeonites) deceived the Israelis (Israelites)

The Givoni (Gibeonite) people lived near Ay (Ai). When they heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had defeated Ay, they were afraid that he would conquer and kill them too. So, they sent messengers who pretended they had come from a long distance away. They deceived the Israelis and made a treaty of friendship with them.

Later, the Israelis learned that the Givonim lied to them, and that they lived quite close to them. They could not kill them because of the treaty, so they made them be water carriers and woodcutters for the Israelis.

Here are some other possible section headings:

The people of Giveon (Gibeon)

The Giveon people tricked the Israelis and made a treaty with them

9:27a

On that day he made them woodcutters and water carriers,

  • But from that day on he made the Givonim cut firewood and draw water.

  • But starting from that day, Yehoshua (Joshua) made the Givonim (Gibeonites) be woodcutters and water carriers,

On that day he made them woodcutters and water carriers: This indicates that Yehoshua carried out the decision of the leaders that was mentioned in 9:21. The Givonim will live among the Israelis (Israelites) and will cut firewood and draw water from the wells for them.

On that day: Here is another way to translate the words that day:

starting from that day

from that day on

9:27b

as they are to this day

  • They are still doing it today

  • and they continue to this day.

as they are to this day: The phrase as they are to this day indicates that when the book of Yehoshua (Joshua) was written, the Givonim (Gibeonites) were still slaves who cut wood and drew water.

9:27c

for the congregation of Yahweh and for the altar

  • for the community and for the altar of Yahweh,

  • They provided for the Israelis (Israelites), and for the altar of Yahweh,

for the congregation of Yahweh and for the altar: The phrase for the congregation of Yahweh and for the altar indicates that the Givonim will supply wood and water for the Israeli (Israelite) community and for the special needs of the altar.

altar: The word altar is used in place of the phrase “house of my God” in 9:23b. Both the word altar and the phrase “house of my God” refer to the same place. This was the tent of worship where the priests burned sacrifices to Yahweh.

9:27d

at the place He would choose.

  • in whatever place Yahweh decides the altar should be.

  • They serve the altar wherever Yahweh decides the altar should be.

at the place He would choose: This indicates that in the future Yahweh may choose a different place for the altar. The Givonim (Gibeonites) will continue to provide wood and water wherever it might be.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

wherever the Lord would choose to build it (NLT)

wherever he chose it to be (NCV)

General Comment on 9:27c-d

It may be more natural in some languages to reorder 27b-d so that the phrase “at the place He would choose” is next to the phrase “for the altar.” For example:

27aBut that day he made the Givonim the woodcutters and water carriers 27cfor the community of Yisrael (Israel) and for the altar of the Lord—27dwherever the Lord would choose to build it. 27bAnd that is what they do to this day. (NLT)

title: Joshua 10:1
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

10:1a

Now Adoni-Tsedek (Adoni-zedek) king of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had captured Ay (Ai)

  • ¶ Adoni-Tsedek, the king of Yerushalem, heard that Yehoshua captured Ay

  • ¶ At this time King Adoni-Tsedek of Yerushalem City heard that Yehoshua defeated

Now: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as Now introduces a series of dependent clauses in 1a-e.

Adoni-Tsedek king of Yerushalem heard: In 9:1–2 the kings who ruled on the west side of the Yarden (Jordan) River heard about Yehoshua and the amazing things that Yahweh had done for the Israelis (Israelites). In 10:1 the kings who ruled in Southern Kena’an (Canaan) heard similar news. The word heard at the beginning of chapters 9, 10, and 11 gives a thematic unity to these chapters. It is recommended that you translate the word heard at the beginning of each of these chapters in a way that keeps this thematic unity but is also natural in your language.

Adoni-Tsedek: The name Adoni-Tsedek means “My master is righteous” in Hebrew. Some English versions hyphenate this name and other versions write it as one word. For example:

Adonizedek (GNT)

Yerushalem: At this time Yerushalem was a Kena’ani (Canaanite) town. The people of Yisrael (Israel) did not yet live there.

that Yehoshua (Joshua) had captured Ay (Ai): The clause Yehoshua had captured Ay indicates that Yehoshua and his army captured the town of Ay, and defeated it.

10:1b

and devoted it to destruction—

  • and destroyed it completely,

  • and completely destroyed Ay City.

and devoted it to destruction: The phrase devoted it to destruction indicates that Yehoshua and his army completely destroyed the town and everything in it. There was nothing left but rubble.

10:1c

doing to Ay and its king as he had done to Yeriho (Jericho) and its king—

  • and killed its king, as he destroyed Yeriho and killed its king.

  • He destroyed it and killed its king, as he destroyed Yeriho City and killed its king.

doing to Ay (Ai) and its king: The clause doing to Ay and its king means that Yehoshua (Joshua) and his army killed the people who lived in the town of Ay and also killed the king of Ay.

as he had done to Yeriho and its king: The clause as he had done to Yeriho means that Yehoshua treated these two towns in the same way. He killed the people of Yeriho along with their king, and he also killed the people who lived in Ay and their king.

10:1d

and that the people of Giveon (Gibeon) had made peace with Yisrael (Israel)

  • He heard that the Givonim (Gibeonites) made peace with Yisrael

  • He also heard that the people of Giveon City made a treaty with Yisrael

and that the people of Giveon: The phrase the people of Giveon refers to the people who lived in the towns of Giveon.

had made peace with Yisrael: The clause made peace with Yisrael refers to the peace treaty that the Givoni (Gibeonite) leaders made with the Israeli (Israelite) leaders.

10:1e

and were living near them.

  • and lived with them.

  • and that they lived among them.

and were living near them: The clause were living near them indicates that the Givonim (Gibeonites) lived in the same area as the Israelis (Israelites).

General Comment on 10:1a-e

This sentence in the BSB is long and complex. The main verb of the sentence does not come until verse 2. Verse 1 consists of background information. The first action in the story is in verse 2. It may be clearer in some languages to translate verse 1 as two or three independent sentences. For example:

1aAdoni-Tsedek (Adoni-zedek), king of Yerushalem (Jerusalem), heard that Yehoshua (Joshua) had captured 1band completely destroyed Ay (Ai) 1cand killed its king just as he had destroyed the town of Yeriho (Jericho) and killed its king. 1dHe also learned that the Givonim had made peace with Yisrael (Israel) 1eand were now their allies. (NLT)

title: Joshua 10:2
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

10:2a

So Adoni-Tsedek (Adoni-zedek) and his people were greatly alarmed,

  • King Adoni-Tsedek and his people were very afraid when they heard this,

  • When he and his people heard this they were frightened.

So Adoni-Tsedek and his people were greatly alarmed: The words greatly alarmed refer to King Adoni-Tsedek. They indicate that the king was very afraid.

There is a textual issue here.

  1. The Hebrew Masoretic text and the Septuagint translation into Greek both read “they feared greatly.” For example:

    he and his people were very much alarmed (NIV) (BSB, NIV, NET, NABRE, GW, NCV, NLT, GNT, CEV, KJV)

  2. Some ancient translations such as the Syriac read “he feared greatly.” For example:

    he feared greatly (ESV) (ESV, RSV, NASB, NJPS, REB)

It is recommended that you follow option (1). Usually we translate the Hebrew text unless it is very difficult. Your translation could say “they” or it could say “the king and his people.” Here is another way to translate this:

the people of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) were greatly alarmed (GNT)

If you have translated 10:1 as an independent sentence, you may need to supply some implicit information here. For example, the NLT supplies this information:

He and his people became very afraid when they heard all this (NLT)

10:2b

because Giveon (Gibeon) was a great city, like one of the royal cities;

  • because Giveon was an important city, like the cities that had a king,

  • They knew that Giveon was a big city, as big as the cities that had kings.

because: The word because introduces the reason why the king and his people were afraid.

Giveon was a great city: In 9:17 it said that Giveon was actually a group of four towns. The phrase a great city indicates that Giveon was a large and important place.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

a large city (NET)

an important city (NIV)

like one of the royal cities: The phrase like one of the royal cities indicates that Giveon (Gibeon) was equal in size and importance to the towns that had a king to rule them. Giveon was ruled by an assembly of leaders and did not have a king.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

as large as any of the cities that had a king (GNT)

10:2c

it was larger than Ay (Ai), and all its men were mighty.

  • and because it was larger than Ay, and the men of Giveon were good fighters.

  • It was larger than Ay, and all its men were soldiers.

it was: The words it was introduce a second reason why the king and his people were afraid.

and all its men were mighty: The clause all its men were mighty indicates that all the men of Ay were good at fighting.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

all its men were warriors (NET)

all its men were good fighters (NIV)

title: Joshua 10:3
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

10:3a

Therefore Adoni-Tsedek (Adoni-zedek) king of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) sent word

  • So Adoni-Tsedek, king of Yerushalem, sent this message

  • So King Adoni-Tsedek of Yerushalem sent messengers with this message

Therefore Adoni-Tsedek king of Yerushalem sent word: The phrase sent word indicates that the king sent messengers to take his message to the other kings.

King Adoni-Tsedek of Yerushalem sent this message to… (NET)

Adoni-Tsedek king of Yerushalem appealed to… (NIV)

King Adoni-Tsedek of Yerushalem sent messengers to… (NLT)

It may be more natural in some languages to put the title “King” before the names of each of the kings in this list.

10:3b

to Hoham king of Hevron (Hebron), Pir’am (Piram) king of Yarmut (Jarmuth),

  • to King Hoham of Hevron, to King Pir’am of Yarmut,

  • to Hoham, king of Hevron City, to Pir’am, king of Yarmut City

to Hoham king of Hevron: Hoham is the name of the king of Hevron. Hevron was a town in the hill country southwest of Yerushalem (Jerusalem).

Pir’am king of Yarmut: Pir’am is the name of the king of Yarmut. Yarmut was a town about 24 kilometers west of Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem) in the Elah Valley. It was southwest of Yerushalem.10:3 Boling and Wright, p. 279.

10:3c

Yafia (Japhia) king of Lakish (Lachish), and Devir (Debir) king of Eglon, saying,

  • to King Yafia of Lakish, and to King Devir of Eglon.

  • to Yafia, king of Lachich City, and to Devir, king of Eglon City.

Yafia king of Lakish: Yafia is the name of the king of Lakish. Lakish was about 40 kilometers southwest of Yerushalem.10:3 Boling and Wright, p. 280.

and Devir king of Eglon, saying: Devir is the name of the king of Eglon. Eglon was about 56 kilometers southwest of Yerushalem.10:3 Bratcher and Newman, p. 138.

title: Joshua 10:4
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

10:4a

“Come up and help me. We will attack Giveon,

  • “Come to me and help me attack Giveon,

  • “Come with me. Let’s attack Giveon,

Come up and help me: The two clauses Come up and help me indicate that the king of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) asked these four kings to join with him in battle against the Givonim (Gibeonites). The word Come up is used because Yerushalem was at a higher elevation than the other four towns. In languages that do not keep track of elevation, it may be more natural to say “come to me.”

We will attack Giveon (Gibeon): The clause We will attack Giveon indicates that the king of Yerushalem asked the other four kings to gather their armies together with his and attack the people of Giveon.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

Come and help me attack Giveon (GNT)

10:4b

because they have made peace with Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis (Israelites).”

  • for they have made a peace treaty with Yehoshua and the Israelis.”

  • because the people of Giveon have made peace with Yehoshua and the people of Yisrael (Israel).”

because they have made peace with Yehoshua and the Israelis: The clause they have made peace states the reason the king of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) wanted to attack the town of Giveon. The Givonim (Gibeonites) had a treaty with the Israelis.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

because its people have made peace with Yehoshua and the Israelis (GNT)

General Comment on 10:4a-b

It may be more natural in some languages to change the order of 4a and 4b, and state the reason first, as in CEV:

4bThe Givonim have made a peace treaty with Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis (Israelites). 4aCome and help me attack Giveon (Gibeon)! (CEV)

title: Joshua 10:5
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

10:5a

So the five kings of the Amorim (Amorites)—

  • Then these five Amori (Amorite) kings,

  • So these five kings of the Amorim,

So the five kings of the Amorim: The phrase the five kings of the Amorim refers to the kings who were mentioned in verse 3. These kings were all “Amori” kings. The term “Amori” referred to people who lived in the hill country. These five kings lived in the southwestern hill country. The towns of the Givonim (Gibeonites) were north of Yerushalem (Jerusalem). These kings wanted to attack Giveon (Gibeon) because they had trade connections with it.10:5 Hess, p. 190. The peace treaty that the Givonim made with the Israelis (Israelites) made it difficult to trade with them.

10:5b

the kings of Yerushalem, Hevron (Hebron), Yarmut (Jarmuth), Lakish (Lachish), and Eglon—

  • the king of Yerushalem City, the king of Hevron City, the king of Yarmut City, the king of Lakish City, and the king of Eglon City,

  • the kings of Yerushalem, Hevron, Yarmut, Lakish, and Eglon

the kings of Yerushalem, Hevron, Yarmut, Lakish, and Eglon: This list of kings is repeated from verse 3. In some languages it may be more natural to avoid some of the repetition.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

Then the five kings of the Amorim (Amorites)—the kings of Yerushalem, Hevron, Yarmut, Lakish and Eglon (NIV)

When these five Amori (Amorite) kings (CEV)

10:5c

joined forces and advanced with all their armies.

  • gathered their armies, and they all went up

  • got their soldiers together. All five armies went up

joined forces: The clause joined forces indicates that the five kings assembled their armies together.

and advanced with all their armies: The clause advanced with all their armies indicates that the five kings led their armies and went to the towns of Giveon (Gibeon).

advanced: The Hebrew text says they advanced. Although the towns of Giveon were at about the same elevation as Yerushalem (Jerusalem), they were higher than the other four towns. In languages that do not keep track of elevation, it may be more natural to say:

they went with all their armies

10:5d

They camped before Giveon and made war against it.

  • and surrounded Giveon, and attacked it.

  • to Giveon, and surrounded it, and fought against it.

They camped before Giveon: The clause camped before Giveon indicates that the armies surrounded the town so that the Givonim (Gibeonites) could not leave it. They could not find food and would soon become weak. Then the five Amori (Amorite) armies could conquer it.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

(they) surrounded Giveon (Gibeon) (GNT)

(they) moved all their troops into place (NLT)

In 9:17 it says that the Givonim lived in four towns: Giveon, Kefirah (Kephirah), Be’erot (Beeroth) and Kiryat (Kiriath) Jearim. Probably this attack was only against the town of Giveon.

and made war against it: The clause made war against it indicates that the five armies attacked the towns of Giveon.

title: Joshua 10:6
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

Paragraph 10:6–11

The Israelis defended the Givonim (Gibeonites) against their enemies.

10:6a

Then the men of Giveon sent word to Yehoshua (Joshua) in the camp at Gilgal:

  • ¶ The Givonim sent messengers to Yehoshua in the camp at Gilgal.

  • ¶ The leaders of the Givonim sent a message to Yehoshua in his camp at Gilgal.

Then: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as Then introduces the next event in the storyline. Introduce this next event in a natural way in your language.

the men of Giveon (Gibeon): The phrase the men of Giveon refers to an indefinite number of people. Probably these men were some of the Givoni (Gibeonite) leaders.

sent word to Yehoshua: The clause sent word to Yehoshua indicates that the Givonim sent messengers to Yehoshua to ask him for his help.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

sent this message to Yehoshua (NET)

sent messengers to Yehoshua (Joshua) (NLT)

in the camp at Gilgal: The phrase the camp at Gilgal refers to the same camping place where the Israelis (Israelites) were staying. Gilgal was where the Givonim (Gibeonites) first met with the Israelis (9:6).

10:6b

“Do not abandon your servants.

  • They said: “Don’t abandon your servants.

  • They pleaded with them: “We are your servants. Don’t throw us away.

In Hebrew this clause begins with the word translated literally as “saying.” It may be more natural in some languages to begin a new sentence here. In this case, the word “saying” may be translated as:

They said

They begged

They pleaded

Use words that show the urgency of their request.

Do not abandon your servants: The Hebrew clause that the BSB translates as Do not abandon is a Hebrew idiom. It could be more literally translated “do not let your hand drop.” This idiom indicates that the Givonim (Gibeonites) asked Yehoshua (Joshua) to protect them from the Amori (Amorite) kings and their armies. They expected the Israelis (Israelites) to help them because of the peace treaty that they had made with them.

your servants: The phrase your servants is used by the Givonim to show their respect for Yehoshua and the Israelis. Many languages have pronouns or nouns that are used when speaking to superiors. Use whatever is most natural in your language to express this relationship.

10:6c

Come quickly and save us! Help us,

  • Come quickly. Save us. Help us.

  • Come now. We desperately need your help.

Come: In Hebrew, the word Come is more literally “come up". The town of Giveon (Gibeon) was higher than the Israelis’s camp at Gilgal. If your language keeps track of elevation, this would be a place to imply going up a steep hill/mountain.

quickly: The word quickly indicates the urgency of the Givonim’s request. They are in danger and want Yehoshua and the Israeli (Israelite) army to come at once to fight with them against the Amori armies.

and save us! Help us: The two verbs save and Help are very similar in meaning. The Hebrew text uses two verbs with similar meanings to emphasize the urgency of the request. It may be more natural in some languages to express this meaning using one verb and some other means of showing emphasis.

10:6d

because all the kings of the Amorim (Amorites) from the hill country have joined forces against us.”

  • For all the Amori (Amorite) kings who live in the hill country are attacking us.”

  • The kings of all the Amori cities in the mountains have gotten together to attack us.”

because: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as because introduces the reason for the Givonim’s (Gibeonites’) request.

all the kings of the Amorim from the hill country: The Givonim referred to the five kings that are mentioned in 10:3. There may also have been other kings of smaller towns in the hill country, as 10:28–39 suggests. In addition, the Givonim may have exaggerated the facts because they were afraid.10:6 Hess, p. 192.

have joined forces against us: The clause joined forces against us indicates that the Amori kings with their armies were preparing to attack the Givonim.

title: Joshua 10:7
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

Paragraph 10:6–11

The Israelis defended the Givonim (Gibeonites) against their enemies.

10:7a

So Yehoshua (Joshua) and his whole army,

  • So Yehoshua with all his soldiers,

  • So Yehoshua and his entire army,

Yehoshua and his whole army: The phrase his whole army refers the Israeli (Israelite) soldiers. These soldiers went with Yehoshua to fight against the Amorim (Amorites).

10:7b

including all the mighty men of valor,

  • including those who were strongest and bravest,

  • including his best warriors,

all the mighty men of valor: The phrase mighty men of valor refers to the strongest and bravest soldiers in the Israeli army.

Here are some other way to translate this phrase:

including the bravest warriors (NET)

including all the best fighting men (NIV)

10:7c

came from Gilgal.

  • went from Gilgal.

  • left Gilgal to go to Giveon (Gibeon).

came from Gilgal: The clause came from Gilgal indicates that when Yehoshua (Joshua) received the message from the Givonim (Gibeonites), he left the Israeli (Israelite) camp at Gilgal to help the Givonim fight against the Amorim (Amorites). Here, as in 10:6c, the Hebrew word indicates elevation, that the army went up a steep hill/mountain since Giveon was a higher elevation than Gilgal.

General Comment on 10:7

It may be more natural in some languages to include the whole subject (Yehoshua and his army) at the beginning of the verse followed by the verb, like the BSB does.

The Hebrew text mentions Yehoshua first as a way to show the importance of Yehoshua as the leader. Use a way that is natural in your language to emphasize Yehoshua’s importance. For an example of the Hebrew word order, the RSV says:

Yehoshua went up from Gilgal, he and all the people of war with him, and all the mighty men of valor (RSV)

title: Joshua 10:8
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

Paragraph 10:6–11

The Israelis defended the Givonim (Gibeonites) against their enemies.

10:8a

Yahweh said to Yehoshua (Joshua),

  • Yahweh said to Yehoshua:

  • Yahweh told Yehoshua:

The Hebrew word that the BSB leaves untranslated but many English versions translate as “and” indicates that the next action in the story is taking place. Use whatever connecting word is natural in your language to express this.

10:8b

“Do not be afraid of them, for I have delivered them into your hand.

  • “Don’t be afraid of them. I will give you power to defeat them.

  • “Don’t be afraid of the Amorim (Amorites). They will lose when you attack them.

Do not be afraid of them: The pronoun them refers to the Amori (Amorite) kings and their armies. It may be necessary to make this explicit in some languages. For example:

don’t be afraid of the Amorim (CEV)

for I have delivered them into your hand: The clause I have delivered them into your hand states the reason that the Israelis (Israelites) did not need to be afraid of the Amori armies. The clause delivered them into your hand is a Hebrew idiom. It indicates that Yahweh will enable the Israelis to defeat the Amorim. The words Yahweh spoke to Yehoshua (Joshua) are similar to the encouraging words he said to Yehoshua in 1:2,5,9.

Here are some other ways to translate this idiom:

I have given you victory over them (NLT)

they will run away when you attack (CEV)

10:8c

Not one of them shall stand against you.”

  • Not one of them will be able to defeat you.”

  • None of them will be able to fight against you.”

Not one of them shall stand against you: The clause Not one of them shall stand against you is a Hebrew idiom. It indicates that the Amorim (Amorites) will not be able to defeat the Israelis (Israelites). All the Amorim will die or will run away. This happened in 10:10–11.

Here are some other ways to translate this idiom:

not one of them can resist you (NET)

none of them will be able to fight and defeat you

title: Joshua 10:9
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

Paragraph 10:6–11

The Israelis defended the Givonim (Gibeonites) against their enemies.

10:9a

After marching all night from Gilgal,

  • After they walked uphill from Gilgal to Giveon during the night,

  • They did this by walking all night from their camp at Gilgal.

After marching all night from Gilgal: The clause marching all night from Gilgal indicates that it took all night for Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israeli (Israelite) army to walk uphill from Gilgal to Giveon (Gibeon). The distance from Gilgal to Giveon was about twenty to twenty-five miles up a fairly steep hill.10:9 Howard, p. 236, note 186.

marching: The English verb marching is used for soldiers who are walking.

10:9b

Yehoshua caught them by surprise.

  • Yehoshua and the Israeli army made a surprise attack on the Amorim (Amorites),

  • And Yehoshua attacked the Amorim when they were not expecting it.

Yehoshua caught them by surprise: Yehoshua was the leader of the Israelis (Israelites), and he attacked the Amorim along with his army. The word them refers to the Amorim.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

Yehoshua and the Israeli army made a surprise attack upon the Amori (Amorite) armies.

caught them by surprise: The phrase caught them by surprise is a Hebrew idiom. It indicates that the Amorim did not know that the Israelis were going to attack them. It was a surprise.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

attacked them by surprise (NET)

attacked them when they were not expecting it

General Comment on 10:9a-b

In some languages it may be more natural to reorder 9a and 9b so that the events are in the Hebrew sentence order. For example:

So Yehoshua (Joshua) came upon them suddenly, having marched up all night from Gilgal (RSV)

title: Joshua 10:10
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

Paragraph 10:6–11

The Israelis defended the Givonim (Gibeonites) against their enemies.

10:10a

And Yahweh threw them into confusion before Yisrael,

  • Yahweh confused the Amori (Amorite) armies when Yisrael attacked.

  • Yahweh made the Amorim (Amorites) be afraid when they saw the Israelis (Israelites).

And Yahweh threw them into confusion before Yisrael (Israel): The clause threw them into confusion indicates that Yahweh caused the Amori armies to be confused and afraid, so that they could not fight the Israelis.

10:10b

who defeated them in a great slaughter at Giveon (Gibeon),

  • The Israeli (Israelite) army defeated them in a great victory at Giveon.

  • The Israelis killed many of them at Giveon City.

who defeated them in a great slaughter: The Hebrew phrase that the BSB translates as defeated them in a great slaughter is more literally “hit them with a great hit.” This Hebrew idiom means that the Israeli army killed many Amori (Amorite) soldiers.

There is an interpretation issue in this clause. The verb defeated (or “hit”) is marked as masculine singular and there is no nominal subject. English versions interpret the subject of the verb in three ways:

  1. The subject of the verb is the Israeli army. For example:

    and the Israelis (Israelites) slaughtered great numbers of them at Giveon (NLT) (BSB, NIV, RSV, ESV, NET, NLT, NAB, GNT, NCV, CEV)

  2. The subject of the verb is Yehoshua (Joshua). For example:

    Yehoshua utterly defeated them at Giveon (Gibeon) (REB) (REB, NEB, NJPS)

  3. The subject of the verb is Yahweh. For example:

    and He struck them down with a great defeat at Giveon (NASB) (NASB, NJB, GW, KJV)

It is recommended that you follow interpretation (1). Verses 8 and 11 make it clear that the Israelis (Israelites) defeated the Amorim (Amorites) only with Yahweh’s help, but verse 11 also makes it clear that the Israelis had a part in the defeat.

at Giveon: The phrase at Giveon refers to the town of Giveon, where the battle took place.

Here are some other ways to translate this part of the verse:

(Yisrael (Israel)) defeated them with a great victory at Giveon (NIV)

Yisrael thoroughly defeated them at Giveon (Gibeon) (NET)

10:10c

pursued them along the ascent to Beyt-Horon (Beth-horon),

  • The Israelitte army chased them along the road going up to Beyt-Horon,

  • They chased them up to the mountain pass at Upper Beyt-Horon (Upper Beth-horon) City,

pursued them along the ascent to Beyt-Horon: The phrase along the ascent to Beyt-Horon indicates that the Israeli (Israelite) army pursued the Amori (Amorite) armies uphill to Beyt-Horon.

Beyt-Horon: There were two towns named Beyt-Horon. Upper Beyt-Horon was 66 meters higher in altitude than Giveon. Lower Beyt-Horon (Lower Beth-horon) is referred to in verse 11. The road from Giveon goes first uphill to Upper Beyt-Horon, and then down to Lower Beyt-Horon.10:10 Woudstra, p. 172, footnote 19. Upper Beyt-Horon was the highest town in that area. It dominated an important mountain pass that led to the lower hills and the plain to the west.10:10 Hess, p. 195.

The English versions spell the name Beyt-Horon in various ways:

Beyt-Horon (BSB, RSV, ESV, NLT, NABRE, NJPS, NASB, KJV)

Beth Horon (NET, NIV, GNT, GW)

Beyt-Horon (Beth-horon) (CEV)

10:10d

and struck them down as far as Azekah and Makedah (Makkedah).

  • and killed more of them all the way to Azekah and Makedah.

  • kept on killing them going down to Azekah City and Makedah City.

and struck them down: The Hebrew idiom that the BSB translates as struck them down is more literally “hit them.” This idiom indicates that the Israeli (Israelite) army killed many of the Amori (Amorite) fighters.

as far as Azekah and Makedah: The phrase as far as Azekah and Makedah indicates that the Israeli army continued to pursue the Amori armies all the way to the towns of Azekah and Makedah. Azekah was about 30 kilometers south of Beyt-Horon and is considerably lower downhill. Makedah was in the southern part of Kena’an (Canaan), about 14 kilometers west of Hevron (Hebron).10:10 Rasmussen, p. 244.

title: Joshua 10:11
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

Paragraph 10:6–11

The Israelis defended the Givonim (Gibeonites) against their enemies.

10:11a

As they fled before Yisrael

  • While the Amori (Amorite) armies ran away from the Israelis (Israelites),

  • The Amorim (Amorites) fled from the Israelis.

As they fled before Yisrael (Israel): This verse is a flashback. It provides additional information about what happened in 10:10. The word they refers to the Amori armies.

fled before Yisrael: The clause fled before Yisrael indicates that the Amori armies turned and ran away from the Israeli (Israelite) army.

10:11b

along the descent from Beyt-Horon (Beth-horon)

  • and while they were running down the mountain slope from Beyt-Horon,

  • They fled down the hill from Beyt-Horon City.

along the descent from Beyt-Horon: The phrase the descent from Beyt-Horon indicates that the Amori (Amorite) armies ran down from the mountain pass. Starting from Upper Beyt-Horon (Upper Beth-horon), they ran southwest and down out of the hill country.

the descent from Beyt-Horon: There is an interpretation issue with this phrase.

  1. This means the descent of Beyt-Horon, or the way down from Beyt-Horon. For example:

    on the road down from Beth Horon (NIV) (BSB, NIV, NET, GNT, CEV, GW, NASB, NCV, NLT, NRSV, NJPS, REB)

  2. This mean the ascent of Beyt-Horon (Beth-horon). For example:

    while they were going down the ascent of Beyt-Horon (ESV) (ESV, RSV)

It is recommended that you follow interpretation (1). The Hebrew text is clear and it is best to follow it. In verse 10 the Amori army fled from the Israelis (Israelites) at Giveon (Gibeon) town and followed the road up the mountain slope to Beyt-Horon town. This was at the peak of the pass through the mountains. In verse 11 the Amori army then fled through the mountain pass and downhill to the foothills and plains below.

10:11c

to Azekah, Yahweh cast down on them large hailstones from the sky,

  • Yahweh made large hailstones fall on them from the sky, all the way to Azekah, and so many of them died.

  • Then Yahweh threw large hailstones on them from the sky on the road to Azekah. This killed many of them.

to Azekah: The phrase to Azekah indicates that the hail continued to fall on the Amori (Amorite) armies all the way to Azekah. The distance that the Amori armies ran away from the Israelis was about twenty miles.10:11 Howard, p. 237.

Yahweh cast down on them large hailstones from the sky: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as large hailstones refers to lumps of hail. Hail is ice that comes down from the sky. Hail storms occur about five to eight times per year in Palestine.10:11 Boling and Wright p. 282.

the sky: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as sky can also be translated “heaven.” For example:

the Lord threw down great stones from heaven upon them (RSV)

10:11d

and more of them were killed by the hailstones than by the swords of the Israelis (Israelites).

  • The hailstones killed more of the Amorim (Amorites) than the Israelis killed with their swords.

  • More of the Amorim were killed by hailstones than were killed by the Israelis.

more of them were killed by the hailstones than by the swords of the Israelis: Here is another way to translate this phrase:

the hailstones killed more of the enemy soldiers than the Israelis killed with their swords

more of them were killed: The clause more of them were killed shows the result of the hailstorm. It may be clearer in some languages to make the connection between the hail and their death explicit. For example:

because of that, they died

and the hail killed them

by the swords of the Israelis (Israelites): The Hebrew phrase that the BSB translates as by the swords is an idiom. This is a Hebrew idiom. It means that they killed the people.

Here is another way to translate this Hebrew idiom:

more were killed by the hailstones than by the Israelis (GNT)

title: Joshua 10:12
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

10:12a

On the day that Yahweh gave the Amorim (Amorites) over to the Israelis,

  • On the same day that Yahweh helped the Israelis to defeat the Amorim,

  • On the day that they defeated the Amorim with the help of Yahweh,

On the day that Yahweh gave the Amorim over to the Israelis (Israelites): This is the same day as the events referred to in 10:10–11. In 10:12–15, the author told the story of the battle of Giveon (Gibeon) again from another perspective and added new information to what he had already said. It may be clearer in some languages to translate the clause the day that Yahweh gave the Amorim over to the Israelis as an independent sentence. For example, you could say:

Yahweh gave the Israelis victory over the Amorim on that day. On that same day Yehoshua (Joshua) spoke to Yahweh…

Yahweh gave the Amorim over to the Israelis: The clause Yahweh gave the Amorim over to the Israelis is a Hebrew idiom. It indicates that Yahweh helped the Israelis to defeat the Amorim. For example:

the Lord gave the men of Yisrael (Israel) victory over the Amorim (GNT)

10:12b

Yehoshua spoke to Yahweh

  • ¶ Yehoshua spoke to Yahweh.

  • ¶ Yehoshua prayed to Yahweh.

Yehoshua (Joshua) spoke to Yahweh: Some English versions follow the Hebrew word order, “spoke Yehoshua to Yahweh.” It puts the verb before the subject. The natural English word order is Yehoshua spoke as in the BSB. Translate this phrase in a way that is natural in your language.

Yehoshua spoke: In some languages it may be more natural to translate the word spoke as “prayed.” For example:

on that same day Yehoshua prayed to Yahweh while the Israelis (Israelites) watched him

10:12c

in the presence of Yisrael (Israel):

  • Yehoshua prayed in front of the Israelis:

  • Yehoshua prayed while Yisrael was watching, and he said:

in the presence of Yisrael: The phrase in the presence of Yisrael indicates that the Israelis who fought the battle watched while Yehoshua prayed to Yahweh.

10:12d

“O sun, stand still over Giveon (Gibeon), O moon, over the Valley of Ayalon (Aijalon).”

  • “Sun, stop moving above Giveon, and moon, stop moving above the valley of Ayalon.”

  • “Let the sun stay in one place over Giveon, and the moon stay in one place over the valley of Ayalon.”

O sun, stand still over Giveon: The expression, O sun, stand still over Giveon is a kind of figurative language called personification. Personification gives human characteristics to non-human things for poetic effect. In 12b Yehoshua (Joshua) spoke to Yahweh. In 12d Yehoshua spoke to the sun. If the reader does not understand that this is figurative language, it is good to make this clear. One way to clarify this is to include some implicit information:

Yehoshua asked Yahweh to make the sun and the moon stand still. He said, “Sun, stay still at Giveon. And moon, stay still in the valley of Ayalon.”

O sun, stand still: The command sun, stand still may not be natural in some languages. The sun does not have legs and it may not be possible to say that the sun can stand.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

Sun, stop moving in the sky

Sun, stay in one place

over Giveon (Gibeon): It may be more natural to translate the phrase over Giveon as “at Giveon,” or “above Giveon.” The sun shone in the sky over the town of Giveon. Use a preposition that is natural in your language.

O moon, over the Valley of Ayalon (Aijalon): The expression O moon, over the Valley of Ayalon is an example of personification. Personification gives human characteristics to non-human things for poetic effect.

the Valley of Ayalon: The phrase Valley of Ayalon refers to the valley where the town of Ayalon was, seven to ten miles west of Giveon.10:12 Bratcher and Newman, p. 143. The Amorim (Amorites) fled from Giveon as far as Azekah (10:10d). Ayalon was between Giveon and Azekah.

Here are some ways to translate 10:12c-d:

Yehoshua (Joshua) prayed to the Lord in front of all the people of Yisrael (Israel). He said, “Let the sun stand still over Giveon, and the moon over the valley of Ayalon.” (NLT)

In the presence of the people of Yisrael, Yehoshua said, “Yahweh, cause the sun to stop moving over Giveon and cause the moon to stop moving over the valley of Ayalon.”

General Comment on 10:12d

In the ancient Near East many people believed that natural objects such as the sun and the moon had a soul or a spirit. The Bible does not teach this. Yehoshua did not actually speak to the sun or the moon, and he did not expect them to respond to his command. The language Yehoshua used is a figure of speech called “personification.” Personification gives human characteristics to non-human things. It is used to add emotional impact to the story. As you translate this verse, keep in mind that this response by the sun and moon to Yehoshua’s command is poetic language. It should not be understood literally.

A miracle of God’s power took place when he lengthened the day. It was God, responding to the prayer of Yehoshua, who caused the miracle. The sun and moon did not actually do anything. God made them stand still.

Yehoshua spoke to both the sun and the moon. Biblical scholars do not agree on why he addressed both the sun and the moon. One possibility is that Yehoshua prayed this prayer in the early morning when the sun was rising in the east and the moon was setting in the west.

title: Joshua 10:13
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

10:13a

So the sun stood still and the moon stopped

  • Then the sun stood still and the moon did not move

  • So the sun and the moon both stopped and remained in one place.

So the sun stood still: The clause So the sun stood still is a result clause. This was what happened as a result of Yehoshua’s (Joshua’s) prayer. Use whatever connecting word indicates a result in your language. The clause the sun stood still indicates that the sun remained in the same place in the sky. God answered Yehoshua’s prayer and caused the sun to stay still.

and the moon stopped: The clause and the moon stopped indicates that the moon remained in one place in the sky, because Yehoshua prayed for this to happen. God answered Yehoshua’s prayer and caused the moon to stay still.

10:13b

until the nation took vengeance upon its enemies.

  • until the Israelis (Israelites) completely defeated their enemies.

  • They stayed there until Yisrael (Israel) finished fighting its enemies.

until the nation took vengeance upon its enemies: The sun and moon did not move through the sky for a long period of time. This allowed Yisrael to finish the battle against their enemies.
