the nation: The phrase the nation refers to the Israelis.

took vengeance upon its enemies: The clause took vengeance upon its enemies indicates that the Israelis defeated the Amorim (Amorites).

10:13c

Is this not written in the Book of Jashar?

  • This event is written in the Book of Jashar.

  • This is written down in the Book of Jashar.

Is this not written in the Book of Jashar?: This is a rhetorical question that functions as a statement. The expected response is “yes, it is.” It may be more natural in some languages to translate this as a statement. For example:

This is what is written down in the Book of Jashar

the Book of Jashar: The term Book of Jashar probably refers to a collection of stories about wars. It is also mentioned one other place in the Old Testament, 2 Samuel 1:18.10:13 Bratcher and Newman, p. 143.

10:13d

“So the sun stopped in the middle of the sky

  • The sun remained in the middle of the sky,

  • The sun stopped in the middle of the sky,

So the sun stopped in the middle of the sky: Here is another way to translate this phrase:

The sun stayed in the midst of heaven (RSV)

10:13e

and delayed going down about a full day.”

  • and did not set for a whole day.

  • and Yahweh delayed it’s going down for almost a whole day.

and delayed going down about a full day: This clause adds information about the length of time the sun did not move in the sky. Yahweh made the sun stay in one place for about one day. The Hebrew clause that the BSB translates as delayed going down is a Hebrew idiom.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

and did not go down for a whole day (GNT)

title: Joshua 10:14
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

10:14a

There has been no day like it before or since,

  • There has never been a day like this before or since,

  • Never before or after this day was there anything like this.

There has been no day like it before or since: The clause There has been no day like it before or since indicates that the day when the Israelis (Israelites) fought the Amorim (Amorites) was an extraordinary day. In the history of the world, there was never a day when God answered such a bold request from a human being.

10:14b

when Yahweh listened to the voice of a man,

  • a day when Yahweh listened to a man pray such a prayer.

  • There was never a day on which Yahweh did something like that for somebody who prayed.

when Yahweh listened to the voice of a man: There are two ways to interpret the clause when Yahweh listened to the voice of a man.

  1. It means that Yahweh listened to Yehoshua (Joshua) and granted his request. For example:

    there has never been a day like this one before or since, when the Lord answered such a prayer (NLT) (BSB, NLT, NIV, RSV, ESV, NASB, NCV, NJPS, REB, CEV, KJV)

  2. It means that Yahweh obeyed Yehoshua. For example:

    never before, and never since, has there been a day like it, when the Lord obeyed a human being (GNT) (GNT, GW, NAB, NET, NJB, NABRE)

It is recommended that you follow option (1). This is followed by a majority of English versions. Sometimes the Hebrew word “to listen” can be translated as “obey.” But it is only used for humans or angels obeying God, not the other way around. A suggestion that God obeyed a human being seems unlikely.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

there has never been a day like it before or since, a day when the Lord listened to a man (NIV)

never before and never since has the Lord done anything like that for someone who prayed (CEV)

10:14c

because Yahweh fought for Yisrael (Israel).

  • Yahweh really did fight for Yisrael.

  • Surely the Israelis (Israelites) won the battle because of what Yahweh did for them.

because: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as because can also mean “surely” or “certainly.” It is used to emphasize a statement. Some examples of its use in English translations are:

surely the Lord was fighting for Yisrael! (NIV)

the Lord really was fighting for Yisrael (CEV)

Yahweh fought for Yisrael: The clause Yahweh fought for Yisrael indicates that the Israelis were able to win the battle because of the miracles that Yahweh did for them.

title: Joshua 10:15
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

10:15

Then Yehoshua (Joshua) returned with all Yisrael to the camp at Gilgal.

  • Then Yehoshua and the Israeli (Israelite) soldiers went back to their camp at Gilgal.

  • After the battle, Yehoshua and all the Israelis (Israelites) went back to their camp at Gilgal.

Then Yehoshua returned with all Yisrael to the camp at Gilgal: The phrase all Yisrael refers to the Israeli army. It may be more natural in some languages to translate the two subjects, Yehoshua and all Yisrael, as one compound phrase. For example:

then Yehoshua and the entire Israeli army returned to their camp at Gilgal

General Comment on 10:6–15

These verses tell the story of the battle against the Amorim (Amorites), which is completed in verse 15. Verses 16–21 tell the story of the five Amori (Amorite) kings who fled and hid in a cave. The CEV supplies some implicit information with verse 15:

After the battle, Yehoshua and the Israelis went back to their camp at Gilgal. (CEV)

This implicit information may help to clarify the transition between verse 15 and 16.

title: Joshua 10:16
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

10:16

Now the five kings had fled and hidden in the cave at Makedah (Makkedah).

  • ¶ However, the five kings ran away and hid in a cave near Makedah.

  • ¶ During the battle, the five Amori (Amorite) kings escaped and hid in a cave at Makedah City.

Now the five kings: The phrase the five kings refers to the five Amori kings who joined together to fight the Israelis (Israelites). There is a list of these kings in 10:3.

had fled: The verb fled indicates that the kings ran away from the battle. There is implicit information: The five kings ran away before the battle finished. They probably ran away when they realized that the Israelis would win the battle. It may be more natural in some languages to include the implicit information in this part of the verse. For example:

During the battle the five kings escaped (NLT)

While the enemy soldiers were running from the Israelis, the five enemy kings ran away (CEV)

and hidden in the cave at Makedah (Makkedah): The phrase in the cave at Makedah refers to a cave near the town of Makedah. 10:10 stated that the Israeli (Israelite) army chased the Amori armies as far as the towns of Azekah and Makedah. The five enemy kings found a cave near Makedah where they could hide from the Israelis.

title: Joshua 10:17
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

10:17a

And Yehoshua (Joshua) was informed:

  • Someone told Yehoshua:

  • And Yehoshua heard the news that

And Yehoshua was informed: The phrase Yehoshua was informed indicates that somebody spoke to Yehoshua. This passive form makes it possible to leave the speaker unnamed. Use a form in your language to indicate that the speaker is not known.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

Someone told Yehoshua

Yehoshua heard the news that

Yehoshua’s (Joshua’s) soldiers told him (CEV)

10:17b

“The five kings have been found; they are hiding in the cave at Makedah (Makkedah).”

  • “We have found the five Amori (Amorite) kings. They are hiding in a cave near Makedah.”

  • they found the five enemy kings hidden in a cave at Makedah City.

The five kings have been found: The clause The five kings have been found is a passive construction. If a passive construction is not natural, it is possible to translate this clause in the active voice.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

We have found the five kings

They have found the five enemy kings.

they are hiding in the cave at Makedah (Makkedah): The town of Makedah was mentioned in 10:10. It may be more natural in some languages to translate the clause hiding in the cave at Makedah as an independent sentence. For example:

They are hiding in a cave near the town of Makkeda

title: Joshua 10:18
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

10:18a

So Yehoshua (Joshua) said, “Roll large stones against the mouth of the cave,

  • So Yehoshua said: “Roll large rocks over the cave opening,

  • Yehoshua told them: “Close the mouth of the cave by rolling big stones against it.

So Yehoshua said: The clause So Yehoshua said is a result clause. Yehoshua gave a command as a result of what the soldiers told him. For example:

Therefore

Use an appropriate means to indicate result in your language.

Yehoshua said: It may be more natural in some languages to translate the word said as “commanded” or “answered.” It may also be more natural to include the addressee in the clause. For example:

So Yehoshua commanded them

Roll large stones against the mouth of the cave: Yehoshua (Joshua) told his soldiers to Roll large stones against the mouth of the cave so that the entrance to the cave was closed. The five kings could not leave the cave until the Israelis (Israelites) finished fighting the battle. It may be more natural in some languages to make this information explicit. For example:

Cover the opening of the cave with large rocks (NLT)

10:18b

and post men there to guard them.

  • and choose some men to guard the kings.

  • Then leave some men there to guard it so that the kings cannot come out.

and post men there to guard them: The clause post men there to guard them indicates that Yehoshua had some soldiers guard the entrance to the cave, so that the five kings would not push away the rocks and get out. The pronoun them refers to the five kings.

title: Joshua 10:19
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

10:19a

But you, do not stop there.

  • But as for you, don’t stay there.

  • However, don’t stay there yourselves.

But you, do not stop there: The Hebrew clause that the BSB translates as you, do not stop there is more literally “you, do not stand.” The pronoun “you” is in an emphatic position. Use whatever way is natural in your language to give this emphasis.

The clause do not stop there indicates that Yehoshua (Joshua) made a distinction between the people who gave the order to guard the cave and the people who guarded it.

10:19b

Pursue your enemies and attack them from behind.

  • Chase after your enemies and kill those who are at the back.

  • Continue chasing the enemy, attack them from behind.

Pursue your enemies: The clause Pursue your enemies indicates that Yehoshua commanded these soldiers to continue fighting and to chase the enemy soldiers.

and attack them from behind: The Amori (Amorite) soldiers were running away from the battlefield. Yehoshua told the Israeli (Israelite) soldiers to attack those who were running from behind.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

attack them from behind

10:19c

Do not let them reach their cities,

  • Don’t let them get into their cities.

  • Don’t let them escape behind their city walls.

Do not let them reach their cities: The clause Do not let them reach their cities indicates that Yehoshua (Joshua) commanded the Israeli army to kill the enemy soldiers before they could return to their walled towns. If they reached their towns they would be protected by the town walls and could continue to fight.

10:19d

for Yahweh your God has delivered them into your hand.”

  • Yahweh your God has already made sure that you will defeat them.”

  • For Yahweh your God has defeated them for you.”

for Yahweh your God has delivered them into your hand: The clause Yahweh your God has delivered them into your hand indicates that Yahweh has decided that the Israelis (Israelites) will defeat the Amorim (Amorites). The Israeli (Israelite) army should not hesitate to chase and attack the enemy soldiers because they can have confidence that Yahweh will enable them to defeat them.

title: Joshua 10:20
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

10:20a

So Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis continued to inflict a terrible slaughter

  • Yehoshua and the Israelis killed many of the Amorim (Amorites),

  • Yehoshua and the Israeli (Israelite) army killed many Amori (Amorite) soldiers,

So Yehoshua and the Israelis (Israelites): The phrase Yehoshua and the Israelis refers to Yehoshua and the Israeli army.

continued to inflict a terrible slaughter: The clause continued to inflict a terrible slaughter is a Hebrew idiom. It indicates that the Israeli army killed many of the Amori soldiers.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

Yehoshua and the Israelis destroyed them completely (NIV)

Yehoshua and the men of Yisrael (Israel) slaughtered them (GNT)

10:20b

until they had finished them off,

  • and destroying almost all of them.

  • until there were hardly any left alive.

until they had finished them off: The clause until they had finished them off indicates that the Israeli (Israelite) army killed almost all the Amori (Amorite) soldiers. This clause restates the information in 10:20a. It emphasizes how completely the Israelis (Israelites) defeated the Amorim (Amorites). If repetition is not a natural way to show emphasis, it may be more natural to combine 20a and b. For example,

So Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis killed the enemy (NCV)

Yehoshua and the Israelis defeated them decisively, almost destroying them (GW)

In some languages there may be grammatical particles or other means that you can use to emphasize this important information in the story.

10:20c

and the remaining survivors retreated to the fortified cities.

  • A few were able to get back to their walled cities.

  • But a few who were still alive escaped back into their strong cities.

and: It may be more natural in many languages to begin a new sentence and to leave the word and untranslated.

the remaining survivors: The phrase the remaining survivors indicates that a few Amori (Amorite) soldiers were still alive.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

and when the survivors (NRSV)

but the few who were left (NIV)

retreated to the fortified cities: The clause retreated to the fortified cities indicates that a few Amori soldiers who remained alive escaped into their own towns. These towns had walls to protect them.

title: Joshua 10:21
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

10:21a

The whole army returned safely to Yehoshua (Joshua) in the camp at Makedah (Makkedah),

  • Then the whole army returned safely to Yehoshua in the camp at Makedah.

  • Then the Israelis (Israelites) went back safely to Yehoshua at Makedah.

The whole army returned safely to Yehoshua in the camp at Makedah: The clause returned safely to Yehoshua in the camp at Makedah indicates that Yehoshua had made a temporary camp at Makedah and waited there for the army to return from battle.

Makedah: The town of Makedah was mentioned in 10:10. Makedah was in the southern part of Kena’an (Canaan), about 14 kilometers west of Hevron (Hebron).10:21 Rasmussen, p. 244. Yehoshua made his camp there temporarily while the Israeli (Israelite) army attacked the towns in the south of Kena’an.

General Comment on 10:20a-21a

It may be clearer in some languages to split this long sentence into several shorter sentences. For example:

20aYehoshua and the Israeli soldiers killed almost all of the Amori (Amorite) soldiers. 20bThere were hardly any left alive. 20cThose who were still alive ran into their fortified towns. 21aThen all the Israeli soldiers returned safely to Yehoshua in the camp at Makedah.

10:21b

and no one dared to utter a word against the Israelis.

  • None of the Kena’ani (Canaanite) people dared to say anything bad about the Israelis.

  • No one was brave enough to threaten the Israelis (Israelites).

no one dared to utter a word against the Israelis: The Hebrew clause that the BSB translates as no one dared to utter a word is more literally “not a man sharpened his tongue.” This Hebrew idiom indicates that none of the Kena’anim (Canaanites) criticized the Israelis or spoke anything bad about them, because they saw how powerful the Israelis were.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

no one dared to speak against any of the Israelis (NRSV)

no one uttered a word against the Israelis (NIV)

no one around there dared say anything bad about the Israelis (CEV)

title: Joshua 10:22
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

10:22a

Then Yehoshua (Joshua) said, “Open the mouth of the cave

  • ¶ Yehoshua told his soldiers: “Now, move the rocks from the entrance to the cave

  • ¶ Then Yehoshua commanded his soldiers: “Take away the rocks from the cave entrance,

Then Yehoshua said: The clause Yehoshua said indicates that Yehoshua gave a command to his soldiers. It may be more natural in some languages to make that information explicit. For example:

Then Yehoshua commanded his soldiers

Open the mouth of the cave: The clause Open the mouth of the cave indicates that Yehoshua commanded some of his soldiers to roll away the rocks that covered the entrance to the cave.

10:22b

and bring those five kings out to me.”

  • and bring the five kings out to me.”

  • and then bring out the five kings who are hiding there.”

and bring those five kings out to me: The five kings refers to the kings of the Amorim (Amorites) who ran away from the battle and hid in the cave.

title: Joshua 10:23
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

10:23a

So they brought the five kings out of the cave—

  • So they obeyed him, and brought the five kings out from the cave.

  • So the soldiers brought the five kings out of the cave,

So they brought: The clause So they brought indicates that the soldiers obeyed Yehoshua’s (Joshua’s) command.

the five kings out of the cave: The phrase the five kings refers to the five Amori (Amorite) kings who fought against the Israelis (Israelites).

It is possible to combine these two clauses into one.

Here are some other ways to translate these clauses:

So Yehoshua’s men brought the five kings out of the cave (NCV)

The soldiers opened the entrance to the cave and brought out the kings (CEV)

10:23b

the kings of Yerushalem (Jerusalem), Hevron (Hebron), Yarmut (Jarmuth), Lakish (Lachish), and Eglon.

  • They were the king of Yerushalem, the king of Hevron, the king of Yarmut, the king of Lakish and the king of Eglon.

  • namely the kings of Yerushalem City, Hevron City, Yarmut City, Lakish City, and Eglon City.

the kings of Yerushalem, Hevron, Yarmut, Lakish, and Eglon: These five kings were first named in 10:3. The Hebrew text states this information in detail to emphasize the importance of what is happening. Some languages may have particles or grammatical means other than repetition to give importance to some information.

title: Joshua 10:24
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

10:24a

When they had brought the kings to Yehoshua (Joshua),

  • When they brought the kings out to Yehoshua,

  • When the soldiers brought them out,

When they had brought the kings to Yehoshua: The clause When they had brought the kings to Yehoshua repeats information already stated in 10:23. It links 10:23 with 10:24 and emphasizes that the soldiers obeyed Yehoshua’s commands. This head-tail linkage is natural in some languages but not in others. It may be more natural to leave some of this information implicit. For example,

When they brought them to Yehoshua (GW)

When they brought them out (NLT)

After this

10:24b

he summoned all the men of Yisrael (Israel) and said to the army commanders who had accompanied him,

  • he called all the soldiers together and told the officers who fought with him:

  • Yehoshua (Joshua) called the soldiers to come and he told the commanders of his army

he summoned all the men of Yisrael: The clause he summoned indicates that he called all the soldiers together.

all the men of Yisrael: The phrase all the men of Yisrael refers to all the soldiers in the Israeli (Israelite) army.

and said to the army commanders who had accompanied him: It may be more natural in some languages to begin a new sentence. For example:

He said to all the commanders of his army (NCV)

He told the army officers

the army commanders: The phrase the army commanders indicates the officers of the Israeli army.

who had accompanied him: The relative clause who had accompanied him refers to the officers of Yehoshua’s army. If translating this clause implies that there were some officers who did not go with Yehoshua, it may be better to leave it untranslated.10:24 Bratcher and Newman, p. 149. Some English versions leave this information implicit. For example:

He said to the commanders of his army (NCV)

Yehoshua (Joshua) told the commanders of his army (NLT)

10:24c

“Come here and put your feet on the necks of these kings.”

  • “Come here. Put your feet on the necks of these five kings.”

  • to put their feet on the necks of the five kings as a sign of victory.

Come here: The clause Come here indicates that Yehoshua commanded his officers to come close to where he was.

and put your feet on the necks of these kings: Yehoshua ordered his officers to put your feet on the necks of these kings because this symbolized victory in the Ancient Near East. There is implied information. Before the army officers could put their feet on the necks of the defeated kings, they must force the kings to lie down. It may be helpful to make this implied information explicit. For example:

Make the five kings lie down and put your feet on their necks

10:24d

So the commanders came forward and put their feet on their necks.

  • So the officers did exactly as Yehoshua (Joshua) told them to do.

  • So the commanders obeyed Yehoshua and put their feet on their necks.

So the commanders came forward: The clause commanders came forward indicates that the army officers came close to Yehoshua as he had told them to.

and put their feet on their necks: Yehoshua’s command to the soldiers in the first part of the verse is repeated using the same words to emphasize that the army officers obeyed Yehoshua exactly. It may not be natural in some languages to repeat this information in the same words. In other languages it may be more natural to make a summary statement. For example:

So the army commanders did exactly as Yehoshua had commanded them

The officers obeyed Yehoshua and did so.

title: Joshua 10:25
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

10:25a

“Do not be afraid or discouraged,” Yehoshua (Joshua) said.

  • Then Yehoshua said to them: “Do not ever be afraid at all.

  • And Yehoshua said to the officers: “Do not be afraid or discouraged.

“Do not be afraid or discouraged,” Yehoshua said: Use whatever connecting word is natural to indicate continuing narrative action.

Do not be afraid or discouraged: The two words afraid and discouraged have a similar meaning. This command is similar to the command that Yahweh gave to Yehoshua in 1:9 and uses the same words that Yahweh spoke to Yehoshua in 8:1. These two words together indicate that the Israelis (Israelites) should not be afraid at all.

10:25b

“Be strong and courageous,

  • Be strong and brave.

  • Be determined and have courage,

Be strong and courageous: The command Be strong and courageous repeats the words that Yahweh spoke to Yehoshua (Joshua) in 1:9. It is recommended that you translate them in the same way as 1:9 if possible.

10:25c

for Yahweh will do this to all the enemies you fight.”

  • Yahweh will defeat all your enemies as he defeated these kings.”

  • because this is what Yahweh is going to do to all the people you fight against.”

for Yahweh will do this to all the enemies you fight: The clause for Yahweh will do this to all the enemies you fight indicates the reason that the Israelis (Israelites) did not have to be afraid. Yahweh will defeat all the Israelis’s enemies as he defeated the Amori (Amorite) kings and their armies.

you: The pronoun you refers to the army commanders.

title: Joshua 10:26
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

10:26a

After this, Yehoshua (Joshua) struck down and killed the kings,

  • Then Yehoshua killed the kings

  • After this, Yehoshua put the five kings to death,

After this: The phrase After this indicates that the next event took place after the officers put their feet on the necks of the kings.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

After the officers had done this

Yehoshua struck down and killed the kings: The two clauses struck down and killed the kings are parallel and have the same meaning. They indicate that Yehoshua killed the five kings. In some languages it may be more natural to use one verb rather than two to indicate this. For example:

Then Yehoshua killed each of the five kings (NLT)

10:26b

and he hung their bodies on five trees

  • and hung their bodies on five poles,

  • and hung their dead bodies on five trees,

and he hung their bodies on five trees: The clause he hung their bodies on five trees indicates that after Yehoshua (Joshua) killed the five kings, he hung them each on a tree as a public sign that God had cursed them. This was the same as Yehoshua did to the king of Ay (Ai) in 8:29, and you should translate it in a similar way. See also Deuteronomy 21:22–23 where Mosheh (Moses) gave rules for how such executions should be done.

10:26c

and left them there until evening.

  • where they hung until evening.

  • and left them there until the evening.

and left them there until evening: The clause and left them there until evening indicates that Yehoshua left the five kings on the trees all day. In the evening, when the sun was setting, he took them down. This was commanded by Mosheh in Deuteronomy 21:23.

title: Joshua 10:27
content:
Section 10:1–27 Five Kena’ani (Canaanite) Kings attacked the Israelis (Israelites)

The kings of five Kena’ani towns joined together to fight against Giveon (Gibeon). Because the Israelis had a peace treaty with Giveon, they helped them in their fight. Yahweh helped the Israelis by sending down hailstones on the Kena’anim (Canaanites), and by causing the sun to stop moving so that the Israelis could continue their victory. The five Kena’ani kings were captured and put to death.

Here are some other possible section headings:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the Kena’an (Canaan) group

The sun stood still

10:27a

At sunset

  • But when the sun went down,

  • When the sun was going down,

At sunset: The phrase At sunset refers to the time when the sun goes down. In some languages it may be more natural to begin a new sentence at this point. For example:

when the sun was setting

10:27b

Yehoshua (Joshua) ordered that they be taken down from the trees

  • Yehoshua commanded his soldiers to take the bodies of the kings down from the trees.

  • Yehoshua told the soldiers: “Take the bodies down,

Yehoshua ordered: It may be more natural in some languages to supply the direct object:

Yehoshua commanded his soldiers.

that they be taken down from the trees: The clause that they be taken down from the trees indicates that Yehoshua’s soldiers took the bodies of the kings down from the trees where they were hanging.

10:27c

and thrown into the cave in which they had hidden.

  • The soldiers threw the bodies into the same cave where the kings hid.

  • and throw them into the same cave where they hid themselves.”

and thrown into the cave in which they had hidden: The clause and thrown into the cave in which they had hidden indicates that Yehoshua’s (Joshua’s) soldiers threw the bodies of the dead kings into the same cave in which they first hid. It may be more natural in some languages to begin a new sentence here. It may also be helpful to make the subject and object explicit. For example:

Then the soldiers threw the bodies into the same cave where they had been hiding

10:27d

Then large stones were placed against the mouth of the cave,

  • They covered the opening of the cave with large rocks,

  • Then the soldiers covered the cave entrance with large stones.

Then large stones were placed against the mouth of the cave: The clause Then large stones were placed against the mouth of the cave indicates that after the soldiers threw the dead bodies into the cave, they covered up the cave entrance again with large rocks. The place where the kings hid themselves to escape Yehoshua’s army became their tomb.

10:27e

and the stones are there to this day.

  • which are there to this day.

  • Those stones are still there to this day.

and the stones are there to this day: In some languages it may be more natural to begin a new sentence at this point. For example:

The stones remain there until this day

to this day: The phrase to this day indicates that, at the time the author wrote the book of Yehoshua (Joshua), the stones were still there.

title: Joshua 10:28
content:
Section 10:28–43 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of southern Kena’an (Canaan)

Yehoshua (Joshua) defeated seven other important towns in Southern Kena’an.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the southern towns

10:28a

On that day Yehoshua captured Makedah (Makkedah)

  • ¶ That day Yehoshua defeated the city of Makedah.

  • ¶ On that same day, Yehoshua and the Israelis attacked and defeated Makedah City.

On that day: The phrase On that day indicates that Yehoshua and the Israeli (Israelite) army attacked and captured Makedah on the same day that they killed the five kings.

Yehoshua (Joshua) captured Makedah: The clause Yehoshua captured Makedah indicates that Yehoshua and the Israeli army captured the town of Makedah. It may be necessary in some languages to make explicit that the Israeli army also fought, and that Yehoshua did not capture Makedah by himself. For example:

Yehoshua and the Israelis (Israelites) captured the town of Makedah on that day

Makedah: The town of Makedah was about 40 kilometers southwest of Giveon (Gibeon).10:28 Bratcher and Newman, p. 151. The cave where the five Amori (Amorite) kings hid was near Makedah. After Yehoshua killed the five kings, he and his army proceeded to capture this nearby town.

10:28b

and put it to the sword, along with its king.

  • He killed the king and the people of the city with his sword.

  • They killed the king and the people of this city.

and put it to the sword, along with its king: This indicates that Yehoshua and the Israeli (Israelite) army killed the king of Makedah (Makkedah) and the people who lived there.

put it to the sword: The phrase put it to the sword is a Hebrew idiom. The word “smote” is the past tense of “smite.” It means “hit.” This idiom means that they killed the king and the people of Makedah.

Here is another way to translate this Hebrew idiom:

Yehoshua (Joshua) killed its king and everyone else in the town (CEV)

10:28c

He devoted to destruction everyone in the city, leaving no survivors.

  • He devoted them to Yahweh for destruction. He killed them all.

  • They killed every single person because Yahweh claimed them.

He devoted to destruction everyone in the city: The Hebrew verb that the BSB translates as devoted to destruction everyone comes from the same root word as the term “devoted for destruction” used in 6:17b. It refers to people or things that are claimed by Yahweh and cannot be bought back by any means. They must be destroyed. If possible, translate this word in the same way as you did in 6:17b. For example:

he devoted to destruction every person in it (ESV)

leaving no survivors: The clause leaving no survivors indicates that not a single person was left alive in the town.

10:28d

So he did to the king of Makedah (Makkedah) as he had done to the king of Yeriho (Jericho).

  • He did the same thing to the king of Makedah that he did to the king of Yeriho.

  • He killed the king of Makedah City in the same way that he killed the king of Yeriho City.

So he did to the king of Makedah as he had done to the king of Yeriho: The pronoun he refers to Yehoshua (Joshua). The clause he did to the king of Makedah as he had done to the king of Yeriho indicates that Yehoshua killed the king of Makedah. It may be clearer to make this information explicit. For example:

and he killed the king of Makedah as he had killed the king of Yeriho (NLT)

A similar phrase was used in 8:2 referring to the king of Ay (Ai).

title: Joshua 10:29
content:
Section 10:28–43 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of southern Kena’an (Canaan)

Yehoshua (Joshua) defeated seven other important towns in Southern Kena’an.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the southern towns

10:29a

Then Yehoshua and all Yisrael with him moved on from Makedah (Makkedah) to Livnah (Libnah)

  • Then Yehoshua and the Israelis went from Makedah to Livnah

  • Yehoshua and the soldiers left Makedah City and went to Livnah City

Then Yehoshua and all Yisrael with him moved on from Makedah: The clause Then Yehoshua…moved on from Makedah indicates that Yehoshua left the town of Makedah.

and all Yisrael with him: The phrase and all Yisrael with him indicates that the whole Israeli (Israelite) army went with him. The terms “Yehoshua (Joshua)” and all Yisrael are both the subjects of this sentence. In some languages it may be more natural to put them together. For example:

Then Yehoshua and all Yisrael with him moved on from Makedah to Livnah (NIV)

Then Yehoshua, along with his whole army, left Makedah and went to fight against Livnah.

to Livnah (Libnah): The town of Livnah was about 11 kilometers southwest of Makedah (Makkedah).

10:29b

and fought against Livnah.

  • and fought against it.

  • and attacked it.

and fought against Livnah: The clause fought against Livnah indicates that Yehoshua (Joshua) and his army attacked the town of Livnah.

title: Joshua 10:30
content:
Section 10:28–43 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of southern Kena’an (Canaan)

Yehoshua (Joshua) defeated seven other important towns in Southern Kena’an.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the southern towns

10:30a

And Yahweh also delivered that city and its king into the hand of Yisrael,

  • Yahweh gave the Israelis the power to defeat the king of Livnah (Libnah) and his people.

  • Yahweh gave the Israelis victory over Livnah and its king,

And Yahweh also delivered that city and its king into the hand of Yisrael: The clause Yahweh also delivered that city and its king into the hand of Yisrael indicates that Yahweh gave Yehoshua and the Israeli (Israelite) army the power to defeat the king and the town of Livnah. They captured the town of Livnah as they had captured the town of Makedah (Makkedah).

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

The Lord also gave that city and its king into Yisrael’s hand (NIV)

The Lord also gave the Israelis (Israelites) victory over this city and its king (GNT)

10:30b

and Yehoshua (Joshua) put all the people to the sword,

  • The Israelis killed every single person in the city with their swords.

  • and they killed the king and all the people.

and Yehoshua: There are two ways to understand the pronoun “he,” which the BSB translates as Yehoshua.

  1. The pronoun “he” refers to Yehoshua and the Israeli (Israelite) army. For example:

    the city and everyone in it Yehoshua put to the sword (NIV) (BSB, NIV, NET, NJPS, GNT, NLT, NCV, CEV)

  2. The pronoun “he” refers to Yahweh. For example:

    and he struck it with the edge of the sword, and every person in it (ESV) (ESV, RSV, GW, NABRE, KJV)

It is recommended that you follow option (1). The pronoun “he” probably to refers to Yehoshua (Joshua) as the representative of the Israeli army, or to the Israeli army itself.

put all the people to the sword: The Hebrew clause that the BSB translates as put all the people to the sword is an idiom. It indicates that Yehoshua and his army killed every person in the town of Livnah (Libnah).

Here is another way to translate this Hebrew idiom:

he killed all the people (GW)

killed every person in it (GNT)

10:30c

leaving no survivors.

  • Not a single person was left alive.

  • They didn’t let any of them live.

leaving no survivors: The clause leaving no survivors indicates that there were no people still alive in Livnah (Libnah) after the Israeli (Israelite) army attacked it. This information was stated in a positive manner in the previous part of the verse. It is restated here negatively. This is a way to emphasize that every single person died.

Here is another way to translate 30b-c:

Yehoshua (Joshua) and his army killed everyone in Livnah with their swords, leaving no survivors

10:30d

And he did to the king of Livnah as he had done to the king of Yeriho (Jericho).

  • And they did the same thing to the king that they did to the king of Yeriho.

  • Yehoshua killed the king of Livnah in the same way that he killed the king of Yeriho.

And he did to the king of Livnah as he had done to the king of Yeriho: The clause he did to the king of Livnah as he had done to the king of Yeriho is similar to the clause in 10:28d. It indicates that Yehoshua killed the king of Livnah. You should translate this in a similar way to 10:28d.

It may be helpful to begin a new sentence here. For example:

Then Yehoshua killed the king of Livnah (Libnah) as he had killed the king of Yeriho (NLT)

title: Joshua 10:31
content:
Section 10:28–43 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of southern Kena’an (Canaan)

Yehoshua (Joshua) defeated seven other important towns in Southern Kena’an.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the southern towns

10:31a

And Yehoshua and all Yisrael with him moved on from Livnah (Libnah) to Lakish (Lachish).

  • ¶ Then Yehoshua and his soldiers went from Livnah to Lakish.

  • ¶ Yehoshua then went with his army from Livnah City to Lakish City.

And Yehoshua and all Yisrael with him moved on from Livnah to Lakish: The clause Yehoshua and all Yisrael with him moved on from Livnah to Lakish has similar wording to 10:29a. It indicates that Yehoshua and his army went from Livnah to Lakish. It is recommended that you translate this clause in the same way that you translated the clause in 10:29a.

Lakish: The town of Lakish was about 17 kilometers south of Livnah.10:31 Bratcher and Newman, p. 152.

10:31b

They laid siege to it and fought against it.

  • They surrounded it, and attacked it.

  • They set up their camp around the city and attacked it.

They laid siege to it: The verb laid siege indicates that Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis (Israelites) set up their camp around the town so that no one could leave the town.

and fought against it: The clause fought against it indicates that the Israeli (Israelite) army attacked the town of Lakish (Lachish).

title: Joshua 10:32
content:
Section 10:28–43 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of southern Kena’an (Canaan)

Yehoshua (Joshua) defeated seven other important towns in Southern Kena’an.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the southern towns

10:32a

And Yahweh delivered Lakish (Lachish) into the hand of Yisrael,

  • Yahweh gave the Israelis victory over Lakish.

  • Yahweh helped the Israelis capture Lakish City.

And Yahweh delivered Lakish into the hand of Yisrael: The clause Yahweh delivered Lakish into the hand of Yisrael is similar to verse 10:30a.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

Yahweh enabled the Israeli (Israelite) army to defeat the people of the town of Lakish.

10:32b

and Yehoshua (Joshua) captured it on the second day. He put all the people to the sword,

  • Yehoshua captured it on the second day of the battle, and killed the people in it with the sword.

  • On the second day they defeated the city, and killed the people in it.

and Yehoshua captured it on the second day: The clause Yehoshua captured it on the second day indicates that it took two days for Yehoshua and his army to defeat the town of Lakish (Lachish), unlike the first two towns, which they defeated in only one day.

He put all the people to the sword: The clause put all the people to the sword is a Hebrew idiom. This is the same wording as the clauses in 10:28b and 10:30b. It is recommended that you translate it in a similar way.

The king of Lakish is not mentioned because he was one of the five kings who led the battle against the Givonim (Gibeonites). Yehoshua killed him by the cave at Makedah (Makkedah) (10:23, 26).

10:32c

just as he had done to Livnah (Libnah).

  • He spared no one, as he did at Livnah.

  • They killed everybody there, as they did at Livnah City.

just as he had done to Livnah: The clause as he had done to Livnah refers to what Yehoshua (Joshua) did to the people of Livnah. It may be more natural in some languages to make this information explicit. For example:

Yehoshua killed all the people of Lakish, as he had killed all the people in Livnah

title: Joshua 10:33
content:
Section 10:28–43 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of southern Kena’an (Canaan)

Yehoshua (Joshua) defeated seven other important towns in Southern Kena’an.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the southern towns

10:33a

At that time Horam king of Gezer went to help Lakish (Lachish),

  • ¶ At this time Horam king of Gezer came to help Lakish,

  • ¶ At that time King Horam of Gezer City came to help the people of Lakish City.

At that time Horam king of Gezer: Horam is the only king in this list of kings and towns who is mentioned by name. The grammar of this sentence is also different from the usual narrative storyline pattern in Hebrew.

The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as At that time indicates that the action that follows has special prominence. This verse stands at the center of the narrative about these seven towns.10:33 Boling and Wright, p. 294. It emphasizes the military leadership of Yehoshua (Joshua) because Horam king of Gezer came to the help of Lakish. However, Yehoshua and the Israelis (Israelites) defeated both Horam’s army and the army of Lakish. Some English versions give prominence to this verse in the following ways:

During this same time King Horam of Gezer came to help Lakish (NCV)

During the attack on Lakish, King Horam of Gezer arrived with his army to help defend the town (NLT)

At that time King Horam of Gezer had come to help Lakish (Lachish) (GW)

Gezer: The town of Gezer is probably about 35 kilometers north of Lakish.10:33 Bratcher and Newman, p. 152.

went to help Lakish: The phrase went to help is used in a military sense. It indicates that the king and his army came prepared to fight a battle.10:33 Boling and Wright, p. 292.

10:33b

but Yehoshua struck him down along with his people, leaving no survivors.

  • But Yehoshua (Joshua) defeated him and his army, and no one was left alive.

  • But Yehoshua killed him and his soldiers, and they all died.

but: The BSB used the word but here to indicate that what happens is surprising and not what was expected.

Yehoshua struck him down along with his people: The clause Yehoshua struck him down along with his people indicates that Yehoshua and the Israeli (Israelite) army killed the king of Gezer and his army.

leaving no survivors: The clause leaving no survivors indicates that the Israeli army continued to attack the army of the king of Gezer until every soldier had died.

title: Joshua 10:34
content:
Section 10:28–43 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of southern Kena’an (Canaan)

Yehoshua (Joshua) defeated seven other important towns in Southern Kena’an.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the southern towns

10:34a

So Yehoshua moved on from Lakish (Lachish) to Eglon, and all Yisrael with him.

  • ¶ Then Yehoshua and all the Israelis went from Lakish to Eglon.

  • ¶ Next, Yehoshua and his soldiers went from Lakish City to Eglon City,

So Yehoshua moved on from Lakish to Eglon, and all Yisrael with him: The clause Yehoshua moved on from Lakish to Eglon, and all Yisrael with him has similar wording as 10:31a. The town of Eglon was about 16 kilometers west of Lakish.10:34 Bratcher and Newman, p. 152. It is possible to translate this clause in the same way as 10:31a. In languages where a repetitious style is not natural, it may be possible to vary the wording a little bit.

10:34b

They laid siege to it and fought against it.

  • They surrounded it, and attacked it.

  • They set up their camp around the city and attacked it.

They laid siege to it and fought against it: The clause They laid siege to it and fought against it is the same as the clause in 10:31b. It is recommended that you translate it the same way.

title: Joshua 10:35
content:
Section 10:28–43 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of southern Kena’an (Canaan)

Yehoshua (Joshua) defeated seven other important towns in Southern Kena’an.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the southern towns

10:35a

That day they captured Eglon and put it to the sword,

  • They captured it that day and killed the people in it with their swords.

  • They captured it that same day, then killed everyone in it.

That day they captured Eglon: The clause That day they captured Eglon indicates that Yehoshua and the Israeli (Israelite) army captured the town and its inhabitants on the same day that they attacked it. In some languages, it is more natural to reverse the order of the words in this phrase. For example:

They captured Eglon City that same day

That day: The Hebrew phrase that the BSB translates as That day is stated twice in this verse for emphasis. It contrasts the fact that the Israelis (Israelites) captured and destroyed the town of Eglon in one day, whereas it took them two days to capture the town of Lakish (Lachish).

and put it to the sword: The clause put it to the sword indicates that the Israeli army killed the people of the town. This is a Hebrew idiom that was used in 10:28, and it is recommended that you translate it the same way in both places.

10:35b

and Yehoshua (Joshua) devoted to destruction everyone in the city,

  • Yehoshua devoted them to Yahweh for destruction on that day

  • On that day they killed every single person because Yahweh claimed them.

and Yehoshua devoted to destruction everyone in the city: The Hebrew clause that the BSB translates as and Yehoshua devoted to destruction everyone in the city has the object stated first because this is a way that the Hebrew language indicates prominence or emphasis. Other languages may have a different way to show emphasis. Indicate emphasis that is natural in your language.

Yehoshua: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as Yehoshua refers to Yehoshua as the representative of the Israeli (Israelite) army. In some languages it may be more natural to include this implied information. For example:

Yehoshua and the Israeli soldiers utterly destroyed the town of Eglon that day

devoted to destruction: The Hebrew verb that the BSB translates as devoted to destruction is the same verb used in 10:28c. It refers to people or things that are claimed by Yahweh and cannot be bought back by any means. They must be destroyed.

10:35c

just as he had done to Lakish (Lachish).

  • as he did to Lakish.

  • This was same as they did to Lakish City.

just as he had done to Lakish: The phrase just as he had done to Lakish may be translated as an independent sentence. For example:

He treated Eglon the same way as he had treated Lakish.

title: Joshua 10:36
content:
Section 10:28–43 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of southern Kena’an (Canaan)

Yehoshua (Joshua) defeated seven other important towns in Southern Kena’an.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the southern towns

10:36a

Then Yehoshua and all Yisrael with him went up from Eglon to Hevron (Hebron)

  • ¶ Then Yehoshua and his soldiers went from Eglon uphill to Hevron,

  • ¶ Then Yehoshua and all the Israeli (Israelite) army marched from Eglon City to Hevron City.

Then Yehoshua and all Yisrael with him went up: The Hebrew text says Yehoshua…went up to Hevron, because Hevron was in the high hill country. Yehoshua walked from Eglon to a higher elevation. In languages that do not keep track of elevation, it may be more natural to say:

Then Yehoshua (Joshua) went

and all Yisrael (Israel) with him: The phrase all Yisrael with him indicates that Yehoshua led the whole Israeli army to Hevron.

from Eglon to Hevron: The town of Hevron was in the hill country, about 36 kilometers from Eglon.10:36 Bratcher and Newman, p. 154.

10:36b

and fought against it.

  • and they attacked it.

  • They attacked it

and fought against it: The clause fought against it indicates that the Israeli (Israelite) army attacked the town of Hevron (Hebron).

title: Joshua 10:37
content:
Section 10:28–43 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of southern Kena’an (Canaan)

Yehoshua (Joshua) defeated seven other important towns in Southern Kena’an.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the southern towns

10:37a

They captured it and put to the sword

  • They captured it and killed the people with their swords.

  • and captured it, and killed its people.

They captured it: The clause captured it indicates that the Israelis (Israelites) captured the town.

put to the sword: The clause put to the sword indicates that the Israeli (Israelite) army killed the people in Hevron (Hebron). This is a Hebrew idiom that was used in 10:28, and it is recommended that you translate it the same way in both places.

10:37b

its king, all its villages, and all the people.

  • They killed its king and every person in it and in the villages around it.

  • They killed the king and all the people, and the people in the small towns near it.

its king, all its villages, and all the people: The phrase its king, all its villages refers to the king of Hevron and the surrounding villages that were under the control of Hevron. All the people in Hevron and its villages were killed.

10:37c

Yehoshua (Joshua) left no survivors, just as he had done at Eglon; he devoted to destruction Hevron and everyone in it.

  • As he did to Eglon, he killed everybody. He devoted them to Yahweh for destruction.

  • Nobody was left alive, as nobody was left alive at Eglon City. Yehoshua claimed the city and all its people for Yahweh by destroying them.

Yehoshua left no survivors: The Hebrew clause that the BSB translates as Yehoshua left no survivors is more literally “not a survivor remained.” This indicates that the Israeli (Israelite) army killed every person in Hevron (Hebron) and its surrounding towns.

just as he had done at Eglon: The clause just as he had done at Eglon is similar to the clause in verse 10:35c. It is recommended that you translate it in a similar way.

he devoted to destruction Hevron and everyone in it: The clause he devoted to destruction Hevron and everyone in it is similar to verse 10:35b. The verb devoted to destruction refers to the action of destroying people and things that Yahweh had claimed and could not be bought back by any means.

General Comment on verse 10:37

It may be more natural in some languages to reorder the parts of 10:37.

Here is another way to translate this verse:

and captured it. They killed the king and everyone else in the city as well as in the nearby towns. Yehoshua (Joshua) condemned the city to total destruction, just as he had done to Eglon. No one in it was left alive. (GNT)

title: Joshua 10:38
content:
Section 10:28–43 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of southern Kena’an (Canaan)

Yehoshua (Joshua) defeated seven other important towns in Southern Kena’an.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the southern towns

10:38

Finally Yehoshua and all Yisrael with him turned toward Devir (Debir) and fought against it.

  • ¶ Then Yehoshua and the Israeli (Israelite) army turned southward to Devir and attacked it.

  • ¶ Then Yehoshua and the Israeli soldiers turned back to Devir City and attacked it.

Yehoshua and all Yisrael with him: The phrase Yehoshua and all Yisrael with him refers to Yehoshua and the entire Israeli army.

turned toward Devir: The clause turned toward Devir indicates that the Israelis (Israelites) changed the direction that they were walking. Earlier they walked from Eglon north to Hevron (Hebron) in the higher hills. Now they turned and walked south to Devir. The town of Devir was 20 kilometers southwest of Hevron.10:38 Bratcher and Newman, p. 155.

and fought against it: The clause fought against it indicates that the Israeli army attacked Devir.

title: Joshua 10:39
content:
Section 10:28–43 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of southern Kena’an (Canaan)

Yehoshua (Joshua) defeated seven other important towns in Southern Kena’an.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the southern towns

10:39a

And they captured Devir (Debir), its king, and all its villages.

  • They captured it with its king and all the towns near it

  • They captured Devir City and its king, and the villages under its control

And they captured Devir, its king, and all its villages: In some languages it may be more natural to begin a new sentence, as in the BSB. The clause they captured Devir, its king, and all its villages is similar to verse 10:37a-b. It indicates that the Israeli (Israelite) army captured the king and all the people of Devir and he also captured the small towns that were close by.

10:39b

They put them to the sword

  • and they killed the people with their swords.

  • and they killed the people there.

They put them to the sword: The clause They put them to the sword indicates that the Israeli army killed the people of Devir (Debir) and the nearby towns. This is a Hebrew idiom that is similar to the clauses in verses 28b, 30b, 32b, 35a, and 37a. It is recommended that you translate it the same way in all these places.

10:39c

and devoted to destruction everyone in the city,

  • They devoted every person to Yahweh for destruction.

  • They claimed them all for Yahweh by destroying them.

10:39d

leaving no survivors.

  • There were nobody who lived.

  • No one was left alive.

10:39c-d

and devoted to destruction everyone in the city, leaving no survivors: These two clauses are similar to verse 10:37.

devoted to destruction: The phrase devoted to destruction indicates that Yahweh had claimed these people for himself and they could not be bought back by any means. They must be destroyed.

leaving no survivors: The clause leaving no survivors indicates that not a single person was left alive in the town of Devir (Debir) and the surrounding towns.

10:39e

Yehoshua (Joshua) did to Devir and its king as he had done to Hevron (Hebron) and as he had done to Livnah (Libnah) and its king.

  • Yehoshua did the same thing to Devir and its king that he did to Hevron and to Livnah and its king.

  • Yisrael (Israel) did to Devir City and its king as they did to Hevron City, and to Livnah City and its king.

Yehoshua did to Devir and its king as he had done to Hevron and as he had done to Livnah and its king:Here is another example of how to translate this verse part:

Yehoshua did the same thing to Devir and its king as he had done to Hevron and as he had done to Livnah and its king

title: Joshua 10:40
content:
Section 10:28–43 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of southern Kena’an (Canaan)

Yehoshua (Joshua) defeated seven other important towns in Southern Kena’an.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the southern towns

Paragraph 10:40–43

This paragraph is a conclusion to the account of the battles that Israelis fought in southern Kena’an. These verses summarize what the Israeli (Israelite) army accomplished. These events were told in detail in 10:28–39.

10:40a

So Yehoshua conquered the whole region—

  • ¶ So Yehoshua defeated the kings of all the cities in this region.

  • ¶ In this way Yehoshua conquered the whole land of Southern Kena’an (Canaan).

So Yehoshua (Joshua) conquered the whole region: Yehoshua is named as the leader of the Israeli army. He defeated the whole region by leading the army as they fought. In some languages it may be more natural to include the Israeli army with Yehoshua as a compound subject. For example:

Yehoshua and the Israeli soldiers defeated the whole land

the whole region: The phrase the whole region refers to the region of southern Kena’an. The towns that the Israeli army captured in chapter 10 were all in southern Kena’an.

10:40b

the hill country, the Negev, the foothills, and the slopes, together with all their kings—

  • He defeated all the people in the mountains, the Negev (Negeb) Desert south of Kena’an, the hills to the west, and the slopes to the east.

  • He conquered the central hill country, the southern desert, the foothills to the west, and the slopes that go down to the Dead Sea.

the hill country: The phrase the hill country refers to the central mountain range that extended from Ay (Ai) and Giveon (Gibeon) in the north to Hevron (Hebron) and Devir (Debir) in the south. See how you translated this term in 9:1.

the Negev: The phrase the Negev refers to the wilderness area south of Kena’an (Canaan).

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

the dry country in the south (GNT)

the Southern Desert (CEV)

the foothills: The phrase the foothills refers to the western foothills that were between the mountains and the coastal plain. This term was used in 9:1 and you should translate it the same way in both places.

and the slopes: The phrase the slopes refers to the steep slopes that lead down from the hill country eastward to the Dead Sea.

together with all their kings: The phrase all their kings refers to the kings of the towns in these areas. It may be more natural in some languages to include the term about the kings in the first part of the verse, as in GNT:

Yehoshua (Joshua) conquered the whole land. He defeated the kings of the hill country, the eastern slopes, and the western foothills, as well as those of the dry country in the south. (GNT)

10:40c

leaving no survivors. He devoted to destruction everything that breathed,

  • He did not let anybody live. He killed all the people.

  • He killed all the people, and none of them were left alive,

leaving no survivors: The clause leaving no survivors has occurred five times in verses 10:28–39. It is repeated to emphasize that Yehoshua obeyed Yahweh’s command in Deuteronomy 20:16–18 to destroy everyone in the land of Kena’an (Canaan). It is recommended that you translate it the same way each time.

He devoted to destruction everything that breathed: The clause devoted to destruction everything that breathed is similar to the clauses in verses 28, 35, 37, and 39.

devoted to destruction: The phrase devoted to destruction translates the Hebrew verb that means a person or thing is claimed by Yahweh and cannot be bought back by any means, but must be destroyed.

everything that breathed: The phrase everything that breathed means “every person.” It does not refer to animals. This expression is also used in Deuteronomy 20:16.

10:40d

just as Yahweh, the God of Yisrael (Israel), had commanded.

  • This was what Yahweh the God of Yisrael commanded.

  • as Yahweh the God of Yisrael said.

just as Yahweh, the God of Yisrael, had commanded: The clause as Yahweh, the God of Yisrael, had commanded refers to the command that Yahweh gave to Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis (Israelites) through Mosheh (Moses) in Deuteronomy 20:16–18. It may be more natural in some languages to state this as an independent sentence. For example:

This was what the Lord God of Yisrael had commanded. (GNT)

It is recommended that you include a footnote or a reference to Deuteronomy 20:16–18.

title: Joshua 10:41
content:
Section 10:28–43 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of southern Kena’an (Canaan)

Yehoshua (Joshua) defeated seven other important towns in Southern Kena’an.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the southern towns

Paragraph 10:40–43

This paragraph is a conclusion to the account of the battles that Israelis fought in southern Kena’an. These verses summarize what the Israeli (Israelite) army accomplished. These events were told in detail in 10:28–39.

10:41a

Yehoshua conquered the area from Kadesh-Barnea (Kadesh-barnea) to Azah (Gaza),

  • Yehoshua defeated the cities from Kadesh Barnea in the south to Azah in the west,

  • Yehoshua conquered them from Kadesh Barnea town in the south to Azah City by the Mediterranean Sea.

Yehoshua (Joshua) conquered the area: The clause Yehoshua conquered the area continues the summary of what Yehoshua did.

from Kadesh-Barnea: Kadesh-Barnea was a town on the southeast boundary of Kena’an (Canaan), more than 80 kilometers south of Devir (Debir). It was the southernmost town that Yehoshua conquered.

Here is another way to spell Kadesh-Barnea:

Kadesh Barnea (NIV, NET)

to Azah: Azah was a town on the southwestern coast of the Mediterranean Sea.

10:41b

and the whole region of Goshen as far as Giveon (Gibeon).

  • and from Goshen to Giveon in the north.

  • He conquered the people in the region of Goshen City, and as far north as Giveon City.

and the whole region of Goshen: The phrase the whole region of Goshen refers to a town in the southern hill country of Kena’an (Canaan) and the region around it. The exact location of the town of Goshen is unknown.10:41 Howard, p. 262.

as far as Giveon: The town of Giveon was the northernmost point of Yehoshua’s (Joshua’s) conquest.

title: Joshua 10:42
content:
Section 10:28–43 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of southern Kena’an (Canaan)

Yehoshua (Joshua) defeated seven other important towns in Southern Kena’an.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the southern towns

Paragraph 10:40–43

This paragraph is a conclusion to the account of the battles that Israelis fought in southern Kena’an. These verses summarize what the Israeli (Israelite) army accomplished. These events were told in detail in 10:28–39.

10:42a

And because Yahweh, the God of Yisrael, fought for Yisrael,

  • Because Yahweh, the God of Yisrael, helped Yisrael to fight,

  • Because Yahweh the God of Yisrael fought for the Israelis (Israelites),

Yehoshua (Joshua) captured all these kings and their land in one campaign: The clause Yehoshua captured all these kings and their land in one campaign indicates that Yehoshua defeated all the kings mentioned in the previous verse and conquered their lands.

in one campaign: The phrase in one campaign indicates that Yehoshua and the Israeli army were able to conquer all the kings and lands in one continuous military campaign. It does not indicate how many days this campaign lasted. The army began their battle against the five Amori (Amorite) kings at Giveon (Gibeon) and then continued on from town to town until they had defeated them all.

10:42b

Yehoshua captured all these kings and their land in one campaign.

  • Yehoshua conquered these kings and their cities all at one time.

  • Yehoshua conquered all these kings and their territory in one continuous battle.

because Yahweh, the God of Yisrael (Israel), fought for Yisrael: In some languages it may help to emphasize the important point made here by supplying implicit information:

They were able to do this because Yahweh the God of Yisrael fought for Yisrael

title: Joshua 10:43
content:
Section 10:28–43 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of southern Kena’an (Canaan)

Yehoshua (Joshua) defeated seven other important towns in Southern Kena’an.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael (Israel) defeated the southern towns

Paragraph 10:40–43

This paragraph is a conclusion to the account of the battles that Israelis fought in southern Kena’an. These verses summarize what the Israeli (Israelite) army accomplished. These events were told in detail in 10:28–39.

10:43

Then Yehoshua returned with all Yisrael to the camp at Gilgal.

  • Then Yehoshua and the Israeli soldiers went back to their camp at Gilgal.

  • After the battle, Yehoshua and all the Israelis (Israelites) went back to their camp at Gilgal.

Then Yehoshua (Joshua) returned with all Yisrael to the camp at Gilgal: This verse is identical to verse 10:15. It is recommended that you translate this verse the same as you translated 10:15.

title: Joshua 11:1
content:
Section 11:1–15 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of northern Kena’an (Canaan)

King Yavin (Jabin), the king of Hatsor (Hazor), brought together the kings of the towns in Northern Kena’an to fight against Yisrael (Israel). With the help of Yahweh, Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis fought and defeated all these towns and killed their kings and their people.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael defeated the northern towns

11:1a

Now when Yavin king of Hatsor heard about these things,

  • ¶ When King Yavin of Hatsor heard about the battles that the Israelis won,

  • ¶ King Yavin, the king of Hatsor, heard what happened.

Now when Yavin king of Hatsor heard about these things: The clause when Yavin king of Hatsor heard about these things has the same structure as the clause that began 10:1. It is recommended that you translate it in a similar way.

Hatsor (Hazor): The town of Hatsor was a large town about 14 kilometers north of the Sea of Galil (Galilee).11:1 Howard, p. 265.

about these things: The phrase about these things refers to Yehoshua’s (Joshua’s) victories over the kings in Southern Kena’an (Canaan).

Here are some other ways to translate this clause:

King Yavin (Jabin) of Hatsor heard about Yehoshua’s victories (CEV)

King Yavin of Hatsor heard what had happened (GW)

11:1b

he sent word to Yovav (Jobab) king of Madon; to the kings of Shimron and Akshaf (Achshaph);

  • he sent a message to King Yovav of Madon, and to the kings of Shimron and Akshaf,

  • So, he sent messengers to many cities and asked them to join him in fighting against Yisrael (Israel). He sent them to King Yovav of Madon City and to the king of Shimron City and the king of Akshaf City.

he sent word to Yovav king of Madon: In the list of kings that follows, King Yovav is the only king listed by name. This indicates that he was Yavin’s most powerful neighbor.

Here is another way to translate this clause:

he sent messengers to King Yovav of Madon to ask for his help to fight against the Israelis (Israelites)

Madon: The town of Madon was 30 kilometers southeast of Hatsor (Hazor).11:1 Bratcher and Newman, p. 158.

to the kings of Shimron: The exact location of the town of Shimron is unknown. In Joshua 19:15, it is listed as part of the territory of Zevulun (Zebulun).11:1 Howard, p. 266.

and Akshaf (Achshaph): The exact location of the town of Akshaf is uncertain. It is listed as part of the territory of Asher in Joshua 19:25.

title: Joshua 11:2
content:
Section 11:1–15 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of northern Kena’an (Canaan)

King Yavin (Jabin), the king of Hatsor (Hazor), brought together the kings of the towns in Northern Kena’an to fight against Yisrael (Israel). With the help of Yahweh, Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis fought and defeated all these towns and killed their kings and their people.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael defeated the northern towns

11:2a

to the kings of the north in the mountains,

  • and to the kings in the northern hills,

  • He sent them to the northern kings in the hills.

to the kings of the north in the mountains: The phrase the kings of the north in the mountains refers to other towns ruled by kings which were further north in the mountains of Galil (Galilee).

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

the northern kings who were in the mountains (NIV)

the kings in the hill country in the north (GNT)

11:2b

in the Aravah (Arabah) south of Kineret (Chinnereth), in the foothills, and in Naphoth-dor to the west;

  • and in the Yarden (Jordan) River Valley south of Lake Galil, and the kings in the lower slopes, and in Naphoth-dor to the west,

  • He sent them to the kings in the valley of the Yarden River south of Lake Galil, and to those in the foothills to the west. He sent a message to the king of Naphoth-dor City in the west.

in the Aravah south of Kineret: The Aravah refers to the valley of the Yarden River, north of the Dead Sea and south of Lake Galil (Galilee).

Kineret: Kineret refers to Lake Galil.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

the Yarden valley south of Lake Galil (GNT)

in the foothills: The phrase the foothills refers to the western foothills that were between the mountains and the coastal plain. This word was used in 9:1 and you should translate it the same way in both places.

and in Naphoth-dor to the west: The town of Dor was a seaport on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea south of Mount Karmel (Carmel). It is not certain to what the term Naphoth refers.

Here are some other ways to translate this term:

the heights of Dor (NET, NASB)

on the coast near Dor (GNT)

the district of Dor (NJPS)

the borders of Dor (KJV)

Naphoth Dor (NIV, GW)

title: Joshua 11:3
content:
Section 11:1–15 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of northern Kena’an (Canaan)

King Yavin (Jabin), the king of Hatsor (Hazor), brought together the kings of the towns in Northern Kena’an to fight against Yisrael (Israel). With the help of Yahweh, Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis fought and defeated all these towns and killed their kings and their people.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael defeated the northern towns

11:3a

to the Kena’anim (Canaanites) in the east and west;

  • and to the Kena’ani (Canaanite) kings east and west of the Yarden (Jordan) River,

  • He sent them to the Kena’anim on both sides of the Yarden River.

to the Kena’anim: The Kena’anim were one of the groups of people who lived in the land of Kena’an (Canaan). It may be more natural to include some implicit information at the beginning of verse 3. For example, you could say:

King Yavin (Jabin) also sent messengers to the kings of the Kena’an people

in the east and west: The phrase in the east and west indicates the east and west sides of the Yarden River.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

to the Kena’ani people on the east and west sides of the Yarden River

11:3b

to the Amorim (Amorites), Hitim (Hittites), Perizim (Perizzites), and Yevusim (Jebusites) in the hill country;

  • and to the kings of Amor, Het (Heth), Periz, and Yevus (Jebus) in the hill country,

  • He sent them to the kings of the Amorim, the Hitim, the Perizim, and the Yevusim in the mountains.

to the Amorim, Hitim, Perizim, and Yevusim: These are groups of people who lived in the land of Kena’an (Canaan) along with the Kena’anim (Canaanites). Yahweh told the Israelis (Israelites) to destroy all these nations with his help (see Deuteronomy 20:16–18). These groups of people were mentioned in Joshua 3:10. You should translate the names the same way you did there.

in the hill country: The phrase hill country indicates the mountainous region that is between the coastal plain and the Yarden (Jordan) River valley. This is the same phrase used in 9:1 and you should translate it the same way in both places.

11:3c

and to the Hivim (Hivites) at the foot of Hermon in the land of Mitspah (Mizpah).

  • and to the king of the Hiv people in the region of Mitspah, near the foot of Mount Hermon.

  • And he sent them to the Hivim, who lived at the foot of Hermon Mountain in the Mitspah Valley.

and to the Hivim at the foot of Hermon: The Hivim were a group of people who lived in the Mitspah Valley south of Mount Hermon. Hermon Mountain is a tall mountain in northeastern Yisrael (Israel). It is 43 kilometers southwest of Damesek (Damascus) and 2,814 meters high. It is the tallest mountain in Yisrael.11:3 Rasmussen, p. 238.

at the foot of Hermon: The Hivim lived near the foot of Hermon Mountain. Hermon Mountain is covered with snow most of the year. It was the dominant feature of the landscape above the Hivi (Hivite) people.
