Here is another way to translate this phrase:

the Hivi kings in the region of Mitspah, near the foot of Mount Hermon (CEV)

in the land of Mitspah: The term Mitspah refers to a valley at the foot of Hermon Mountain. There are several towns mentioned in the Bible that are named Mitspah, but they are in other places. The Mitspah mentioned here is only mentioned again in Joshua 11:8.11:3 Rasmussen, p. 245.

General Comment on verses 11:1–3

These verses contain a list of the names of towns and their kings to whom King Yavin (Jabin) of Hatsor (Hazor) sent messengers. He asked them to help him fight the Israelis (Israelites). In some languages it may be helpful to state this information at the beginning of 11:1. For example:

When King Yavin of Hatsor heard the news of the Israelis’s victories, he sent messengers to the towns of Northern Kena’an (Canaan) and their kings asking for their help to fight the Israelis. He sent to King Yovav (Jobab) of Madon…11:3 Bratcher and Newman, p. 158.

title: Joshua 11:4
content:
Section 11:1–15 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of northern Kena’an (Canaan)

King Yavin (Jabin), the king of Hatsor (Hazor), brought together the kings of the towns in Northern Kena’an to fight against Yisrael (Israel). With the help of Yahweh, Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis fought and defeated all these towns and killed their kings and their people.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael defeated the northern towns

11:4a

So these kings came out with all their armies, a multitude

  • They came out with all their soldiers, a lot of them.

  • The kings of these cities gathered together, and there were many soldiers.

So: The Hebrew connector that the BSB translates as So introduces the next event in the story. Here it also indicates result. The kings and their armies marched out in response to the message they had received from King Yavin of Hatsor.

these kings: The pronoun these kings indicates the kings of the towns referred to in verse 3.

came out with all their armies: The verb came out indicates that the kings gathered their troops together and came out of their towns to fight against the Israelis (Israelites).

Here is another way to translate this clause:

the kings of these towns came out with all their soldiers

a multitude: The phrase a multitude indicates that there were many soldiers.

11:4b

as numerous as the sand on the seashore,

  • There were as many soldiers as the grains of sand on the seashore,

  • There were so many soldiers they could not be counted. There were as many as the grains of sand beside the sea.

as numerous as the sand on the seashore: The phrase as numerous as the sand on the seashore indicates a comparison. The number of Kena’ani (Canaanite) soldiers gathered to fight against the Israelis (Israelites) is compared to the grains of sand on the beach by the sea. There were so many that it was impossible to count them. In some languages it may be helpful to make this comparison clearer. For example:

there were so many soldiers that they could not be counted. It was like counting the sand that is on the seashore

11:4c

along with a great number of horses and chariots.

  • and they had many horses and chariots.

  • They had many horses which pulled war carts.

along with a great number of horses and chariots: The horses were used to pull the chariots. At that time, the Israeli (Israelite) army did not have any horses or chariots. The Kena’ani army had more soldiers and had better weapons than the Israelis. This made the Israeli victory even more remarkable and showed that it was only possible because God fought for them.

chariots: The chariots were light carts that were each pulled by one or two horses. There was room in the chariot for two soldiers. One drove the horses and the other was free to fight with a sword or with bow and arrows.

Here are some other ways to translate this term:

war cart

horse-drawn war cart

title: Joshua 11:5
content:
Section 11:1–15 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of northern Kena’an (Canaan)

King Yavin (Jabin), the king of Hatsor (Hazor), brought together the kings of the towns in Northern Kena’an to fight against Yisrael (Israel). With the help of Yahweh, Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis fought and defeated all these towns and killed their kings and their people.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael defeated the northern towns

11:5a

All these kings joined forces

  • All these kings brought their soldiers together

  • All these kings came with their armies

All these kings: The phrase All these kings indicates the kings of each of the towns mentioned in the above verses.

joined forces: The clause joined forces indicates that the kings told their armies to fight together as one army against the Israelis (Israelites).

11:5b

and encamped at the waters of Merom

  • at the waters of Merom, and camped there

  • to the Merom River and set up their camp together there.

and encamped: The clause and encamped indicates that all the armies set up their camps as if they were one army.

at the waters of Merom: The exact location of the waters of Merom is uncertain. It was probably a riverbed where waters flowed during rainstorms. It was probably somewhere between the Sea of Galil (Galilee) and the Mediterranean coast.11:5 Howard p. 267 and footnote 264.

Here is another way to translate this term:

Merom Brook (GNT)

11:5c

to fight against Yisrael (Israel).

  • ready to fight Yisrael.

  • Then they got ready to fight with the Israelis (Israelites).

to fight against Yisrael: The clause to fight against Yisrael indicates the intention of the armies. They gathered and set up camp in order to fight against the Israelis. This can also be translated as an independent sentence. For example:

Then they got ready to fight with Yisrael.

title: Joshua 11:6
content:
Section 11:1–15 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of northern Kena’an (Canaan)

King Yavin (Jabin), the king of Hatsor (Hazor), brought together the kings of the towns in Northern Kena’an to fight against Yisrael (Israel). With the help of Yahweh, Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis fought and defeated all these towns and killed their kings and their people.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael defeated the northern towns

11:6a

Then Yahweh said to Yehoshua, “Do not be afraid of them,

  • Then Yahweh said to Yehoshua: “Do not be afraid of them.

  • Then Yahweh told Yehoshua: “Do not be afraid of the Kena’ani (Canaanite) armies

Then: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as Then indicates the continuing action of the narrative. Yahweh gave instructions to Yehoshua after the armies gathered to fight against the Israelis (Israelites).

Do not be afraid of them: Yahweh told Yehoshua (Joshua) not to be afraid of the enemies. Yahweh gave him this same encouragement before the battle of Ay (Ai) (Joshua 8:1) and the battle at Giveon (Gibeon) (Joshua 10:8).

11:6b

for by this time tomorrow I will deliver all of them slain before Yisrael (Israel).

  • By this time tomorrow I will kill all of them and hand them over to Yisrael.

  • because I am going to give them to you Israelis. At this time tomorrow they will all be dead.

for by this time tomorrow: The phrase by this time tomorrow indicates the time that Yahweh will help the Israelis to defeat the armies of the northern kings.

I will deliver all of them slain before Yisrael: The clause I will deliver all of them slain before Yisrael indicates that Yahweh will kill the enemies of the Israelis. It is evident from verses 6–7 that the Israelis had a part in pursuing their enemies and killing them. However, this happened only because Yahweh enabled them to do it.

slain: The word slain is from the verb “to slay” which means “to kill.” Yahweh said that he would kill the enemies.

before Yisrael: Yahweh said he would give the Kena’ani (Canaanite) soldiers before Yisrael. Since Yahweh was talking to Yehoshua, it may be clearer in some languages to translate this:

to you

to you Israelis (Israelites)

11:6c

You are to hamstring their horses

  • Then you must cut the hamstrings of their horses

  • You must cut the legs of their horses so that they cannot be used in battle

You are to hamstring their horses: The word to hamstring means to cut the large tendon, the “hamstring,” that runs down the back of the horse’s hind leg. The Israelis were to cut the hamstrings of the Kena’ani (Canaanite) horses so that they would not be able to walk. They did this so that the enemy armies could not use the horses that survived.

Here are some other ways to translate this clause:

cut the hamstrings of their horses

cut the legs of their horses so that they cannot be used to fight

11:6d

and burn up their chariots.”

  • and burn their chariots.”

  • and burn up their chariots with fire.”

and burn up their chariots: The Hebrew text includes the words “with fire", which may be helpful to specific in some languages. For example:

and burn their chariots with fire

In other languages, adding this might make it redundant, because it is already implied in the verb burn.

title: Joshua 11:7
content:
Section 11:1–15 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of northern Kena’an (Canaan)

King Yavin (Jabin), the king of Hatsor (Hazor), brought together the kings of the towns in Northern Kena’an to fight against Yisrael (Israel). With the help of Yahweh, Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis fought and defeated all these towns and killed their kings and their people.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael defeated the northern towns

11:7a

So by the waters of Merom,

  • At waters of Merom.

  • At Merom River.

So by the waters of Merom: The waters of Merom were mentioned in 11:5b. The battle between the Israelis (Israelites) and the enemy armies took place near this riverbed.

11:7b

Yehoshua (Joshua) and his whole army came upon them suddenly and attacked them,

  • Yehoshua and all his soldiers caught them by surprise.

  • Yehoshua and his army made a surprise attack against the Kena’anim (Canaanites).

Yehoshua and his whole army came upon them suddenly: The clause Yehoshua and his whole army came upon them suddenly indicates that Yehoshua and his army attacked the Kena’ani (Canaanite) armies by surprise. These words are similar to the words in 10:9, and you may be able to translate them in a similar way.

and his whole army: The phrase and his whole army indicates that Yehoshua’s entire army was with him. In Hebrew, this is more literally “all the people of war with him”.

Here are some other ways to translate this clause:

Yehoshua and his whole army caught them by surprise (NET)

So Yehoshua and his whole army came against them suddenly (NIV)

and attacked them: The clause and attacked them indicates that Yehoshua (Joshua) and his army attacked the enemy armies. It may be more natural in some languages to combine this clause with the clause in 11:7a, for example:

So Yehoshua and all his men attacked them by surprise at Merom Brook (GNT)

Yehoshua and his army made a surprise attack against the enemy camp at Merom Pond (CEV)

title: Joshua 11:8
content:
Section 11:1–15 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of northern Kena’an (Canaan)

King Yavin (Jabin), the king of Hatsor (Hazor), brought together the kings of the towns in Northern Kena’an to fight against Yisrael (Israel). With the help of Yahweh, Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis fought and defeated all these towns and killed their kings and their people.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael defeated the northern towns

11:8a

and Yahweh delivered them into the hand of Yisrael,

  • Yahweh gave the Kena’anim (Canaanites) to Yisrael, and the Israelis defeated them.

  • Yahweh helped the Israelis to have victory over them.

and Yahweh delivered them into the hand of Yisrael: The clause Yahweh delivered them into the hand of Yisrael indicates that Yahweh helped the Israeli (Israelite) army defeat the Kena’anim.

Here are some other ways to translate this clause:

The Lord gave the Israelis (Israelites) victory over them (GNT)

The Lord helped Yisrael (Israel) defeat the enemy (CEV)

11:8b

who struck them down and pursued them all the way to Greater Tsidon (Sidon) and Misrefot-Mayim (Misrephoth-maim),

  • The Israelis fought them and chased them as far as Great Tsidon (Great Sidon), and Misrefot-Mayim,

  • The Israelis attacked them and chased them as far north as Great Tsidon City and Misrefot-Mayim City,

who struck them down: The word struck comes from the verb “to strike” which means “to hit.” This is an idiom for killing. The clause struck them indicates that the Israeli (Israelite) army killed many soldiers in the enemy army. It may be more natural in some languages to begin a new sentence here. For example:

The Israelis (Israelites) killed them

and pursued them: The clause pursued them indicates that the Israeli army chased the Kena’anim (Canaanites) as they ran away and killed the people whom they overtook.

all the way to Greater Tsidon: The town of Greater Tsidon was to the northwest on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea.11:8 Hess, p. 112, Map B.

and Misrefot-Mayim: The location of the town of Misrefot-Mayim is uncertain. It was probably north of Galil (Galilee), near Tsidon, possibly near the Litani River.11:8 Rasmussen, p. 245. Some scholars think it was on the coast near the modern border between Levanon (Lebanon) and Yisrael (Israel).11:8 Boling and Wright, p. 308.

11:8c

and eastward as far as the Valley of Mitspah (Mizpeh).

  • and eastward to the valley of Mitspah.

  • and then as far east as the valley of Mitspah.

and eastward as far as the Valley of Mitspah: The Israeli (Israelite) army chased them in a circular path around the borders of Galil. They went northwest towards Greater Tsidon (Sidon) and then south towards the town of Misrefot-Mayim (Misrephoth-maim). Then they turned eastward to the Valley of Mitspah.

This Valley of Mitspah is probably the same place as the “land of Mitspah” mentioned in verse 11:3c. It is recommended that you spell this name the same way in both places.

11:8d

They struck them down, leaving no survivors.

  • They kept on killing them until none of them were still alive.

  • They attacked them until they were all dead.

They struck them down: The clause They struck them down indicates that the Israeli army killed the enemy soldiers. This clause is like the clause in 11:8b. It is repeated here for emphasis.

leaving no survivors: The clause leaving no survivors indicates that the Israeli army killed all the soldiers who had gathered to attack them.

It may be more natural in some languages to translate this clause as an independent sentence. For example:

None of the enemy soldiers escaped alive (CEV)

They killed them until all of them were dead

title: Joshua 11:9
content:
Section 11:1–15 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of northern Kena’an (Canaan)

King Yavin (Jabin), the king of Hatsor (Hazor), brought together the kings of the towns in Northern Kena’an to fight against Yisrael (Israel). With the help of Yahweh, Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis fought and defeated all these towns and killed their kings and their people.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael defeated the northern towns

11:9a

Yehoshua treated them as Yahweh had told him;

  • Yehoshua did what Yahweh told them to do.

  • Then Yehoshua ordered his soldiers to obey Yahweh’s command.

Yehoshua treated them: The word them refers to the Kena’ani (Canaanite) armies.

as Yahweh had told him: The clause as Yahweh had told him indicates that Yehoshua (Joshua) obeyed Yahweh’s commands.

11:9b

he hamstrung their horses and burned up their chariots.

  • They cut the hamstrings of the Kena’ani horses and burned their chariots.

  • He told them to cut the legs of their horses so that they couldn’t walk and to burn their chariots.

he hamstrung their horses: The clause he hamstrung their horses indicates that Yehoshua had the tendons in the back legs of the enemy horses cut so that they could not walk. Probably Yehoshua ordered his soldiers to do this. He did not do it himself. It may be clearer in some languages to make this information explicit. Translate this using similar words to 11:6c.

and burned up their chariots: The clause burned up their chariots indicates that Yehoshua had his soldiers burn the enemy chariots. Translate this using similar words to 11:6d.

Here is another way to translate these phrases:

Yehoshua told his soldiers to cut the hamstrings of their horses and burn their chariots as Yahweh had commanded them

title: Joshua 11:10
content:
Section 11:1–15 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of northern Kena’an (Canaan)

King Yavin (Jabin), the king of Hatsor (Hazor), brought together the kings of the towns in Northern Kena’an to fight against Yisrael (Israel). With the help of Yahweh, Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis fought and defeated all these towns and killed their kings and their people.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael defeated the northern towns

11:10a

At that time Yehoshua turned back

  • ¶ Then Yehoshua went back

  • ¶ After that, Yehoshua went back southwards

At that time Yehoshua turned back: The verb phrase turned back indicates that Yehoshua changed directions. He and his soldiers turned south to walk to town of Hatsor.

At that time: The phrase At that time indicates that Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis (Israelites) turned back as part of the same battle as verse 9.

11:10b

and captured Hatsor (Hazor) and put its king to the sword,

  • and captured Hatsor, and killed its king with the sword,

  • and captured Hatsor City and killed its king.

and captured Hatsor: The clause and captured Hatsor indicates that Yehoshua and his army captured the town of Hatsor City. Hatsor City was mentioned in 11:1.

and put its king to the sword: The clause put its king to the sword indicates that they killed the king of Hatsor City. “Put to the sword” is a Hebrew idiom that was used in 10:32, and it is recommended that you translate it the same way in both places.

Here is another way to translate this Hebrew idiom:

captured Hatsor and killed its king (GNT)

11:10c

because Hatsor (Hazor) was formerly the head of all these kingdoms.

  • because at that time the king of Hatsor City was the leader of all the Kena’ani (Canaanite) kingdoms.

  • They did this because he was the leader of all the kings who fought against the Israelis (Israelites).

because: The word because introduces the reason why they attacked the town of Hatsor.

Hatsor was formerly the head of all these kingdoms: The word formerly indicates the viewpoint of the author of this book, who wrote at a time later than Yehoshua (Joshua).

Here are some other ways to translate this word:

at that time (GNT, NET)

up to this time (CEV)

the head of all these kingdoms: The phrase the head of all these kingdoms indicates that the king of Hatsor (Hazor) was the leader of the kingdoms who fought against the Israelis.

title: Joshua 11:11
content:
Section 11:1–15 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of northern Kena’an (Canaan)

King Yavin (Jabin), the king of Hatsor (Hazor), brought together the kings of the towns in Northern Kena’an to fight against Yisrael (Israel). With the help of Yahweh, Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis fought and defeated all these towns and killed their kings and their people.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael defeated the northern towns

11:11a

The Israelis put everyone in Hatsor to the sword, devoting them to destruction.

  • The Israelis killed everybody that lived in the city with the sword, completely destroying them.

  • Yisrael killed everyone in Hatsor City and destroyed them completely.

The Israelis (Israelites) put everyone in Hatsor to the sword: The clause The Israelis put everyone in Hatsor to the sword indicates that Yehoshua and his army killed every person in the town of Hatsor. This is a Hebrew idiom that was used in 10:32. It is recommended that you translate it the same way in both places.

Here is another way to translate this Hebrew idiom:

they put everyone there to death (GNT)

devoting them to destruction: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as devoting them to destruction indicates destroying people or things that were devoted to Yahweh and cannot be saved by any means. This is the same kind of destruction that Yahweh commanded Yehoshua (Joshua) to carry out at Yeriho (Jericho) and Ay (Ai) (6:24 and 8:8). You should translate this phrase in the same way that you translated it there.

11:11b

Nothing that breathed remained,

  • Not one person still lived.

  • Nobody was left alive.

Nothing that breathed remained: The clause Nothing that breathed remained indicates that every person in the town was killed. This information is repeated to emphasize it. Yehoshua obeyed Yahweh’s command to kill all the Kena’anim (Canaanites) so that the Israelis (Israelites) could live in the land God had promised them.

11:11c

and Yehoshua burned down Hatsor (Hazor) itself.

  • Then Yehoshua burned Hatsor.

  • And he told his soldiers to burn the town of Hatsor.

and Yehoshua (Joshua) burned down Hatsor itself: The clause Yehoshua burned down Hatsor itself indicates that Yehoshua had his soldiers burn the town of Hatsor completely.

title: Joshua 11:12
content:
Section 11:1–15 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of northern Kena’an (Canaan)

King Yavin (Jabin), the king of Hatsor (Hazor), brought together the kings of the towns in Northern Kena’an to fight against Yisrael (Israel). With the help of Yahweh, Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis fought and defeated all these towns and killed their kings and their people.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael defeated the northern towns

11:12a

Yehoshua captured all these kings and their cities

  • ¶ Yehoshua captured all these cities and their kings.

  • ¶ Yehoshua took all these cities and killed their kings.

Yehoshua captured all these kings and their cities: Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

Yehoshua (Joshua) captured all the cities where the enemy kings had ruled (CEV)

Yehoshua captured: The clause Yehoshua captured indicates that Yehoshua and his soldiers defeated the kings and captured their towns. You should follow the word order that is natural in your language.

11:12b

and put them to the sword. He devoted them to destruction,

  • He killed them with the sword, and completely destroyed them,

  • He killed everybody in them.

and put them to the sword: The clause put them to the sword indicates that Yehoshua and his army killed the people in the towns and their kings. This is a Hebrew idiom that was used in 10:32. You should translate it in the same way in both places.

Here is another way to translate this Hebrew idiom:

putting everyone to death (GNT)

He devoted them to destruction: This is the same word as in 11:11a, and you should translate it in the same way.

11:12c

as Mosheh (Moses) Yahweh’s servant had commanded.

  • as Yahweh’s servant Mosheh commanded him to do.

  • He did this as Mosheh, the servant of Yahweh, told him.

as Mosheh Yahweh’s servant had commanded: The title that is given to Mosheh Yahweh’s servant is the same as in Joshua 1:1, and you should translate it in the same way.

had commanded: Mosheh commanded the Israelis (Israelites) to defeat and destroy all their enemies in Numbers 33:51–52 and in Deuteronomy 7:2. He did this because Yahweh commanded him to do so.

title: Joshua 11:13
content:
Section 11:1–15 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of northern Kena’an (Canaan)

King Yavin (Jabin), the king of Hatsor (Hazor), brought together the kings of the towns in Northern Kena’an to fight against Yisrael (Israel). With the help of Yahweh, Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis fought and defeated all these towns and killed their kings and their people.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael defeated the northern towns

11:13a

Yet Yisrael did not burn any of the cities built on their mounds,

  • But the Israelis did not burn any of the cities built on mounds,

  • But Yehoshua and the Israelis did not burn any of the cities built on small hills

Yet Yisrael did not burn any of the cities built on their mounds: Here is another way to translate this sentence:

But Yisrael (Israel) burned none of the towns that stood on mounds (NRSV)

Yisrael: The noun Yisrael indicates Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israeli (Israelite) army.

their mounds: Some towns were built on top of the ruins of other older towns. When this happened many times at these sites, the mounds, or small hills, were formed. Yehoshua did not destroy these towns.

Here is another way to translate this word:

small hills (CEV)

11:13b

except Hatsor (Hazor), which Yehoshua burned.

  • except the city of Hatsor, which they burned.

  • except for Hatsor City. Yehoshua ordered his army to burn that city.

except Hatsor, which Yehoshua (Joshua) burned: The clause except Hatsor indicates that Hatsor was the only town on a mound that the Israelis (Israelites) captured and burned during the battle in the north.

title: Joshua 11:14
content:
Section 11:1–15 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of northern Kena’an (Canaan)

King Yavin (Jabin), the king of Hatsor (Hazor), brought together the kings of the towns in Northern Kena’an to fight against Yisrael (Israel). With the help of Yahweh, Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis fought and defeated all these towns and killed their kings and their people.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael defeated the northern towns

11:14a

The Israelis took for themselves all the plunder and livestock of these cities,

  • The Israeli (Israelite) soldiers took all the valuable things and the animals in these cities.

  • The Israeli army kept for themselves all the goods of these cities and the domestic animals,

The Israelis (Israelites): The phrase The Israelis indicates the Israeli army.

took for themselves: The Hebrew verb that the BSB translates as took for themselves is more literally “took” or “seized.”

Here are some other ways to translate this part of the verse:

The Israelis kept the animals and everything of value from these towns (CEV)

The Israelis took for themselves all the animals and the other things from those towns

all the plunder and livestock of these cities: The phrase all the plunder and livestock of these cities refers to the things such as clothing or jewelry that a soldier might want to take. Yahweh allowed the Israelis to take these things for their own use. The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as plunder is the same word as was used in 8:27.

and livestock of these cities: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as livestock can refer to other kinds of animals as well as cattle. It is recommended that you use a more general term, such as “domestic animals.” The same Hebrew word was also used in 8:27.

11:14b

but they put all the people to the sword

  • But they killed all the people there with their swords.

  • but they killed every single person.

they put all the people to the sword: The phrase put all the people to the sword indicates that the Israeli (Israelite) army killed the people. This is a Hebrew idiom that was used in 10:32, and it is recommended that you translate it the same way in both places.

Here is another way to translate this Hebrew idiom:

they put every person to death (GNT)

all the people: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as all the people refers to both men and women.

11:14c

until they had completely destroyed them, not sparing anyone who breathed.

  • They destroyed them all. They left no one alive.

  • They completely destroyed all of them. No one was left alive.

until they had completely destroyed them: The clause until they had completely destroyed them indicates that the Israeli (Israelite) army completed the task that Yahweh had given them through Mosheh (Moses).

not sparing anyone who breathed: The clause not sparing anyone who breathed indicates that the army killed every single person. The Hebrew text states this information three times using different words to emphasize that the Israelis (Israelites) obeyed Yahweh’s command to completely destroy their enemies.

General Comment on verses 11:12–14

In each of these verses, the object comes before the subject and the verb. The Hebrew text uses this word order to emphasize the object. In some languages this order may be difficult to understand. Use the natural grammatical or lexical means in your language to indicate this emphasis.

title: Joshua 11:15
content:
Section 11:1–15 The Israelis (Israelites) conquered the towns of northern Kena’an (Canaan)

King Yavin (Jabin), the king of Hatsor (Hazor), brought together the kings of the towns in Northern Kena’an to fight against Yisrael (Israel). With the help of Yahweh, Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis fought and defeated all these towns and killed their kings and their people.

Here is another possible section heading:

Yisrael defeated the northern towns

11:15a

As Yahweh had commanded His servant Mosheh (Moses),

  • Yahweh commanded Mosheh his servant to do this,

  • Yahweh told his servant Mosheh to kill all the people in Kena’an,

As Yahweh had commanded His servant Mosheh: The clause As Yahweh had commanded His servant Mosheh refers to Yahweh’s command to Mosheh to destroy the inhabitants of the land. Yahweh gave Mosheh this command in Numbers 33:51–52. Verse 11:15 emphasizes that Yehoshua followed these commands completely.

In some languages it may help to include some implicit information. For example:

As Yahweh had commanded his servant Mosheh to destroy all the inhabitants of the land

11:15b

so Mosheh commanded Yehoshua (Joshua). That is what Yehoshua did,

  • and Mosheh (Moses) commanded Yehoshua to do it, and so Yehoshua did it.

  • and Mosheh gave this command to Yehoshua, and Yehoshua obeyed.

so Mosheh commanded Yehoshua. That is what Yehoshua did: The clause so Mosheh commanded Yehoshua. That is what Yehoshua did indicates that Mosheh told Yehoshua what Yahweh had commanded, and Yehoshua obeyed the command to destroy the people living in the land of Kena’an (Canaan).

Here are some other ways to translate 15a-b:

The command that Yahweh gave to Mosheh his servant, Mosheh told to Yehoshua, and Yehoshua obeyed.

Yahweh had commanded Mosheh his servant to kill all the people in the land. Mosheh gave this command to Yehoshua, and Yehoshua obeyed it.

11:15c

leaving nothing undone of all that Yahweh had commanded Mosheh (Moses).

  • Yehoshua (Joshua) did everything that Yahweh told Mosheh to do.

  • Yehoshua did not fail to do anything that Yahweh commanded Mosheh.

leaving nothing undone of all that Yahweh had commanded Mosheh: The phrase leaving nothing undone is a double negative. Here are some other ways to translate this part of the verse:

he did everything that Yahweh had commanded Mosheh

he did not fail to do anything that Yahweh had commanded Mosheh

This clause repeats the information that Yehoshua completely obeyed Yahweh’s command. It is repeated for emphasis. Use a way that is most natural to show how completely Yehoshua followed Yahweh’s commands.

title: Joshua 11:16
content:
Section 11:16–23 The towns that the Israelis (Israelites) conquered

In this section there is a summary of the towns that the Israelis conquered in the land of Kena’an (Canaan).

11:16a

So Yehoshua (Joshua) took this entire region:

  • ¶ Yehoshua conquered all that land.

  • ¶ Yehoshua and his army captured the whole land.

So Yehoshua took this entire region: The clause Yehoshua took this entire region indicates that Yehoshua conquered all the towns in the regions listed in 11:16–17. The places mentioned in 11:16 are similar to the places listed in 10:40. These places were mostly in the southern part of Kena’an.

The BSB translates verse 16 and part of verse 17 as one continuous sentence. In some languages it may be more natural to translate 11:16a as one sentence and to begin a new sentence with verse 11:16b. For example:

So Yehoshua took all that land. He took the hill country…

11:16b

the hill country, all the Negev, all the land of Goshen, the western foothills,

  • Yehoshua (Joshua) conquered the hill country and the Negev (Negeb) and all the area around Goshen and the lower slopes of the hills,

  • They captured the mountains, the Negev in southern Kena’an (Canaan), all the area near Goshen City, the foothills to the west,

the hill country: The hill country indicates the central mountain range that extended from Ay (Ai) and Giveon (Gibeon) in the north to Hevron (Hebron) and Devir (Debir) in the south. This is the same phrase as in 9:1 and you should translate it the same way in both places.

all the Negev: The Negev indicates the southern wilderness area of Kena’an. This term was used in 10:40 and you should translate it the same way in both places.

all the land of Goshen: Goshen refers to a town in the southern hill country of Kena’an and the region around it. The exact location of Goshen is unknown.11:16 Howard, p. 262.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

the land around the town of Goshen

the western foothills: The phrase the western foothills refers to the western foothills that were between the mountains and the coastal plain. This word was used in 9:1 and you should translate it the same way in both places.

11:16c

the Aravah (Arabah), and the mountains of Yisrael (Israel) and their foothills,

  • and the valley of the Yarden (Jordan) River. And so, he conquered the mountains and the hills near them.

  • and the Yarden River Valley. In this way they captured the high areas and the low areas.

the Aravah: The term Aravah indicates the Yarden River Valley, which is south of the Sea of Galil (Galilee) and north of the Dead Sea.11:16 Rasmussen p. 226. This word was used in 8:14 and you should translate it the same way in both places.

and the mountains of Yisrael and their foothills: The phrase the mountains of Yisrael and their foothills is a summary of the places that were mentioned previously in this verse. Translate this phrase so that the readers will understand that it does not refer to new places. It emphasizes that Yehoshua (Joshua) captured all the mountains and foothills of Yisrael. For example:

He Yehoshua controlled the mountains of Yisrael and all the hills near them. (NCV)

And so, Yehoshua conquered the highlands and lowlands of Yisrael.

title: Joshua 11:17
content:
Section 11:16–23 The towns that the Israelis (Israelites) conquered

In this section there is a summary of the towns that the Israelis conquered in the land of Kena’an (Canaan).

11:17a

from Mount Halak, which rises toward Se’ir (Seir),

  • Yehoshua (Joshua) conquered the land from Mount Halak near Edom,

  • They conquered the land from Mount Halak near the country of Edom in the south,

from Mount Halak: Mount Halak was the southernmost place that the Israelis captured. The location of Mount Halak is uncertain, It may be the modern Jebel Halaq, which is 45 kilometers southeast of Be’er-Sheva (Beersheba).11:17 Rasmussen, p. 237.

which rises toward Se’ir: The clause which rises toward Se’ir indicates that Mount Halak was near the territory of Edom, which was also called Se’ir. Edom was south of the Dead Sea.11:17 Bratcher and Newman, p. 166.

11:17b

as far as Ba’al-Gad (Baal-gad) in the Valley of Levanon (Lebanon) at the foot of Mount Hermon.

  • to Ba’al-Gad in the valley of Levanon, below Mount Hermon.

  • and north to Ba’al-Gad City in the Levanon Valley at the foot Hermon Mountain.

as far as Ba’al-Gad: Ba’al-Gad was a town in the valley of Levanon at the western foot of Mount Hermon.11:17 Rasmussen, p. 228. The exact location of Ba’al-Gad is unknown. This was the northernmost place that the Israelis (Israelites) captured.11:17 Howard, p. 272. Some English versions spell this “Ba’al (Baal) Gad.”

in the Valley of Levanon at the foot of Mount Hermon: Mount Hermon was a high mountain in the northeast of Yisrael (Israel). The Valley of Levanon was near Mount Hermon. It may be the modern Beqa Valley. It may also include the valley of the Litani River further south.11:17 Hess, p. 216.

11:17c

He captured all their kings and struck them down, putting them to death.

  • Yehoshua (Joshua) captured all the kings in the land and killed them.

  • They caught all the kings of this territory and killed them.

He captured all their kings: The clause He captured all their kings indicates that Yehoshua and the Israeli (Israelite) army captured all the kings who ruled the towns in the regions mentioned.

and struck them down, putting them to death: The two clauses struck them down and putting them to death have the same meaning. In some languages it may be more natural to combine these two clauses into one clause.

Here is another way to translate these clauses:

Yehoshua ordered his soldiers to kill these kings

title: Joshua 11:18
content:
Section 11:16–23 The towns that the Israelis (Israelites) conquered

In this section there is a summary of the towns that the Israelis conquered in the land of Kena’an (Canaan).

11:18

Yehoshua (Joshua) waged war against all these kings for a long period of time.

  • Yehoshua fought against them for a long time.

  • The battles against these kings lasted a long time.

Yehoshua waged war against all these kings for a long period of time: The clause Yehoshua waged war against all these kings for a long period of time indicates that it took a long time for Yehoshua and his army to defeat the enemy kings and kill them.Some commentators believe this was about seven years.11:18 Woudstra, p. 196.

This verse adds more information to the summary statements of verses 16–17. In some languages it may be clearer to combine verses 17 and 18. For example:

Yehoshua was at war with the kings of this territory for a long time, but he captured them all and put them to death. (GNT)

title: Joshua 11:19
content:
Section 11:16–23 The towns that the Israelis (Israelites) conquered

In this section there is a summary of the towns that the Israelis conquered in the land of Kena’an (Canaan).

11:19a

No city made peace with the Israelis except the Hivim (Hivites) living in Giveon (Gibeon);

  • Not one city made a peace treaty with the Israelis except for the Hivim in Giveon City.

  • The only city that made peace with Yisrael (Israel) was Giveon City where the Hivim lived.

No city made peace with the Israelis: Every town in this area fought against Yisrael. No town (except Giveon) tried to make peace.

the Israelis: Another term for the Israelis is “the people of Yisrael.”

except the Hivim living in Giveon: In 9:7 the people who lived in the town of Giveon were identified as Hivim. The Hivim were one of the nations who lived on the west side of the Yarden (Jordan) River in the land of Kena’an (see 9:3).

It may be more natural in some languages to translate the clause “No city made peace with the Israelis (Israelites)” in positive rather than negative terms. For example:

The people of only one city in all the land had made peace with Yisrael (NCV)

The only city that made peace with the people of Yisrael was Giveon (Gibeon) (GNT)

11:19b

all others were taken in battle.

  • The Israelis defeated all the other cities.

  • The Israelis fought and defeated everyone else.

all others were taken in battle: The clause all others were taken in battle indicates that the Israeli (Israelite) army fought against all the other enemy nations and captured them.

title: Joshua 11:20
content:
Section 11:16–23 The towns that the Israelis (Israelites) conquered

In this section there is a summary of the towns that the Israelis conquered in the land of Kena’an (Canaan).

11:20a

For it was of Yahweh to harden their hearts

  • These things happened because Yahweh made their hearts stubborn and rebellious,

  • The Israelis defeated their enemies because Yahweh caused them to be unwilling to make peace.

For: The word For indicates that the following clause contains the reason why the Israelis defeated all the towns that were named in the previous verses. Another way to translate this word is:

These things happened because

it was of Yahweh: The clause it was of Yahweh indicates that Yahweh caused these things to happen.

to harden their hearts: The clause harden their hearts indicates that Yahweh caused the enemy people to be stubborn and rebellious, so that they were not willing to make peace treaties with the Israelis (Israelites). Like Par’oh (Pharaoh) in Exodus 5:2, the kings of the towns decided to oppose God and his plans instead of submitting to them.

Here are some other ways to translate this sentence:

These things happened because Yahweh made their hearts stubborn and rebellious

The Israelis defeated these enemies because Yahweh caused them to be unwilling to make peace

11:20b

to engage Yisrael (Israel) in battle,

  • so that they wanted to fight against the Israelis.

  • Instead, they fought against Yisrael.

to engage Yisrael in battle: The clause that to engage Yisrael in battle indicates that the enemy nations were determined to fight against the Israelis (Israelites).

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

so that they wanted to fight against the Israelis

Instead they fought against the Israelis

11:20c

so that they would be set apart for destruction

  • The Israelis had to destroy them completely.

  • God wanted the Israelis to kill them all.

so that they would be set apart for destruction: The clause so that they would be set apart for destruction indicates that the Israelis (Israelites) had to kill all their enemies. In some languages it may be more natural to begin a new sentence here. For example:

This happened so that they would all die

11:20d

and would receive no mercy, being annihilated

  • They could not be merciful. They had to kill every single person,

  • They should show them no mercy but kill them all,

and would receive no mercy: The clause receive no mercy indicates that the Israelis were not to show mercy to their enemies or allow any of them to live.

being annihilated: The clause being annihilated indicates that the Israelis must destroy the Kena’anim (Canaanites). This clause repeats the information of verse 20c using different words to emphasize how important this was. In some languages repetition may not be a natural way to show emphasis. There may be other lexical or grammatical means to indicate emphasis. Use whatever means is natural to indicate emphasis in your language.

11:20e

as Yahweh had commanded Mosheh (Moses).

  • as Yahweh commanded Mosheh.

  • because this was what Yahweh commanded Mosheh to tell them to do.

as Yahweh had commanded Mosheh: It may be more natural in some languages to begin a new sentence here. The clause as Yahweh had commanded Mosheh refers to the command that Yahweh gave Mosheh in Deuteronomy 7:2. Yahweh commanded the Israelis (Israelites) to destroy the Kena’ani (Canaanite) people so that the Israelis would not be tempted to worship their gods.

title: Joshua 11:21
content:
Section 11:16–23 The towns that the Israelis (Israelites) conquered

In this section there is a summary of the towns that the Israelis conquered in the land of Kena’an (Canaan).

11:21a

At that time Yehoshua (Joshua) proceeded to eliminate the Anakim from the hill country

  • ¶ During this time Yehoshua killed all the Anakim (Anakites) who lived in the mountains

  • ¶ At this time Yehoshua destroyed all the Anak people who lived in the hill country.

At that time Yehoshua proceeded: The Hebrew verb proceeded indicates continuation of action, rather than movement.11:21 Bratcher and Newman, p. 167. Some English versions leave this verb untranslated, for example:

Now Yehoshua fought… (NCV)

At that time: The phrase At that time indicates an indefinite time. It is close to the same time that Yehoshua and his army finished fighting the other enemy soldiers.

Some other ways to translate this phrase are:

During this period (NLT)

At this time (GNT)

to eliminate: The Hebrew verb that the BSB translates as to eliminate indicates that Yehoshua (Joshua) and his army killed all the Anakim.

the Anakim: The Anakim were a group of people who were descendants of Anak. The descendants of Anak were first referred to in Numbers 13:22–33. At that time the Israelis (Israelites) were afraid of the Anakim and refused to enter the promised land. They did not trust Yahweh, and so they had to walk through the wilderness for forty years. Now the Israelis killed the Anakim.

Here are some other ways to translate this term:

descendants of Anak (NLT)

people of Anak (GW)

Anakim (Anakites) (NIV, NET)

from the hill country: The term hill country indicates the central mountain range of the land of Yisrael (Israel). This is the same phrase used in 9:1 and you should translate it the same way that you did there.

11:21b

of Hevron (Hebron), Devir (Debir), and Anav (Anab),

  • in the area of Hevron, Devir, and Anav,

  • They lived in Hevron City, Devir City, and Anav Village,

of Hevron: Yehoshua (Joshua) destroyed the town of Hevron in 10:36–37. Hevron was in the hill country of Yehudah (Judah), 32 kilometers southwest of Yerushalem (Jerusalem).11:21 Rasmussen, p. 238.

Devir: Yehoshua destroyed the town of Devir in 10:38–39. Devir was 14 kilometers southwest of Hevron, in the hill country of Yehudah.11:21 Rasmussen, p. 232.

and Anav: Anav was a village in the hill country of Yehudah. Anav was 19 kilometers southwest of Hevron.11:21 Rasmussen, p. 226.

11:21c

and from all the hill country of Yehudah and of Yisrael (Israel).

  • and in the mountains of Yehudah and the mountains of Yisrael.

  • and in the hill country of Yehudah and Yisrael.

and from all the hill country of Yehudah: The hill country of Yehudah indicates the central mountain range in the southern part of the land of Yisrael.

and of Yisrael: The and of Yisrael indicates the mountains in the northern part of the country.

It may be clearer to combine these two phrases into one. For example:

from all the hill country of Yehudah (Judah) and Yisrael

11:21d

Yehoshua (Joshua) devoted them to destruction, along with their cities.

  • Yehoshua completely destroyed them and their cities.

  • Yehoshua killed them all and destroyed their cities.

Yehoshua devoted them to destruction, along with their cities: The phrase with their cities indicates that Yehoshua destroyed the Anakim people, and also the towns in which they lived.

title: Joshua 11:22
content:
Section 11:16–23 The towns that the Israelis (Israelites) conquered

In this section there is a summary of the towns that the Israelis conquered in the land of Kena’an (Canaan).

11:22a

No Anakim were left in the land of the Israelis;

  • There were no Anakim (Anakites) left living in the land of the Israelis,

  • None of the Anak people were left in the land of Yisrael (Israel).

No Anakim were left in the land of the Israelis: The clause No Anakim were left in the land of the Israelis repeats the information of verse 21 in different words, to emphasize its importance.

the land of the Israelis: The phrase the land of the Israelis indicates the entire country of the Israelis. It includes both the southern part, which was called Yehudah (Judah) in verse 21, and the northern part, which was called Yisrael.

11:22b

only in Azah (Gaza), Gat (Gath), and Ashdod did any survive.

  • but there were a few left in Azah, Gat, and Ashdod.

  • However, some still remained in the towns of Azah, Gat, and Ashdod which Yisrael did not capture.

only in Azah, Gat, and Ashdod: The towns of Azah, Gat, and Ashdod were in the territory of the Pelishtim (Philistines). They were in southwestern Kena’an (Canaan), on the Mediterranean Sea.11:22 Howard, p. 275.

did any survive: The clause did any survive indicates that some Anakim still lived in the towns of Azah, Gat and Ashdod. The Israelis (Israelites) did not capture these towns.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

However, there were still some Anakim who lived in Azah, Gat, and Ashdod.

title: Joshua 11:23
content:
Section 11:16–23 The towns that the Israelis (Israelites) conquered

In this section there is a summary of the towns that the Israelis conquered in the land of Kena’an (Canaan).

11:23a

So Yehoshua (Joshua) took the entire land,

  • ¶ So Yehoshua conquered of all the land

  • ¶ In this way, Yehoshua and the Israeli (Israelite) people took control of the entire land of Yisrael (Israel).

So Yehoshua took the entire land: The clause Yehoshua took the entire land indicates that Yehoshua and the Israeli army conquered the whole land of Kena’an. This verse is the conclusion to the first section of the book of Yehoshua. Chapter 12 contains a list of conquered kings and territories and forms a kind of appendix to chapter 11.11:23 Howard, p. 275.

11:23b

in keeping with all that Yahweh had spoken to Mosheh (Moses).

  • as Yahweh told Mosheh to do long ago.

  • This was what Yahweh instructed Mosheh long ago.

in keeping with all that Yahweh had spoken to Mosheh: The phrase in keeping with all that Yahweh had spoken to Mosheh indicates that Yehoshua (Joshua) followed every command that Yahweh gave to Mosheh. Yahweh told Mosheh to drive out all the other nations from the land of Kena’an (Canaan).

11:23c

And Yehoshua gave it as an inheritance to Yisrael (Israel) according to the allotments to their tribes.

  • Then Yehoshua divided up the land and gave a part to each of the clans of Yisrael.

  • And Yehoshua gave it to the people of Yisrael, giving a part to each clan.

And Yehoshua gave it as an inheritance to Yisrael: The clause Yehoshua gave it as an inheritance to Yisrael indicates that Yehoshua divided up the land for each tribe of Yisrael to live in. Each of the twelve tribes of Yisrael got a certain part of the land.

inheritance: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as inheritance is more literally “property.” Yahweh gave land to each tribe for that tribe to own. Each family could pass this land on to their children and grandchildren.

Here are some other ways to translate this term:

a possession (GW)

a gift (NLV)

In some languages it may be more natural to translate this term as a clause. For example:

The Lord gave that land to Yisrael (Israel) as he promised (ERV)

Yehoshua (Joshua) gave it to the Israelis (Israelites) as their own (GNT)

according to the allotments to their tribes: The phrase according to the allotments to their tribes indicates that Yehoshua divided the land into sections and each tribe received one section of the land for their people to live in.

11:23d

Then the land had rest from war.

  • And there was peace in the land.

  • So, there was no more fighting in the land.

Then the land had rest from war: The clause the land had rest from war indicates that the Israeli (Israelite) army no longer fought. The soldiers could rest. The countryside was peaceful and no longer destroyed by battles.

Here are some other ways to translate this clause:

Then there was peace in the land

Then there was no war in the land

title: Joshua 12:1
content:
Section 12:1–24 The kings that Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis (Israelites) defeated

In this section there is a list of the kings that the Israelis defeated on the east side and the west side of the Yarden (Jordan) River.

Here is another possible section heading:

The kings that the Israelis defeated on both sides of the Yarden River

Paragraph 12:1–6

The kings that the Israelis defeated on the east side of the Yarden River.

12:1a

Now these are the kings of the land

  • ¶ These are the kings of the land

  • ¶ These are the names of the two kings

Now: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as Now introduces a list of two kings that the Israelis (Israelites) defeated. Many English versions do not translate this word. Use a word that is appropriate to introduce a list in your language.

these are the kings: In some languages it may be more natural to say that these are the names of the kings.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

These are the names of the kings (REB)

of the land: The phrase the land indicates the land east of the Yarden (Jordan) River. This is not stated until 12:1c. It may be more natural in some languages to reorder this verse. A way to reorder the verse is found at the end of the notes for this verse.

12:1b

whom the Israelis struck down

  • whom the Israeli (Israelite) soldiers defeated

  • whom the Israelis defeated before they crossed the Yarden River.

whom the Israelis (Israelites) struck down: The Israelis defeated these kings at an earlier time, before they crossed the Yarden River. This story is found in Numbers 21:21–35. It may be helpful to express this implicit information.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

The people of Yisrael (Israel) had defeated these kings before they crossed the Yarden River

Israelis: The word Israelis indicates the Israeli army.

12:1c

and whose lands they took beyond the Yarden (Jordan) to the east,

  • and whose territory the Israelis took east of the Yarden River.

  • The Israelis captured their land east of the Yarden River.

and whose lands they took: The clause whose lands they took indicates that after the Israelis (Israelites) defeated the kings and their armies, they occupied their land and controlled it.

beyond the Yarden to the east: The phrase beyond the Yarden to the east indicates that the land was on the east side of the Yarden River.

12:1d

from the Arnon Valley to Mount Hermon, including all the Aravah (Arabah) eastward:

  • Their land went from the valley of the Arnon River to Mount Hermon, including all the eastern side of the Yarden River.

  • These kings ruled the land from the Arnon River gorge in the south, to Mount Hermon in the north. They ruled all the land on the east side of the Yarden (Jordan) River.

from the Arnon Valley to Mount Hermon: The Arnon Valley and Mount Hermon were at the south and the north of the area that the Israelis conquered east of the Yarden River.

the Arnon Valley: The Arnon River flows through a deep Valley that is dry during part of the year. It runs into the Dead Sea. Its valley is halfway between the southern and northern ends of the Dead Sea. This was the southern limit of the land that the Israelis conquered on the east side of the Yarden River.12:1 Bratcher and Newman, p. 170.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

the valley of the Arnon River

Valley: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as Valley refers to a riverbed that has water in it only during the rainy season. This kind of riverbed is sometimes referred to by its Arabic term, wadi.

Here are some ways to translate this word:

gorge (NLT, NIV)

ravine (NCV)

wadi (NRSV, REB, NJPS)

Use the word in your language that best fits this context.

Mount Hermon: Mount Hermon is west of Damesek (Damascus). It was the northern limit of the land that the Israelis (Israelites) conquered on the east side of the Yarden (Jordan) River.

including all the Aravah (Arabah) eastward: The Aravah is the valley of the Yarden River. The land that the Israelis conquered included all the Yarden River valley and the land to the east of it.

General Comment on 12:1

Here are some other ways to translate verse 1. These examples have partially reordered the parts of the verse. They have also broken the verse into two sentences.

These are the kings of the land east of the Yarden River that the people of Yisrael (Israel) defeated. Yisrael also took possession of their land from the Arnon Valley to Mount Hermon, and all the eastern plains. (GW)

Before Mosheh (Moses) died, he and the Israelis had defeated two kings east of the Yarden River. These kings had ruled the region from the Arnon River Gorge in the south to Mount Hermon in the north, including the eastern side of the Yarden River Valley. (CEV)

General Comment on 12:1–5

In the Hebrew text these verses are one long sentence, and the BSB translates them this way. It is recommended that you translate these verses as several sentences. Use the sentence breaks that are most natural in your language. There are some examples of how to do this the end of each verse.

title: Joshua 12:2
content:
Section 12:1–24 The kings that Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis (Israelites) defeated

In this section there is a list of the kings that the Israelis defeated on the east side and the west side of the Yarden (Jordan) River.

Here is another possible section heading:

The kings that the Israelis defeated on both sides of the Yarden River

Paragraph 12:1–6

The kings that the Israelis defeated on the east side of the Yarden River.

12:2a

Sihon king of the Amorim (Amorites), who lived in Heshbon.

  • Sihon was the Amori (Amorite) king who lived in Heshbon.

  • The first king that the Israelis (Israelites) defeated was King Sihon of the Amor people. He lived in Heshbon City.

Verses 12:2–3 give a detailed description of the territory that King Sihon ruled. Verse 2 describes the eastern part of his territory starting from its south end. Verse 3 describes the western part of his territory that was in the Yarden (Jordan) River valley.

Sihon king of the Amorim: The story of how Mosheh (Moses) and the Israelis conquered Sihon king of the Amorim is in Numbers 21:21–35.

the Amorim: The word Amorim refers to a group of people who lived on the east side of the Yarden River. This word was used in 3:10| and you should translate it the same way in both places.

who lived in Heshbon: King Sihon lived in Heshbon, which was the capital town of the Amorim. Heshbon was about 25 kilometers northeast of the Dead Sea.12:2 Bratcher and Newman, p. 171.

12:2b

He ruled from Aroer on the rim of the Arnon Valley,

  • His kingdom went from Aroer, on the edge of the Arnon River valley,

  • His territory started at Aroer City in the south. Aroer City was on the edge of the Arnon River gorge.

He ruled from Aroer: The town of Aroer was beside the Arnon River. King Sihon’s territory started at Aroer in the south and went north from there.

Here is another way to translate this clause:

King Sihon’s territory started at the town of Aroer

on the rim of the Arnon Valley: The clause on the rim of the Arnon Valley indicates that the town of Aroer was on the bank of the Arnon River. The Arnon River runs into the Dead Sea.

12:2c

along the middle of the valley, up to the Yabok (Jabbok) River (the border of the Amonim (Ammonites)),

  • from the middle of this valley to the Yabok River, which is the border of Amonim.

  • It went north from the middle of the Arnon River gorge to the Yabok River. The Yabok River starts the territory of the Amon (Ammon) people.

along the middle of the valley: The words the valley refers to the Arnon River valley. There is an interpretation issue here.

  1. The Hebrew text reads “and the middle of the valley.” For example:

    from the middle of the gorge (NIV) (BSB, NIV, RSV, ESV, GW, CEV, NLT, NABRE, KJV)

  2. Some English versions say “from the town in the middle of the valley.” They add the word “town” because of Joshua 13:9 and 16 which describe the same place. For example:

    including the city in the middle of the valley (NET) (NET, GNT)

It is recommended that you follow option (1) and translate the middle of the valley as in the BSB. This follows the Hebrew text.

up to the Yabok (Jabbok) River: The phrase up to the Yabok River indicates that the Yabok River was the northern boundary of King Sihon’s territory. It was also that beginning of Amoni (Ammonite) territory.

the border of the Amonim (Ammonites): The phrase the border of the Amonim indicates that the Yabok River formed the boundary between the territory of King Sihon and the territory of the Amonim.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

all the way to the Yabok Valley bordering Amoni territory (NET)

to the Yabok River, which is the border of the Amonim (NIV)

the Amonim: The term Amonim indicates a group of people who lived in the country of Amon (Ammon). Amon was a region or an area, not a town.

12:2d

that is, half of Gilead,

  • This was half of the region of Gilead.

  • This territory of King Sihon was the southern half of the Gilead area.

that is, half of Gilead: The clause half of Gilead indicates that the territory which King Sihon ruled was half of the region of Gilead.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

This included half of Gilead (NIV)

This territory included the southern half of the territory of Gilead (NLT)

Gilead: The term Gilead indicates the mountainous region north of the Dead Sea. The Gilead Region stretched from the east of the Yarden (Jordan) River to the desert.12:2 Rasmussen, p. 236.

General Comment on 12:2

Here is another way to translate 12:2. This example has divided the verse into three sentences.

King Sihon of the Amorim (Amorites), who lived in Heshbon, was defeated. His kingdom included Aroer, on the edge of the Arnon Gorge, and extended from the middle of the Arnon Gorge to the Yabok (Jabbok) River, which serves as a border for the Amonim (Ammonites). This territory included the southern half of the territory of Gilead. (NLT)

title: Joshua 12:3
content:
Section 12:1–24 The kings that Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis (Israelites) defeated

In this section there is a list of the kings that the Israelis defeated on the east side and the west side of the Yarden (Jordan) River.

Here is another possible section heading:

The kings that the Israelis defeated on both sides of the Yarden River

Paragraph 12:1–6

The kings that the Israelis defeated on the east side of the Yarden River.

12:3a

as well as the Aravah (Arabah) east of the Sea of Kineret (Chinnereth)

  • It included the land east of the Yarden River valley, from Lake Galil (Galilee),

  • King Sihon’s territory included the valley of the Yarden River and the land east of it, from Lake Galil in the north

Verse 12:3 continues the description of King Sihon’s territory. It describes the territory that he ruled in the valley of the Yarden (Jordan) River, starting from its north end. It may be clearer to start a new sentence here.

as well as the Aravah: The Aravah is the valley of the Yarden River.

east of the Sea of Kineret: The Sea of Kineret is another name for the Sea of Galil. In the Yarden River valley, the territory of King Sihon extended north beyond the Yabok (Jabbok) River to the Sea of Galil.

east of: The phrase east of indicates that King Sihon’s territory was east of the Yarden River. It extended eastward from the Yarden River to the desert.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

King Sihon’s territory included the east side of the Yarden River valley to the Sea of Galil in the north

12:3b

to the Sea of the Aravah (Arabah) (the Salt Sea),

  • and the Dead Sea,

  • to the Dead Sea,

to the Sea of the Aravah: The Sea of the Aravah is another name for the Dead Sea.

the Salt Sea: The Salt Sea is another name for the Dead Sea. The Dead Sea is referred to by two different names in this verse. See how you translated this phrase in Joshua 3:16.

12:3c

eastward through Beyt-Hayeshimot (Beth-jeshimoth),

  • to Beyt-Hayeshimot,

  • and went south to Beyt-Hayeshimot City,

through Beyt-Hayeshimot: Beyt-Hayeshimot is a town referred to in Numbers 33:49. It was the last place that the Israelis (Israelites) camped before crossing the Yarden (Jordan) River into Kena’an (Canaan). It is beside the Yarden River, at the northeast tip of the Dead Sea.12:3 Rasmussen, p. 229.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

and his territory went south to the town of Beyt-Hayeshimot

Some English versions spell this name as two separate words:

Beth Jeshimoth (NIV, NET, GNT)

12:3d

and southward below the slopes of Pisgah.

  • and on to the slopes of Mount Pisgah in the south.

  • and on south to the foot of Pisgah Mountain.

southward below the slopes of Pisgah: Mount Pisgah was the southern boundary of King Sihon’s territory. The exact location of Mount Pisgah is uncertain, but it is probably at the north end of the Dead Sea.12:3 Rasmussen, p. 248.

General Comment on 12:3

Here is another way to translate 12:3. This example includes some connecting words to make the meaning clear.

Sihon also controlled the Yarden (Jordan) Valley and regions to the east—from as far north as the Sea of Galil (Galilee) to as far south as the Dead Sea, including the road to Beyt-Hayeshimot (Beth-jeshimoth) and southward to the slopes of Pisgah. (NLT)

title: Joshua 12:4
content:
Section 12:1–24 The kings that Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis (Israelites) defeated

In this section there is a list of the kings that the Israelis defeated on the east side and the west side of the Yarden (Jordan) River.

Here is another possible section heading:

The kings that the Israelis defeated on both sides of the Yarden River

Paragraph 12:1–6

The kings that the Israelis defeated on the east side of the Yarden River.

12:4a

And Og king of Bashan,

  • Og king of Bashan

  • The second king that the Israelis (Israelites) defeated was King Og, king of Bashan Country,

And Og king of Bashan: King Og was the second king that the Israelis defeated. The story of how Mosheh (Moses) and the Israelis defeated Og king of Bashan is found in Numbers 21:33–35.

Bashan is a country northeast of the Sea of Galil (Galilee). This country appeared in Joshua 9:10 and you should translate it the same way in both places.

Verse 4 is part of the long Hebrew sentence that begins at 12:1. In some languages it may be more natural to begin a new sentence here.

Here are some other ways to translate this phrase:

They also defeated King Og of Bashan (GNT)

Next, Mosheh and the Israelis defeated King Og of Bashan (CEV)

12:4b

one of the remnant of the Refaim (Rephaim),

  • was among the last group of the Refaim.

  • He was one of the last of the Repha people.

one of the remnant of the Refaim: The word one introduces a relative clause. Use the relative clause marker that is most natural in your language. It is also possible to translate this relative clause as an independent sentence.

Here are some other ways to translate this relative clause:

who was one of the remnant of the Refaim

King Og was one of the last of the Repha people

remnant: The word remnant indicates that only a few of the Refaim (Rephaim) were still alive.

Here are some other ways to translate this word:

one of the few remaining Refaim (NET)

one of the last of the Refaim (NIV)

among the last group of the Repha people

the Refaim: The term Refaim indicates a group of people who lived in the land of Kena’an (Canaan) before the Israelis (Israelites). They are mentioned in Deuteronomy 2:10–11, where it is said that they are strong and tall.

Here are some other ways to translate this name:

Refaim (NIV, NCV, NLT, NET)

Repha people

12:4c

who lived in Ashtarot (Ashtaroth) and Edre’i (Edrei).

  • He lived in Ashtarot and Edre-i.

  • He lived at Ashtarot City and Edre-i City.

who lived in Ashtarot: The town of Ashtarot was the capital town of King Og. Ashtarot was twenty-two miles east of the Sea of Galil (Galilee).

and Edre’i: King Og also had a residence in the town of Edre’i. Edre’i was sixty miles south of Damesek (Damascus).12:4 Rasmussen, p. 233. The king was living there when the Israelis (Israelites) defeated him.

Here is another way to spell the name of Edre’i:

Edre-i (RSV)

Here are some other ways to translate these phrases:

Og king of Bashan was one of the last of the Refaim (Rephaites). He ruled the land in Ashtarot (Ashtaroth) and Edre’i (Edrei) (NCV)

They also defeated King Og of Bashan, who was one of the last of the Refaim; he ruled at Ashtarot and Edre’i. (GNT)

title: Joshua 12:5
content:
Section 12:1–24 The kings that Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis (Israelites) defeated

In this section there is a list of the kings that the Israelis defeated on the east side and the west side of the Yarden (Jordan) River.

Here is another possible section heading:

The kings that the Israelis defeated on both sides of the Yarden River

Paragraph 12:1–6

The kings that the Israelis defeated on the east side of the Yarden River.

12:5a

He ruled over Mount Hermon, Salkah (Salecah),

  • He ruled the territory that went from Mount Hermon and Salkah City in the north

  • His kingdom went north to Mount Hermon, and east to Salkah City,

He ruled over Mount Hermon, Salkah: Mount Hermon is a high mountain that was the northern limit of Yehoshua’s (Joshua’s) conquests. It formed the northwest end of King Og’s kingdom.

Salkah: The town of Salkah was on the eastern boundary of the territory of Bashan. It was southeast of the Sea of Galil (Galilee).12:5 Rasmussen, p. 250.

Here are some ways to translate this part of the verse:

He ruled a territory stretching from Mount Hermon and Salkah in the north (NLT)

His kingdom stretched north to Mount Hermon, east to the town of Salkah, (CEV)

12:5b

all of Bashan up to the border of the Geshurim (Geshurites) and Ma’akatim (Maacathites),

  • and all of Bashan to where the Geshurim and the Ma’akatim lived.

  • and included the land of Bashan as far west as the land of the Geshur people and the Ma’akah (Maacah) people.

all of Bashan up to the border of the Geshurim: The term Geshurim can also be translated “Geshur people.” They were a small group who lived northeast of the Sea of Galil (Galilee). Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis (Israelites) were not able to conquer them.12:5 Rasmussen, p. 236.

and Ma’akatim: The term Ma’akatim can also be translated “Ma’akah people.” This was a small kingdom in modern Aram (Syria) whose people continued to live in their land. Yehoshua and the Israelis failed to drive them out.12:5 Rasmussen, p. 243.

12:5c

and half of Gilead to the border of Sihon king of Heshbon.

  • He ruled half the land of Gilead up to the border of Sihon king of Heshbon.

  • His territory included the northern half of Gilead, as far as the boundary of King Sihon of Heshbon.

and half of Gilead: King Og ruled over the northern half of Gilead. King Sihon ruled over the southern half of Gilead. You should translate the word Gilead the same way you did in 12:2d.

to the border of Sihon king of Heshbon: King Og’s territory extended south to the area that King Sihon ruled.

title: Joshua 12:6
content:
Section 12:1–24 The kings that Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis (Israelites) defeated

In this section there is a list of the kings that the Israelis defeated on the east side and the west side of the Yarden (Jordan) River.

Here is another possible section heading:

The kings that the Israelis defeated on both sides of the Yarden River

Paragraph 12:1–6

The kings that the Israelis defeated on the east side of the Yarden River.

12:6a

Mosheh (Moses), the servant of Yahweh, and the Israelis had struck them down

  • Mosheh the servant of Yahweh and the Israelis destroyed the people of King Sihon and King Og

  • These were the people that Mosheh, Yahweh’s servant, and the people of Yisrael (Israel) defeated.

Verse 6 is a summary of how Mosheh and the Israeli (Israelite) army conquered the land east of the Yarden (Jordan) River and divided it among Re’uven (Reuben), Gad and half of Menasheh (Manasseh).

Mosheh, the servant of Yahweh: You should translate the phrase the servant of Yahweh the same way you did in Joshua 1:1.

and the Israelis (Israelites): The word Israelis indicates the Israeli army.

had struck them down: The pronoun them refers to King Sihon and King Og. It may be helpful to make this reference explicit. For example:

Mosheh, the servant of the Lord, had destroyed the people of King Sihon and King Og. (NLT)

12:6b

and given their land as an inheritance

  • and gave away all their land

  • He gave their land

In the Hebrew text, the phrase “Mosheh (Moses), the servant of Yahweh” is repeated here to emphasize the status of Mosheh as the one who led the Israelis out of Mitsrayim (Egypt). In some languages, it may be natural to repeat this phrase, as the Hebrew text does.

and given their land as an inheritance: The clause given their land as an inheritance indicates that Mosheh divided the land on the east side of the Yarden (Jordan) River between the two and a half tribes, who became the owners of it.

12:6c

to the Re’uvenim (Reubenites), the Gadim (Gadites), and the half-tribe of Menasheh (Manasseh).

  • to the clans of Re’uven (Reuben), Gad, and half the clan of Menasheh for them to own.

  • to the clans of Re’uven and Gad and East Menasheh as their own.

to the Re’uvenim, the Gadim, and the half-tribe of Menasheh: The phrase the Re’uvenim, the Gadim, and the half-tribe of Menasheh indicates the descendants of Re’uven, the descendants of Gad, and the descendants of Makir, who was a son of Menasheh. The people of Re’uven and Gad asked to settle east of the Yarden River because it was good land for shepherding herds and flocks. This story is told in Numbers 32:1–5. The descendants of Makir, from the tribe of Menasheh, conquered the land of Gilead and settled there in Numbers 32:39–40).

the half-tribe of Menasheh: Some English versions translate this as East Menasheh, because these people lived on the east side of the Yarden River.

title: Joshua 12:7
content:
Section 12:1–24 The kings that Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis (Israelites) defeated

In this section there is a list of the kings that the Israelis defeated on the east side and the west side of the Yarden (Jordan) River.

Here is another possible section heading:

The kings that the Israelis defeated on both sides of the Yarden River

Paragraph 12:7–24

The kings that the Israelis defeated on the west side of the Yarden River.

12:7a

And these are the kings of the land that Yehoshua and the Israelis conquered beyond the Yarden to the west,

  • ¶ This is a list of the kings that Yehoshua and the Israelis defeated west of the Yarden River,

  • ¶ Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israeli (Israelite) army also defeated the kings on the west side of the Yarden River.

And: The Hebrew word that the BSB translates as And indicates the next event in the narrative. Some English versions do not translate this word.

these are the kings of the land: The clause these are the kings of the land introduces the list of kings whom Yehoshua and the Israelis (Israelites) defeated on the west side of the Yarden (Jordan) River. However, the actual list does not start until verse 9.

that Yehoshua and the Israelis conquered beyond the Yarden to the west: Here are some other ways to translate this sentence:

Yehoshua and the people of Yisrael (Israel) defeated all the kings in the territory west of the Yarden (GNT)

Yehoshua and the Israelis also defeated kings in the land west of the Yarden River. (NCV)

The following is a list of the kings that Yehoshua and the Israeli armies defeated on the west side of the Yarden (NLT)

12:7b

from Ba’al-Gad (Baal-gad) in the Valley of Levanon (Lebanon) to Mount Halak, which rises toward Se’ir (Seir)

  • from Ba’al-Gad in the valley of Levanon to Mount Halak which is near Se’ir.

  • This land went from Ba’al-Gad in the Levanon Valley in the north, to Halak Mountain near Edom in the south.

from Ba’al-Gad in the Valley of Levanon: The term Ba’al-Gad indicates a town in the valley of Levanon at the western foot of Mount Hermon.12:7 Rasmussen, p. 228. The exact location of Ba’al-Gad is unknown, but it was the northern point of Yehoshua’s (Joshua’s) conquests.12:7 Howard, p. 272.

Some English versions spell this name as two words:

Ba’al (Baal) Gad (NIV, NET, GW)

the Valley of Levanon: The Valley of Levanon was near Mount Hermon. It may be the modern Beqa Valley. It may also include the valley of the Litani River further south.12:7 Hess, p. 216. This term occurred in 11:17 and you should translate it the same way as you did there.

to Mount Halak, which rises toward Se’ir: The term Mount Halak indicates a mountain that marked the southern point of the Israelis’s (Israelites’) conquests. Its location is uncertain, but it may be Jebel Halaq, 28 miles southeast of Be’er-Sheva (Beersheba).12:7 Rasmussen, p. 237.

rises toward Se’ir (Seir): Se’ir is another word for the territory of Edom, which was south of the Dead Sea. The clause rises toward Se’ir indicates that Mount Halak was near the territory of Edom.12:7 Bratcher and Newman, p. 166.

Here is another way to translate this phrase:

Mount Halak near the country of Edom (CEV)

General Comment on 12:7b

Verse 12:7b describes the land by naming its northern and southern points. In 12:8a-b the same land is described by naming its geographical regions. 12:8c describes this land again by naming the Kena’ani (Canaanite) peoples who lived there.

12:7c

(according to the allotments to the tribes of Yisrael (Israel), Yehoshua (Joshua) gave them as an inheritance

  • Yehoshua gave this land to the clans of Yisrael for them to own, giving some to each clan,

  • Yehoshua divided this land among the clans and gave it to them as their own.

according to the allotments to the tribes of Yisrael, Yehoshua gave them as an inheritance: The BSB puts verse 12:7d-12:8c in parentheses. Most English versions do not use parentheses here.

according to the allotments to the tribes of Yisrael: Here is another way to translate this phrase:

according to their tribal divisions (NIV)

Yehoshua gave them as an inheritance: These words are like the words in 12:6 and you should translate them in the same way. Yehoshua gave land to each of the ten- and one-half tribes of Yisrael who settled on the west side of the Yarden (Jordan) River. These tribes became owners of that land.

title: Joshua 12:8
content:
Section 12:1–24 The kings that Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israelis (Israelites) defeated

In this section there is a list of the kings that the Israelis defeated on the east side and the west side of the Yarden (Jordan) River.

Here is another possible section heading:

The kings that the Israelis defeated on both sides of the Yarden River

Paragraph 12:7–24

The kings that the Israelis defeated on the west side of the Yarden River.

12:8a

the hill country, the foothills, the Aravah (Arabah),

  • including the mountains, the lowlands to the west, the Yarden Valley,

  • This land included the central mountains, the western foothills of the central mountains, the valley of the Yarden River,

Verse 12:8a-b lists all the geographical areas of Yisrael (Israel) on the west side of the Yarden (Jordan) River.

the hill country: The phrase the hill country indicates the central mountain range on the west side of the Yarden River. This word was used in 9:1 and you should translate it the same way in both places.

the foothills: The phrase the foothills refers to the western side of the central mountain range, between the mountains and the coastal plain. This word was used in 9:1 and you should translate it the same way in both places.

the Aravah: The term Aravah refers to the valley of the Yarden River. This word was used in 8:14 and you should translate it the same way in both places.

12:8b

the slopes, the wilderness, and the Negev—

  • the mountain slopes, the Yehudi (Judean) wilderness, and the Negev.

  • the eastern slopes of the central mountains, the desert of Judea, and the desert in southern Kena’an (Canaan).
